docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 7 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Itihāsa–Purāṇa: Epics and Purāṇas. After an introductory chapter on the genre, it treats the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (Chapters 2–3), the Mahābhārata and the Harivaṃśa (Chapters 4–5), the Bhagavad Gītā (Chapter 6), and the Mahāpurāṇas, Upapurāṇas and māhātmyas (Chapters 7–8). Three thematic chapters then take up what the narrative chapters leave open: the hard cases and the limits of epic dharma (Chapter 9), the women of the epics (Chapter 10) and the philosophy of the Mokṣadharma and the Nārāyaṇīya (Chapter 11). The last chapter follows the epics’ afterlife in the regional languages, in Persian at the Mughal court and in the Sikh Dasam Granth, in Southeast Asia, in sculpture, dance, ritual theatre, film and festival, and in modern debates about their historicity.

Two perspectives run through the book. The first is that of the tradition, for which these texts are sacred history and scripture. The second is that of modern textual and historical scholarship, which dates their composition (academic dates are given first throughout, with traditional dates labelled as such), studies their growth through critical editions, and reads them alongside the Jain, Buddhist, regional and oppositional retellings — including feminist and Dalit critiques — that are part of their history. Quotations from the Sanskrit texts are given only where their wording and reference could be checked; claims that archaeology or astronomy confirm the epics are presented as the contested proposals they are. Where a heading or a sentence reports what the tradition holds, it says so. The book is a work of synthesis and introduction; a note on texts, translations and abbreviations follows, and readers are referred to the select bibliography for the standard scholarship on which it draws.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: A Note on Texts, Translations and Abbreviations
docs.text:
Critical Edition and vulgate. Both epics exist in two forms that a reader will meet. The Critical Edition (CE) is the text reconstructed by modern editors from manuscripts of all regions: for the Mahābhārata, the Poona edition of the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI, 1933–1966), with the Harivaṃśa edited separately (1969–1971); for the Rāmāyaṇa, the Baroda edition (1960–1975). The vulgate is the text printed before the critical editions and still most widely read: for the Mahābhārata, the northern text of Nīlakaṇṭha (late seventeenth century), found in the Calcutta and Bombay editions, the Gita Press edition and Ganguli’s translation; for the Rāmāyaṇa, the southern text printed with the commentaries of Govindarāja and others. How the critical editions were made, and the debate over them, are described in Sections 2.3 and 4.8.

References. Mahābhārata references give book (parvan), chapter (adhyāya) and verse in the CE, so that 12.67 is chapter 67 of the twelfth book, the Śānti Parva; the eighteen books are numbered as in Table 4.1. Rāmāyaṇa references give book (kāṇḍa), canto (sarga) and verse in the CE. Where a passage exists only in the vulgate, or a vulgate number is given, this is said; chapter numbers in the two texts differ, sometimes widely. The Bhagavad Gītā is cited by chapter and verse, which are the same in all editions. Purāṇas are cited by book, chapter and verse of the usual printed editions, whose numbering varies.

Abbreviations. BORI, Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute; CE, Critical Edition; c., circa; r., reigned; trad., traditional. Within the text the epics are named in full; “Mbh.” and “Rām.” appear only in tables.

Transliteration. Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST), with ṃ for the anusvāra; Tamil follows the transliteration of the Tamil Lexicon of the University of Madras (so ḻ, ṟ, ṉ, as in Āḻvār). Modern places are given in their usual modern spelling (Ayodhya, Varanasi) where the modern town is meant, and with diacritics where the place of the text is meant (Ayodhyā). Persian, Hindi and Punjabi names are given in simplified form. Translations of passages are the author’s unless a translation is cited; they aim at the sense and should be checked against the editions below.

Dates. The mainstream academic date or range is given first, and traditional dates are labelled as traditional (see Table 1.5).

A short guide to translations. For the Mahābhārata, the only complete English translation of the critical text is Bibek Debroy’s, in ten volumes (Debroy 2010–2014). The Chicago translation begun by J. A. B. van Buitenen covers Books 1–5 (van Buitenen 1973–1978) and was continued by James Fitzgerald with Books 11 and the first part of 12 (Fitzgerald 2004); its introductions are the best scholarly guide to the books they cover. K. M. Ganguli’s prose translation of the vulgate (1883–1896) is complete, freely available and still useful, but it translates a different text and its English is dated (Ganguli 1883–1896). A reader who wants a single volume should begin with John D. Smith’s abridgement of the critical text, which translates the main narrative and summarises the rest (Smith 2009). For the Harivaṃśa there is Simon Brodbeck’s translation of the critical text (Brodbeck 2019). For the Bhagavad Gītā, van Buitenen prints the CE text with a facing translation and Franklin Edgerton gives a deliberately literal version (van Buitenen 1981; Edgerton 1944). For the Rāmāyaṇa, the annotated Princeton translation of the critical text by Robert Goldman and his collaborators is the standard (Goldman 1984–2017); the notes record the major vulgate passages that the CE excludes. For the Purāṇas, Dimmitt and van Buitenen’s reader gives a selection of myths in good translation (Dimmitt and Buitenen 1978); Edwin Bryant has translated the tenth book of the Bhāgavata (Bryant 2003) and Thomas Coburn the Devī Māhātmya (Coburn 1991). Translations of the Tamil, Khmer and other versions are cited where those versions are discussed.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction — What is Itihāsa?
docs.text:
ṛgvedaṃ bhagavo ’dhyemi yajurvedaṃ sāmavedam ātharvaṇaṃ caturtham itihāsapurāṇaṃ pañcamam … “Sir, I know the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Ātharvaṇa as the fourth, and Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth …”

— Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.2 (Nārada to Sanatkumāra)

The word itihāsa names a genre of Sanskrit literature that presents itself as an account of what really happened, transmitted by authoritative narrators and directed towards instruction in dharma. The genre does not correspond neatly to the modern discipline of history: it combines genealogy, narrative, didactic discourse and religious teaching, and its claim to truth is a claim made by the tradition rather than one that can be tested by documentary evidence. This volume treats the two great epics — the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata — together with the related Purāṇa literature, both as the tradition understands them and as modern textual and historical scholarship has studied them (Brockington 1998; Rocher 1986).

docs.title: 1.1 The Word and Its Claim
docs.text:
The word itihāsa is formed from the particles iti (“thus”) and ha (“indeed”) and the verb form āsa (“it was”, from the root as, “to be”): “thus indeed it was.” It already occurs in late Vedic texts, often in the compound itihāsa-purāṇa, as the name of a body of narrative lore recited alongside the Vedas. The lexicon Amarakośa (c. 5th–7th century CE) glosses it briefly as itihāsaḥ purāvṛttam, “itihāsa is an account of past events.”

The gloss expresses the conviction that the events narrated in the epics actually took place, even though they are told in poetry (kāvya) and directed towards instruction in dharma. Modern historians have asked a different question: not whether the events happened, but what kind of historical consciousness the genre expresses. The colonial claim that India “had no history” before the Muslim chroniclers has been rejected. Romila Thapar has argued that early India possessed “embedded” historical traditions — genealogies (vaṃśānucarita), heroic narratives and dynastic lists preserved in the epics and Purāṇas — which later became “externalised” in chronicles, inscriptions and royal biographies, and that later dynasties legitimised their rule by attaching themselves to the Solar and Lunar lineages of these genealogies (Thapar 2013). On this view the epics are evidence for how communities remembered and used their past, and for the periods in which they were composed and transmitted, rather than records that can be read off as political history. Earlier attempts, notably Pargiter’s, to reconstruct a dynastic chronology from the Purāṇic genealogies are now generally regarded as over-confident (Pargiter 1922; Rocher 1986). Table 1.1 sets itihāsa beside the neighbouring categories of narrative.

Table 1.1. Itihāsa and Neighbouring Narrative Categories Category Basis as understood in the tradition Purpose Itihāsa Events held to have occurred (purāvṛtta) Instruction in dharma through exemplary lives Purāṇa “Ancient” lore: cosmogony, genealogy, theology, ritual Comprehensive religious instruction Kāvya Poetic composition, often on an epic theme Aesthetic experience (rasa) Kathā / Ākhyāyikā Prose narrative (invented or based on tradition) Entertainment and instruction Arthavāda Explanatory or laudatory passages in the Veda (in Mīmāṃsā usage) Supporting Vedic injunctions

docs.title: 1.2 The “Fifth Veda” and the Authority of Itihāsa
docs.text:
The tradition gives the itihāsa-purāṇa literature the title of Pañcama Veda, the “fifth Veda,” as in the epigraph above, and the Mahābhārata states its relation to the Veda in a frequently quoted line:

Mahābhārata 1.1.204 (Critical Edition)

itihāsapurāṇābhyāṃ vedaṃ samupabṛṃhayet Translation: “One should amplify (upabṛṃh-) the Veda by means of Itihāsa and Purāṇa.”

On this view what the Vedas state in compressed form, the epics and Purāṇas unfold through narrative, dialogue and exemplary lives. The claim had a social side. Vedic learning was restricted to the initiated men of the three dvija (“twice-born”) varṇas; the epics and Purāṇas were recited to everyone. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (1.4.25) explains that Vyāsa composed the Bhārata out of compassion because “the triple Veda is not within the hearing of women, Śūdras and degenerate members of the twice-born classes.” The epics thus became the main vehicle of religious education for the majority of the population — but within a framework that took the hierarchy of varṇa and gender for granted, as the same verse shows. Table 1.2 gives examples of the kinds of knowledge the epics carried.

Table 1.2. Itihāsa as Educator: Knowledge Domains Accessible Through the Epics Domain Epic Source Specific Teaching Governance Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva Rājadharma: duties of kings, taxation, justice Medicine Rāmāyaṇa, Yuddha Kāṇḍa Suṣeṇa’s treatment of the wounded; Hanumān’s mountain of herbs Military science Mahābhārata, Bhīṣma and Droṇa Parvas Battle arrays (vyūha), weapons, codes of combat Geography Rāmāyaṇa, Kiṣkindhā Kāṇḍa Sugrīva’s description of the four quarters of the earth Law Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva Āpaddharma: conduct in times of emergency Philosophy Bhagavad Gītā; Mokṣadharma Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Vedānta and the theory of action (karman)

In the formal classification of learning the epics held a more modest place. A verse of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa lists the fourteen branches of knowledge (caturdaśa vidyās):

Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.6.27

aṅgāni vedāś catvāro mīmāṃsā nyāyavistaraḥ purāṇaṃ dharmaśāstraṃ ca vidyā hy etāś caturdaśa Translation: “The (six) auxiliaries, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya, Purāṇa and Dharmaśāstra — these are the fourteen branches of knowledge.”

Here itihāsa is not listed separately but is subsumed under purāṇa. In the classification of authoritative texts, too, the epics and Purāṇas are smṛti (“remembered” tradition) rather than śruti (the Veda, held to be revealed). The Mīmāṃsā school, which developed the most explicit theory of textual authority, held that smṛti is authoritative because it is presumed to rest on Vedic texts, perhaps now lost, and that where it contradicts an extant Vedic text it is to be disregarded (Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1.3.1–3 with Śabara’s commentary); narrative passages within the Veda itself were classed as arthavāda, authoritative only in so far as they support an injunction. In practice the epics — especially the Bhagavad Gītā — came to rival the Veda in religious influence, and the Vedāntic schools counted the Gītā among their three foundational texts (prasthānatraya). Figure 1.1 shows the mediating role that the tradition assigns to itihāsa-purāṇa.

Figure 1.1. The mediating role of Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the tradition conceives it

docs.title: 1.3 Itihāsa and Purāṇa Distinguished
docs.text:
Although itihāsa and purāṇa are often named together, the tradition distinguishes them (Table 1.3).

Table 1.3. Key Distinctions: Itihāsa vs. Purāṇa Criterion Itihāsa Purāṇa Meaning “Thus it was” — historical narrative “Ancient” — ancient lore Number Two: Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata Eighteen Mahāpurāṇas + Upapurāṇas Central Focus Life of a single hero or royal lineage Cosmology, genealogy, Dharma teachings Narrative Style One main story, framed and interrupted by many embedded episodes Encyclopaedic, dialogical, nested narratives Defining Feature Purāvṛtta (ancient happening) Pañca Lakṣaṇa (five characteristics) Authorship (traditional) Vālmīki (Rāmāyaṇa), Vyāsa (Mahābhārata) Attributed to Vyāsa

docs.title: 1.3.1 The Pañca Lakṣaṇa of Purāṇas
docs.text:
A verse found in several Purāṇas defines the genre by five characteristics (pañca lakṣaṇa):

Kūrma Purāṇa 1.1.12; the verse recurs in several other Purāṇas

sargaś ca pratisargaś ca vaṃśo manvantarāṇi ca vaṃśānucaritaṃ caiva purāṇaṃ pañcalakṣaṇam Translation: “Creation, secondary creation, genealogy (of gods and sages), the Manvantara periods, and the deeds of the royal lineages — (this is) a Purāṇa, possessing five characteristics.”

As Rocher and others have pointed out, the extant Purāṇas fit this definition poorly: some of the five topics occupy only a small part of most Purāṇas, while much of their bulk is devoted to ritual, pilgrimage, sectarian theology and dharma (Rocher 1986). The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (12.7) gives an expanded list of ten characteristics. Figure 1.2 sets out the classical five.

Figure 1.2. The Pañca Lakṣaṇa — Five Defining Characteristics of a Purāṇa

docs.title: 1.4 Scale and Literary Form
docs.text:
Tradition assigns the Rāmāyaṇa 24,000 ślokas in seven kāṇḍas, and the Mahābhārata 100,000 ślokas (it calls itself the śatasāhasrī saṃhitā) in eighteen parvans. The critical editions are shorter: the Poona Critical Edition of the Mahābhārata contains roughly 75,000 verses, and the Baroda Critical Edition of the Rāmāyaṇa is likewise appreciably shorter than the vulgate. A śloka is a couplet of two sixteen-syllable lines, each roughly comparable in length to a Greek hexameter; counted in this way, the critical text of the Mahābhārata is about five times the combined length of the Iliad and Odyssey (c. 28,000 lines), and the vulgate’s traditional 100,000 ślokas would be about seven times. The Purāṇic tradition assigns the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas a total of 400,000 ślokas (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.13); actual printed texts vary considerably (Table 1.4).

Table 1.4. Scale of Itihāsa-Purāṇa Literature Text Traditional count of ślokas Divisions Rāmāyaṇa 24,000 7 Kāṇḍas Mahābhārata 100,000 (CE c. 75,000) 18 Parvas, 100 Upaparvans Harivaṃśa (appendix) 12,000 (CE c. 6,000) 2–3 Parvas Bhagavad Gītā 700 18 Adhyāyas 18 Mahāpurāṇas 400,000 (traditional total) Varying

The forms through which this mass of material is organised recur throughout the volume. The frame narrative sets stories within stories: in the Mahābhārata the bard Ugraśravas Sauti recites to Śaunaka and the sages of the Naimiṣa forest the epic he heard Vaiśaṃpāyana recite to King Janamejaya, the great-grandson of its heroes (Section 4.18). Teaching is given in dialogue (saṃvāda) — Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, Bhīṣma and Yudhiṣṭhira, Vidura and Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Self-contained embedded stories (upākhyāna) such as Nala, Sāvitrī and the Rāmopākhyāna comment on the main story. Genealogical lists, set descriptions (varṇana) of seasons, cities and battles, and extended philosophical discourse complete the repertoire. Because the corpus gathers law, statecraft, cosmology, philosophy, geography and the arts as well as narrative, the tradition has treated it as a knowledge system in its own right; Rocher’s survey shows, however, that much Purāṇic and māhātmya material is ritual, sectarian or local in purpose, so that any single unifying aim is better described as the tradition’s ideal than as a description of the texts.

docs.title: 1.4.1 Dharma as the Tradition’s Axis
docs.text:
For the tradition, the unifying principle of the corpus is dharma: on this reading every narrative, discourse and genealogy serves to show the nature, practice and fruits of dharma and the consequences of adharma. One of the closing verses of the Mahābhārata, put in Vyāsa’s mouth, voices the tradition’s complaint that this teaching goes unheeded:

Mahābhārata, Svargārohaṇa Parva 18.5.49 (Critical Edition)

Sanskrit: ūrdhvabāhur viraumy eṣa na ca kaścic chṛṇoti me dharmād arthaś ca kāmaś ca sa kimarthaṃ na sevyate Translation: “With upraised arms I cry out, but none heeds my call: from Dharma flow Artha (prosperity) and Kāma (fulfilment); why then is Dharma not pursued?”

docs.title: 1.5 Dating: Two Chronologies
docs.text:
The chronology of the itihāsa-purāṇa texts must be approached on two levels. The tradition places the events of the Rāmāyaṇa in the Tretā Yuga and the Bhārata war at the junction of the Dvāpara and Kali Yugas; the Kali Yuga is conventionally reckoned from 3102 BCE, an epoch used by Āryabhaṭa (499 CE), and the Aihole inscription of Pulakeśin II (634 CE) dates itself 3,735 years after the Bhārata war. Modern scholarship, working from language, metre, internal cross-references, the material culture the texts describe and their relation to datable literature, dates the composition of the texts as we have them much later, and treats each as the product of centuries of growth. Table 1.5 sets out both views; academic ranges are given first throughout this volume. Attempts to confirm the traditional dates by archaeology or by the planetary positions mentioned in the epics are examined in Section 12.11.

Table 1.5. Chronological Perspectives on the Itihāsa-Purāṇa Literature Text Academic dating of composition Traditional dating Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Core (Books 2–6) c. 5th–3rd century BCE; Books 1 and 7 added later; substantially complete by c. 2nd–3rd century CE (Brockington). Goldman places the earliest stratum somewhat earlier, c. 750–500 BCE. Composed by Vālmīki, a contemporary of Rāma, in the Tretā Yuga Mahābhārata Composite text growing c. 400 BCE–400 CE (Brockington); Hiltebeitel argues for a written composition between the mid-2nd century BCE and the turn of the era Composed by Vyāsa, a participant in the events, at the end of the Dvāpara Yuga (war conventionally c. 3102 BCE) Bhagavad Gītā Usually c. 2nd century BCE–1st century CE; estimates range from the 5th century BCE, and some scholars see layers Spoken by Kṛṣṇa on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra Harivaṃśa c. 1st–3rd century CE Appendix (khila) by Vyāsa Mahāpurāṇas Earliest layers of the oldest Purāṇas c. 3rd–5th century CE (Hazra); Bhāgavata c. 9th–10th century CE in most current estimates; all were revised and expanded until the early modern period (Rocher) Composed by Vyāsa at the beginning of the Kali Yuga

Within the tradition the ṛṣis are regarded as seers (draṣṭā) of truths that are sanātana (eternal), so the date of a text’s composition is not thought to determine the validity of its teaching. The academic dates concern the texts as literary artefacts; they neither confirm nor refute the religious claims made for them (Hazra 1940; Rocher 1986; Brockington 1998; Hiltebeitel 2001).

docs.title: 1.6 Transmission and Recitation
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata describes its own transmission as a chain of narrators: Vyāsa taught the epic to his five disciples, among them Vaiśaṃpāyana; Vaiśaṃpāyana narrated it to King Janamejaya during the snake sacrifice (sarpasattra); and Ugraśravas Sauti, who heard it there, re-narrated it to the sages assembled under Śaunaka in the Naimiṣa forest (Figure 1.3). This layered frame is a literary device, but it also mirrors the real social setting of epic recitation: the sūtas (bards attached to royal courts) and, later, brahmin reciters (paurāṇikas, kathāvācakas) who performed the epics, often at rituals and festivals. The connection of the frame with Janamejaya’s sacrifice has been analysed as a deliberate ritual structure (Minkowski 1989).

Figure 1.3. Transmission Chain of the Mahābhārata as the Epic Describes It

The epic and Purāṇic corpus was preserved by a combination of oral performance and manuscript copying. Unlike the Vedas, which were preserved word for word through techniques such as the jaṭā and ghana recitations, the epics were transmitted through a more flexible tradition of narrative recitation that allowed both the preservation of core content and adaptation to local audiences. The result, visible in the manuscripts, is a large number of regional versions and recensions — the reason critical editions were needed (Sections 2.3 and 4.8). The best-known story of the writing of the Mahābhārata, in which Gaṇeśa serves as Vyāsa’s scribe, is absent from most manuscripts and from the Critical Edition (Section 4.1).

Recitation was also a religious act. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.11.1) instructs the departing student, svādhyāyān mā prama­daḥ, “Do not neglect your recitation”; in the tradition, hearing and reciting the epics and Purāṇas came to be regarded as a form of this svādhyāya, promising merit (puṇya) to reciter and listener alike, and the phalaśruti passages at the end of the epics and of individual Purāṇas spell out the rewards. Table 1.6 lists the main forms that this engagement has taken; four of them are studied in Section 12.5.

Table 1.6. Traditional Forms of Itihāsa-Purāṇa Engagement Form Sanskrit Term Description Complete recitation Pārāyaṇa Full text recited over 7–30 days; considered a sacred act Scholarly discourse Pravācana A learned speaker expounds episodes with commentary Dramatic performance Nāṭya / Līlā Rāmlīlā, Kṛṣṇa Līlā, Yakṣagāna Devotional singing Bhajana / Kīrtana Epic episodes rendered in song Temple sculpture Śilpa / Mūrti Narrative panels on temple walls Manuscript painting Citra / Paṭa Illustrated manuscripts (Mughal, Rajput, Pahari, Odia and other schools) Shadow puppetry Chāyā Nāṭaka Tolu Bommalata (Andhra), Tolpāvakkūttu (Kerala), Togalu Gombeyata (Karnataka)

docs.title: 1.7 Commentators and Levels of Meaning
docs.text:
The interpretation of the epics and Purāṇas has been shaped by a commentarial tradition that is, for the most part, medieval and early modern. The Bhagavad Gītā attracted the largest number of commentaries, from Śaṅkara’s (c. 8th century), the earliest to survive, through Rāmānuja and Madhva to Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (Table 6.3); the Bhāgavata Purāṇa was expounded by Śrīdhara Svāmin and by the theologians of the Kṛṣṇa schools (Table 7.5); and the Rāmāyaṇa found its principal commentators in the south from the sixteenth century, above all the Śrīvaiṣṇava Govindarāja (Section 2.10). The whole Mahābhārata had fewer interpreters. Madhva’s Mahābhārata­tātparya­nirṇaya is a verse digest reading the whole epic theologically, and the only complete commentary in common use is the Bhārata­bhāva­dīpa (“Lamp on the Meaning of the Bhārata”) of Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara, a Mahārāṣṭrian scholar working in Benares in the late seventeenth century. Nīlakaṇṭha collated many manuscripts to establish his text, which became the basis of the widely printed “vulgate” (the northern recension as he constituted it); he often offers alternative explanations of disputed passages, and his Advaitic reading of the epic remains the main traditional point of reference.

Traditional readers have long recognised that an epic narrative can be read on more than one level at once: as an account of events, as moral instruction, as philosophical allegory and as the play (līlā) of God. The Mahābhārata itself remarks that some learned brahmins begin the Bhārata with Manu, others with Āstīka and others with Uparicara (1.1.50 in the Critical Edition), and Madhva is commonly understood to have taken this as a hint that the epic carries historical, moral and spiritual senses simultaneously, while insisting that the historical sense is not cancelled by the others. Later devotional readers, especially in the Rāma and Kṛṣṇa traditions, read the narratives above all as divine līlā. A modern version of the same idea is V. S. Sukthankar’s: in lectures given shortly before his death, the editor of the Critical Edition read the epic on a mundane, an ethical and a metaphysical plane at once (Sukthankar 1957).

Classical critics were equally aware that the epics are literature. The ninth-century theorist Ānandavardhana, in the fourth chapter of his Dhvanyāloka, treats the Mahābhārata as at once a śāstra (a teaching) and a kāvya (a poem), whose dominant sentiment is the tranquillity (śānta rasa) born of disillusion with worldly ends, shown in the ruin of the Yādavas and the Pāṇḍavas’ bleak victory; and he regards the Rāmāyaṇa as founded on pathos (karuṇa), the grief of separation that begins with the poem’s own origin story (Section 2.1). These two judgements have shaped the reading of both epics ever since, and later chapters refer back to them here.

docs.title: 1.8 The Epics in Comparative Perspective
docs.text:
Comparison with other epic traditions brings out both the distinctive features of the Sanskrit epics and how much they share with heroic poetry elsewhere — bardic origins, formulaic diction, heroic codes and a long period of oral and written growth (Smith 1977; Brockington 1998). Table 1.7 sets them beside the Homeric poems and the Epic of Gilgamesh. A different kind of comparison asks whether the Mahābhārata preserves, in transposed form, myths that the Indo-European peoples inherited in common; that question is taken up in Section 4.4.

Table 1.7. The Sanskrit Epics in Comparative Perspective Feature Sanskrit epics Homeric epics Epic of Gilgamesh Length c. 75,000 ślokas (CE MBh; 100,000 trad.) and 24,000 (Rām., trad.) c. 28,000 lines c. 3,000 lines (Standard Babylonian version) Central ethical frame Dharma, often contested within the text Honour (timē) and glory (kleos) Mortality and the limits of kingship Didactic content Extensive (Gītā, Śānti and Anuśāsana Parvas) Limited Limited Later life Continuously recited, retold, performed and worshipped Central to classical education and literature Lost; recovered through archaeology in the 19th century

Three features stand out. The Sanskrit epics have been recited, performed and retold without a break for some two millennia, and remain central to religious life. They carry extended teaching on dharma, statecraft, philosophy and devotion inside the narrative. And they exist in many versions, for every region and community produced its own, including Jain, Buddhist, folk and oppositional retellings (Sections 2.8 and 4.10).

docs.title: 1.9 Approach and Scope of This Volume
docs.text:
This volume keeps two perspectives in view. It presents the texts as the tradition has understood them, respecting their status as sacred literature for many readers, and it reports the findings of modern textual criticism, comparative study and archaeology where they bear on the texts. It sets the major interpretive traditions — Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, devotional, Jain, Buddhist and regional — beside modern critical readings, including feminist and Dalit critiques, without making any one of them the measure of the others; where a heading or a judgement belongs to the tradition rather than to the author, it says so. Key ślokas are given in transliteration with translation, only where their wording and reference could be checked. The sociologist Maurice Halbwachs’s idea of “collective memory” — the shared stock of narratives that gives a group its identity — offers a useful modern analogy to the Indian idea of smṛti, “that which is remembered,” and helps to explain why the epics are not only studied but recited, performed, celebrated and contested.

The volume has twelve chapters. After this introduction, Chapters 2 and 3 treat Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa, first as a whole — its structure, recensions, versions and reception — and then book by book; the contested episodes of Vālin, Sītā’s ordeal and Śambūka are discussed in full in Chapter 3. Chapters 4 and 5 do the same for the Mahābhārata: Chapter 4 covers its growth, the Critical Edition and its critics, the Indo-European comparative reading and the Harivaṃśa’s life of Kṛṣṇa, and Chapter 5 surveys the eighteen books. Chapter 6 is devoted to the Bhagavad Gītā, Chapter 7 to the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas with a fuller study of the Bhāgavata, and Chapter 8 to the Upapurāṇas, the māhātmyas of sacred places and the Tamil talapurāṇams. Three thematic chapters follow: Chapter 9 on the hard cases and the limits of epic dharma, Chapter 10 on the women of the epics, and Chapter 11 on the philosophy of the Mokṣadharma and the Nārāyaṇīya. The last chapter, Chapter 12, follows the epics’ afterlife: regional retellings, the Persian translations of the Mughal court and the Sikh Dasam Granth, Southeast Asia, sculpture, dance and ritual theatre, film and festival, and the modern debate over archaeology, astronomy and the historicity of the epics.

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa: The Ādikāvya
docs.text:
Few works of world literature have had the cultural reach of the Rāmāyaṇa attributed to Vālmīki, the ādikavi or “first poet.” Composed in the anuṣṭubh śloka that became the standard measure of later Sanskrit narrative verse, it tells the story of Rāma — for the tradition the ideal man, the ideal king and the embodiment of dharma — and has been retold, performed, worshipped and argued over across South and Southeast Asia for more than two millennia (Brockington 1998; Goldman 1984–2017).

The tradition calls the Rāmāyaṇa the ādikāvya, the first poem. According to the opening cantos of the text itself, the śloka form was born from Vālmīki’s cry of anguish on witnessing the killing of a bird: grief (śoka) became verse (śloka). The metre itself is older — the anuṣṭubh occurs throughout the Veda — but the story makes Vālmīki the founder of secular poetry (kāvya), and later poeticians accepted that role for him.

docs.title: 2.1.1 The Life and Transformation of Vālmīki
docs.text:
The epic itself says little about its author. In the Uttarakāṇḍa Vālmīki appears as a sage who shelters the banished Sītā in his hermitage, raises her twin sons Kuśa and Lava, and teaches them to sing the poem; there he calls himself a son of Pracetas (hence the patronymic Prācetasa). The famous story that he had been a robber named Ratnākara, who was reformed by the seven sages and meditated so long that an ant-hill (valmīka) grew over him, is not found in the critical text. It belongs to later tradition — it is told, for instance, in the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, in Purāṇic māhātmyas and in regional Rāmāyaṇas — and the name is derived from valmīka by folk etymology.

The tradition knows him by several titles: ādikavi, the first poet and author of the first kāvya; Prācetasa, the son of Pracetas; and, in later devotional sources, a brahmarṣi who reached that rank through his austerities.

docs.title: 2.1.2 The Birth of the Śloka: Grief into Poetry
docs.text:
The second sarga of the Bālakāṇḍa tells how poetry itself began. Vālmīki, walking by the river Tamasā with his disciple Bharadvāja, saw a pair of krauñca birds (usually identified as cranes or curlews) mating, when a hunter’s arrow killed the male. Moved by the cry of the female, Vālmīki cursed the hunter:

Rāmāyaṇa 1.2.14 (Critical Edition)

mā niṣāda pratiṣṭhāṃ tvam agamaḥ śāśvatīḥ samāḥ / yat krauñcamithunād ekam avadhīḥ kāmamohitam // Translation: “Hunter (niṣāda), may you find no rest for endless years, since you killed one of this pair of krauñcas while it was lost in love.”

Vālmīki was astonished at what he had uttered, a verse with four equal quarters fit to be sung to the lute:

Rāmāyaṇa 1.2.17 (Critical Edition)

pādabaddho ’kṣarasamas tantrīlayasamanvitaḥ / śokārtasya pravṛtto me śloko bhavatu nānyathā // Translation: “Bound in metrical feet, with an equal number of syllables, fit for the rhythm of the lute — this utterance that came from me in my grief shall be called a śloka, and nothing else.”

The god Brahmā then appears, tells Vālmīki that this speech came forth by his will, and commissions him to compose the whole story of Rāma in the same form. Many centuries later the critic Ānandavardhana made the episode the emblem of his theory of poetry: “the very soul of poetry is that (suggested) meaning, as, long ago, the grief of the first poet, arising from the separation of the pair of krauñcas, became verse (śokaḥ ślokatvam āgataḥ)” (Dhvanyāloka 1.5).

docs.title: 2.2 Structure: Seven Kāṇḍas
docs.text:
The Rāmāyaṇa describes itself (Bālakāṇḍa, sarga 4 of the vulgate) as a poem of 24,000 ślokas in 500 sargas, arranged in six books “and the Uttara” — a formulation that itself hints that the seventh book was felt to be an addition. The printed vulgate texts come close to the traditional figure; the Baroda Critical Edition is shorter. A later tradition, the “Gāyatrī Rāmāyaṇa,” holds that each thousand ślokas begins with one of the twenty-four syllables of the Gāyatrī mantra; this is a devotional reading, not a feature of the text as transmitted (Table 2.1).

Table 2.1. Structure of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Kāṇḍa Name Sargas (vulgate) Sargas (CE) Primary Content 1 Bāla Kāṇḍa 77 76 Birth of Rāma; breaking of Śiva’s bow; marriage 2 Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa 119 111 Exile; death of Daśaratha; Bharata’s refusal 3 Araṇya Kāṇḍa 75 71 Forest life; Śūrpaṇakhā; abduction of Sītā 4 Kiṣkindhā Kāṇḍa 67 66 Alliance with Sugrīva; killing of Vālin; search 5 Sundara Kāṇḍa 68 66 Hanumān in Laṅkā 6 Yuddha Kāṇḍa 128 116 War; death of Rāvaṇa; Sītā’s ordeal; coronation 7 Uttara Kāṇḍa 111 100 Origins of Rāvaṇa; banishment of Sītā; Śambūka; end of Rāma’s reign Total 645 606

Scholarly Note: The growth of the text

Since Hermann Jacobi’s study of 1893, most scholars have regarded Books 2–6 as the oldest part of the poem, and Books 1 and 7 as later additions: they differ in style, they contain most of the passages that present Rāma as an incarnation of Viṣṇu, and the table of contents at the opening of Book 1 originally appears to have ended with the return to Ayodhyā. Brockington distinguishes several stages of growth extending over many centuries; Goldman dates the earliest stratum c. 750–500 BCE, while others prefer the 5th–3rd centuries BCE (see Table 1.5) (Jacobi 1893; Brockington 1984; Goldman 1984–2017).

docs.title: 2.3 The Recensions: Northern and Southern Traditions
docs.text:
The manuscripts of the Rāmāyaṇa fall into distinct regional recensions. The editors of the Critical Edition prepared at the Oriental Institute, Baroda (1960–1975) grouped the manuscripts into two major families, each with sub-recensions defined largely by script (Figure 2.1; Table 2.2):

Figure 2.1. Major Recensions and Sub-Recensions of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa

docs.title: 2.3.1 Key Differences Between Recensions
docs.text: Table 2.2. Major Differences Between Northern and Southern Recensions Feature Northern Recension Southern Recension Sub-recensions Northwestern and Northeastern, which differ considerably from each other Telugu, Grantha and Malayalam, which are relatively uniform Relation between recensions Large parts of the text are shared, but each recension contains many verses (and some whole passages) absent from the other, and wording differs widely Basis of the Critical Edition Used for comparison; northern-only passages relegated to the apparatus and appendices Chosen as the basis of the constituted text because of its greater homogeneity Commentaries Fewer surviving commentaries The major commentaries (Govindarāja, Maheśvaratīrtha, the Tilaka) follow southern texts

docs.title: 2.3.2 The Baroda Critical Edition (1960–1975)
docs.text: The Oriental Institute of the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda produced the Critical Edition of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa in seven volumes between 1960 and 1975, under the general editorship of G. H. Bhatt and U. P. Shah (Bhatt and Shah 1960–1975). Unlike the Poona edition of the Mahābhārata, which gives preference to the northern recension, the Baroda editors judged the southern recension to be more homogeneous and generally closer to the archetype and therefore used it as their base, recording the rest in the critical apparatus. The resulting text is the basis of the complete English translation by Robert Goldman and his collaborators (Goldman 1984–2017). Critics have pointed out that the constituted text is a scholarly reconstruction that never circulated as such, and that the excluded passages are themselves part of the Rāmāyaṇa’s history; but the edition remains the indispensable basis for historical study of the poem.

docs.title: 2.4.1 The Rasa Aesthetic
docs.text: Sanskrit critics after Ānandavardhana took pathos (karuṇa) to be the dominant rasa of the poem, with the heroic (vīra) subordinate (Section 1.7). The grief that gave birth to the first śloka returns in Daśaratha’s death, Kausalyā’s lament and, above all, the separation (viraha) of Rāma and Sītā.

docs.title: 2.4.2 The Anuṣṭubh Metre: The Heartbeat of Sanskrit Poetry
docs.text: The anuṣṭubh śloka consists of four pādas (quarter-verses) of eight syllables each, thirty-two syllables in all. The overwhelming majority of the Rāmāyaṇa is composed in this metre. Longer metres of the triṣṭubh family (indravajrā, upajāti) and others such as vaṃśastha occur mainly in the closing verses of sargas, a convention later standard in courtly mahākāvya.

docs.title: 2.5.1 Rāma as the Ideal: Vālmīki’s Frame
docs.text:
The opening sarga of the Bālakāṇḍa frames the whole poem as the answer to a question. Vālmīki asks the divine sage Nārada whether there is anyone in the world who possesses every virtue:

Rāmāyaṇa 1.1.2: Vālmīki’s Question

ko nv asmin sāmprataṃ loke guṇavān kaś ca vīryavān / dharmajñaś ca kṛtajñaś ca satyavākyo dṛḍhavrataḥ // Translation: “Who in this world today is virtuous and who is valiant, who knows dharma, who is grateful, truthful in speech and firm in his vows?”

Vālmīki’s question continues for two more verses (1.1.3–4), listing some sixteen qualities in all: besides virtue, valour, knowledge of dharma, gratitude, truthful speech and firm vows, the ideal man is of good conduct, benevolent to all beings, learned, capable, pleasing to behold, self-possessed, free of anger and envy, radiant, and one whom even the gods fear when he is roused in battle. Nārada answers that such a man exists — Rāma of the Ikṣvāku line — and summarises his story. The poem thus presents itself from its first verses as the portrait of an ideal; the later Hindi epithet Maryādā Puruṣottama, “the supreme person who keeps within the bounds,” expresses the same ideal.

docs.title: 2.5.2 Recitation as a Meritorious Act
docs.text: The Rāmāyaṇa tradition holds the text to be puṇya (meritorious) to recite and to hear. The Yuddhakāṇḍa of the vulgate closes with a phalaśruti that promises long life, prosperity, sons and freedom from sin to those who listen to the poem, a promise repeated and amplified in later devotional Rāmāyaṇas.

docs.title: 2.6 Relationship with Vālmīki’s Other Works
docs.text: The Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (also called the Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa), a long philosophical work cast as a dialogue between the sage Vasiṣṭha and the young Rāma, is attributed by tradition to Vālmīki. Modern scholarship regards it as a much later work: its earliest recoverable form, the Mokṣopāya, was composed in Kashmir around the tenth century, and the text was later reworked in an Advaitic direction. The traditional attribution shows how the authority of Vālmīki’s name could be used to frame new philosophical teaching.

docs.title: 2.7 The Rāmāyaṇa Tradition: Versions and Adaptations
docs.text:
The Rāmāyaṇa was retold in virtually every language and cultural region of South and Southeast Asia, and in Jain and Buddhist as well as Hindu forms. Table 2.3 presents a selection:

Table 2.3. Major Versions of the Rāma Story Title Author Language Notable Feature Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa attributed to Vālmīki Sanskrit Earliest full surviving version; model for most later Hindu versions Rāmopākhyāna (Mahābhārata 3.257–275) Sanskrit Condensed telling within the Mahābhārata Dasaratha Jātaka Buddhist canon (Jātaka 461) Pāli Rāma as a previous birth of the Buddha; no abduction Paumacariya Vimalasūri Prakrit Earliest Jain version; Rāvaṇa a Vidyādhara, not a demon Padmacarita Raviṣeṇa (late 7th c.) Sanskrit (Jain) Sanskrit reworking of the Jain story Irāmāvatāram Kampaṉ (c. 12th c.) Tamil Independent literary masterpiece Rāmacaritamānas Tulsīdās (begun 1574) Awadhi Most influential North Indian version Saptakāṇḍa Rāmāyaṇa Mādhava Kandalī (14th c.) Assamese One of the earliest vernacular versions; Kandalī’s five books were completed by Mādhavadeva and Śaṅkaradeva Kṛttivāsī Rāmāyaṇ Kṛttivās (15th c.) Bengali Devotional; the classic Bengali version Candrāvatī Rāmāyaṇ Candrāvatī (16th c.) Bengali By a woman poet; centred on Sītā Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kilippāṭṭu Eḻuttacchaṉ (16th c.) Malayalam Based on the Sanskrit Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa Torave Rāmāyaṇa Narahari (Kumāravālmīki) (c. 16th c.) Kannada Popular devotional version Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu Goṇa Budda Rāḍḍi (13th–14th c.) Telugu Influential in Andhra Jagamohana Rāmāyaṇa Balarāma Dāsa (16th c.) Odia Classic Odia version Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇ Eknāth (16th c.) Marathi Devotional retelling by the Vārkarī poet Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa attributed to Yogīśvara (9th c.) Old Javanese Southeast Asian courtly adaptation Bhānubhakta Rāmāyaṇa Bhānubhakta Ācārya (19th c.) Nepali The first great work of Nepali literature Hikayat Seri Rama Unknown Malay Version shaped by an Islamic milieu

A. K. Ramanujan’s essay “Three Hundred Rāmāyaṇas” (first presented in 1987, published 1991) took its title from the count of versions made by earlier scholarship and argued that the Rāma story is best seen not as one text with derivatives but as a “pool of signifiers” from which each telling draws (Ramanujan 1991). The essay’s inclusion in the history syllabus of the University of Delhi was challenged by protesters, and the university’s Academic Council removed it in 2011 — an episode that itself illustrates how contested the plurality of Rāmāyaṇas remains.

docs.title: 2.8 Jain, Buddhist and Questioning Rāmāyaṇas
docs.text: Vālmīki’s poem is the earliest complete version to survive, but it was never the only one. Camille Bulcke’s monumental Hindi study Rāmkathā (1950) first surveyed the whole field, and Paula Richman’s edited volumes Many Rāmāyaṇas (1991) and Questioning Rāmāyaṇas (2001) brought it into the centre of modern scholarship (Bulcke 1950; Richman 1991, 2001).

docs.title: 2.8.1 The Buddhist Dasaratha Jātaka
docs.text: The Pāli Dasaratha Jātaka (no. 461 in the Jātaka collection) tells a very different story (Cowell 1895–1907). King Dasaratha of Vārāṇasī sends his children Rāma-paṇḍita, Lakkhaṇa and Sītā to the Himalaya to protect them from a scheming queen; when news of the king’s death reaches them, Rāma alone remains calm, explaining to his grieving siblings that all that lives must die. He returns after the agreed period, reigns for sixteen thousand years, and takes Sītā — in this version his sister — as his queen. There is no abduction, no Rāvaṇa and no war. The Buddha tells the story to console a landowner mourning his father, and identifies himself as Rāma in a former life. Scholars disagree about the relation of the Jātaka to Vālmīki: some have seen in it an older form of the story, but Richard Gombrich and others have argued that it presupposes knowledge of the Sanskrit epic and recasts it to teach equanimity (Gombrich 1985).

docs.title: 2.8.2 Jain Rāmāyaṇas
docs.text: The Jains developed their own Rāma tradition, beginning with Vimalasūri’s Prakrit Paumacariya (“The Deeds of Padma”); its colophon places it in the first century CE, though many scholars date it several centuries later. It was followed by Raviṣeṇa’s Sanskrit Padmacarita (late 7th century), Svayambhū’s Apabhraṃśa Paumacariu (9th century), Nāgacandra’s Kannada Rāmacandracaritapurāṇa (c. 1100) and Hemacandra’s account in the Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacarita (12th century). In these works Rāma (Padma) is the eighth Baladeva, Lakṣmaṇa the corresponding Vāsudeva and Rāvaṇa the Prativāsudeva of the Jain universal history. The Rākṣasas and Vānaras are not demons and monkeys but clans of vidyādharas, human beings with magical knowledge, named after their banners; Rāvaṇa is a learned and pious king undone by desire. Vimalasūri explicitly rejects as absurd the “false” stories of other poets — of monkeys who build bridges and of Kumbhakarṇa sleeping for six months. Consistently with Jain ethics, it is Lakṣmaṇa, not Rāma, who kills Rāvaṇa and who goes to hell for it, while Rāma renounces the world, becomes a Jain monk and attains liberation. The Jain versions thus offer a rationalised and non-violent counter-tradition that was itself widely read (Kulkarni 1990).

docs.title: 2.8.3 Oppositional and Marginal Voices
docs.text: Within Hindu South Asia, too, the epic has been retold from the margins. Women’s songs in Telugu, Bengali, Maithili and other languages dwell on Sītā’s pregnancy, her banishment and the sufferings of women in Rāma’s household, often implicitly criticising Rāma (Narayana Rao 1991). The sixteenth-century Bengali poet Candrāvatī composed a Rāmāyaṇa that tells the story largely from Sītā’s point of view. In the twentieth century, E. V. Ramasamy (Periyar) and the Dravidian movement in Tamil Nadu read the Rāmāyaṇa as a story of Aryan conquest of the Dravidian south, inverted its moral polarities and staged public burnings of Rāma’s image; B. R. Ambedkar, in Riddles in Hinduism, criticised Rāma’s treatment of Sītā and of the Śūdra ascetic Śambūka (Richman 2001; Ambedkar 1987). Feminist and Dalit critiques of the epic, and the continuing debate over Sītā’s ordeal and banishment, are discussed in Chapters 3 and 10.

docs.title: 2.9 The Rāmāyaṇa in Daily Religious Life
2.9.1 Pārāyaṇa: The Nine-Day Recitation
docs.text:
The complete recitation of the Rāmāyaṇa (pārāyaṇa) is traditionally completed over nine days (navadina pārāyaṇa) or other fixed periods. It is especially associated with:

  • Rāmanavamī (Rāma’s birthday) and the spring Navarātri that precedes it

  • The autumn festival season culminating in Dasarā (Vijayadaśamī)

  • Household ceremonies and vows (vrata)

The story is also enacted. The Rāmlīlā of North India re-enacts it every autumn, culminating at Dasarā; the month-long Rāmlīlā of Ramnagar near Varanasi, under the patronage of the Mahārājā of Benares, is the best known (Section 12.5). UNESCO proclaimed Rāmlīlā a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005, and it was inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008 (Lutgendorf 1991).

docs.title: 2.10.1 Modern Studies
docs.text:
European scholarship on the Rāmāyaṇa began with partial translations by William Carey and Joshua Marshman (1806–1810) and the verse translation of Ralph T. H. Griffith (1870–1874). Major contributions since then include:

  • Hermann Jacobi, Das Rāmāyaṇa (1893) — the first systematic analysis of the epic’s growth (Jacobi 1893)

  • Camille Bulcke, Rāmkathā (1950) — a survey of the Rāma story in all its versions (Bulcke 1950)

  • G. H. Bhatt, U. P. Shah and colleagues, the Baroda Critical Edition (1960–1975) (Bhatt and Shah 1960–1975)

  • J. L. Brockington, Righteous Rāma (1984) — analysis of the epic’s evolution (Brockington 1984)

  • Robert P. Goldman and collaborators, The Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki (Princeton, 7 vols., 1984–2017) — the annotated translation of the Critical Edition (Goldman 1984–2017)

  • Sheldon Pollock — studies of Rāma’s divinity and of the epic’s political uses (Pollock 1993)

  • Paula Richman (ed.), Many Rāmāyaṇas (1991) and Questioning Rāmāyaṇas (2001) (Richman 1991, 2001)

docs.title: 2.10.2 Traditional Sanskrit Commentaries
docs.text:
The Rāmāyaṇa attracted a substantial commentarial tradition, mostly from the sixteenth century onwards and mostly in the south:

  • Govindarāja, Bhūṣaṇa (16th century) — an extensive Śrīvaiṣṇava commentary

  • Maheśvaratīrtha, Tattvadīpikā — an Advaitic commentary

  • The Tilaka, attributed to Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa or his patron Rāma (18th century) — widely printed with the vulgate

  • Tryambaka Makhin, Dharmākūta (18th century, Thanjavur) — reads the epic as a source of dharma

docs.title: 2.11 The Rāmāyaṇa’s Geography: Sacred Landscape
docs.text:
The Rāmāyaṇa maps a geography that spans much of the subcontinent, from Ayodhyā in the Gangetic plain through the forests of central India to the southern sea. The detail is most precise for the north and becomes vaguer further south, which many scholars take as a sign of the poem’s northern origin. Later tradition turned this landscape into a sacred geography, identifying sites across India with the stages of Rāma’s journey (Table 2.4).

Table 2.4. Key Geographical Sites in the Rāmāyaṇa and Their Modern Identifications Rāmāyaṇa Name Kāṇḍa Modern Location Significance Ayodhyā Bāla, Ayodhyā Ayodhya, U.P. Rāma’s birthplace; capital of Kośala Citrakūṭa Ayodhyā Chitrakoot, M.P. Bharata visits Rāma; Pādukā episode Daṇḍakāraṇya Araṇya Central-South India Forest of exile; sages’ hermitages Pañcavaṭī Araṇya Nāsik, Maharashtra Sītā’s abduction occurs here Kiṣkindhā Kiṣkindhā Hampi, Karnataka (traditional) Vānara capital; Sugrīva’s kingdom Ṛṣyamūka Parvata Kiṣkindhā Hampi hills (traditional) Rāma meets Hanumān Rāmeśvaram Yuddha (later tradition) Rāmeśvaram, T.N. Worship of the Śiva liṅga before the crossing (not in Vālmīki; later tradition) Setu (Bridge) Yuddha Adam’s Bridge (traditional) Nala’s bridge to Laṅkā Laṅkā Sundara, Yuddha Sri Lanka (traditional; disputed) Rāvaṇa’s fortress city

docs.title: 2.11.1 The Concept of Rāma’s Footsteps (Rāma-Padāṅka)
docs.text:
The later Rāma tradition holds that places where Rāma set foot became sacred. The belief gave rise to a large network of pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) stretching from Ayodhyā in the north to Rāmeśvaram in the south, many of them first attested in Purāṇic māhātmyas and regional Rāmāyaṇas rather than in Vālmīki. Figure 2.2 maps these sites together with the principal places of the Mahābhārata (Section 12.10).

Figure 2.2. Places of the two epics with their usual modern identifications. Most identifications are traditional rather than archaeological (Section 12.11), and the route drawn for Rāma is the one that later pilgrimage tradition follows. Schematic map: coastline and rivers simplified, positions approximate

docs.title: 2.12 Character Studies: The Major Figures of the Rāmāyaṇa
docs.text: The tradition reads the figures around Rāma as embodiments of particular virtues or vices; Vālmīki’s text, and its later retellings, give several of them more room than that reading allows. The women of the poem are discussed in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 2.12.1 Hanumān
docs.text: In the later tradition Hanumān is the model of dāsya bhakti, devotion expressed as service. Son of the wind god Vāyu, he combines immense strength with learning and courage, and devotes all of them to Rāma. The Sundarakāṇḍa is essentially Hanumān’s book. Already on their first meeting in the Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa, Rāma remarks on the correctness and eloquence of Hanumān’s speech, observing that he must have studied grammar thoroughly. Hanumān’s importance grew steadily in later centuries, until he became one of the most widely worshipped deities of India in his own right (Lutgendorf 2007).

docs.title: 2.12.2 Rāvaṇa
docs.text: Rāvaṇa is more than a simple villain. The Uttarakāṇḍa presents him as a figure of great austerity and power, a devotee of Śiva, whose fatal flaw is uncontrolled desire. A popular later interpretation reads his ten heads as mastery of the four Vedas and six auxiliary sciences. After Rāvaṇa’s death, when Vibhīṣaṇa hesitates to cremate his brother, Rāma tells him that “enmities end with death” (maraṇāntāni vairāṇi, 6.99.39 in the Critical Edition) and that Rāvaṇa should receive the full funeral rites. In some regional and modern retellings, and in the Jain tradition, Rāvaṇa becomes a far more sympathetic figure; in the Dravidian movement he was recast as a Dravidian hero.

docs.title: 2.12.3 Lakṣmaṇa
docs.text: For the tradition Lakṣmaṇa is the devoted younger brother. He leaves the palace, and his wife Ūrmilā, to serve Rāma and Sītā throughout the exile. A popular later legend, absent from Vālmīki, holds that Lakṣmaṇa did not sleep for the fourteen years, the goddess of sleep visiting Ūrmilā in his place; Ūrmilā’s neglected suffering became a theme for modern poets (Section 10.7).

docs.title: 2.12.4 Bharata
docs.text: Bharata refuses the throne that his mother’s scheming had procured for him and rules as Rāma’s regent, placing Rāma’s sandals (pādukās) on the throne and living as an ascetic at Nandigrāma for fourteen years. The tradition holds up his regency as the ideal of disinterested rule, the king as trustee rather than owner of the kingdom; the episode also shows how completely the poem subordinates the younger brother’s claim to the elder’s.

docs.title: 2.13 Poetic Metres and Literary Techniques in the Rāmāyaṇa
docs.text: Vālmīki uses the full range of figures of speech (alaṅkāra) later codified by the poeticians — simile (upamā), metaphor (rūpaka), poetic fancy (utprekṣā), hyperbole (atiśayokti) and corroboration of a particular by a general truth (arthāntaranyāsa) — but sparingly by the standards of later kāvya. His descriptions of the seasons, of the forests of the Araṇya and Kiṣkindhā books, and of the rains that delay the search for Sītā became models for later poets; Brockington has traced how the more ornate passages tend to belong to later strata of the text (Brockington 1984).

docs.title: 2.13.1 Vālmīki and the Poeticians
docs.text: Later ālaṅkārikas (poeticians) such as Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta treated Vālmīki as the paradigm of the inspired poet. The transformation of śoka into śloka was, for Ānandavardhana, the very model of suggested emotion (rasa-dhvani) as the soul of poetry. The Rāmāyaṇa also became a principal source of plots for courtly epic and drama; the plays are surveyed in Section 3.13.

docs.title: 2.14 The Rāmāyaṇa in Modern Indian Life
docs.text:
The Rāmāyaṇa’s presence in modern Indian life extends far beyond the temple and the recitation hall, into ethical vocabulary, the arts, mass media and politics (Table 2.5).

Table 2.5. The Rāmāyaṇa in Contemporary Indian Culture Domain Rāmāyaṇa’s Influence Political discourse Gandhi’s ideal of “Rāmrājya” as just government; later the Rāmajanmabhūmi movement of the 1980s–1990s Social Values Concepts of filial duty, fraternal loyalty, and marital fidelity drawn from the epic Festival Culture Rāmanavamī, Dasarā, Dīpāvalī directly celebrate Rāmāyaṇa events Performing Arts Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Bharatanatyam repertoires heavily feature Rāmāyaṇa episodes Visual Arts Pahari, Rājasthāni, Tanjore, and Kalamkari painting traditions Cinema & Television Ramanand Sagar’s television serial Ramayan (1987–88), watched by a very large share of the national audience; numerous films in all Indian languages

The epic’s centrality also makes it politically potent. Sheldon Pollock has argued that the Rāmāyaṇa offered medieval Indian kings a powerful imaginative framework for representing their enemies as demonic others, and that this framework was reactivated in modern politics (Pollock 1993). The national broadcast of Sagar’s serial in 1987–88 coincided with the rise of the Rāmajanmabhūmi campaign at Ayodhyā, and the image of Rāma has since been central to Hindu nationalist mobilisation. At the same time, the Rāma of Gandhi, of Kabīr’s nirguṇa devotion, of women’s songs and of Dalit critique shows how many different Rāmas coexist in modern India.

docs.title: 2.15 The Rāmāyaṇa’s Philosophical Substratum
docs.text: Beneath the narrative surface of the Rāmāyaṇa lies a sophisticated philosophical framework that engages with the central questions of Indian metaphysics. While the Mahābhārata makes its philosophical content explicit through extended discourses (the Bhagavad Gītā, the Śānti Parva), Vālmīki embeds his philosophical vision within the fabric of narrative itself.

docs.title: 2.15.1 Rāma’s Divinity
docs.text: In the Bāla and Uttara Kāṇḍas, and in a few passages of the Yuddhakāṇḍa (notably the hymn in which the gods reveal Rāma’s identity after Sītā’s ordeal), Rāma is explicitly an incarnation (avatāra) of Viṣṇu. In the central books he appears mostly as a human hero, unaware of any divine identity. Since Jacobi, many scholars have therefore regarded the divinisation as a later development. Sheldon Pollock has argued instead that the central books already portray Rāma as a divine king of a particular kind, a human being endowed with the qualities of the gods, and that the explicit avatāra passages develop rather than invent this conception (Pollock 1984). Traditional commentators such as Govindarāja read Rāma as fully divine throughout, interpreting his grief and confusion as part of his divine play (līlā); later devotional Rāmāyaṇas such as the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa and Tulsīdās go further, so that the real Sītā is never abducted at all but replaced by an illusory double.

docs.title: 2.15.2 Ethical Themes
docs.text: As the tradition reads it, the Rāmāyaṇa teaches that dharma must be upheld even at great personal cost: Rāma accepts exile rather than let his father break his word, lives as an ascetic in the forest and keeps faith with his ally Sugrīva. Its treatment of conflicts between filial duty, royal duty and duty to a spouse complicates the more schematic presentations of the Dharmaśāstras. Three of its themes proved especially influential. Rāma’s acceptance of Rāvaṇa’s brother Vibhīṣaṇa, against his counsellors’ advice, became for Śrīvaiṣṇava theologians the model of God’s protection of the one who takes refuge (śaraṇāgati). His fidelity to a single wife (ekapatnīvrata) is set against the polygyny of his father. And his order that Rāvaṇa be cremated with honour, since “enmities end with death,” was remembered as a rule of chivalry. Other acts of the hero have been contested from the commentators to the present: the killing of Vālin from hiding, the mutilation of Śūrpaṇakhā, Sītā’s ordeal and banishment, and the killing of Śambūka. Each is discussed once, in Chapter 3 (Sections 3.4, 3.3, 3.6.3 and 3.7.4).

docs.title: 2.16 The Rāmāyaṇa in Southeast Asian Civilisations
docs.text:
The Rāmāyaṇa was adapted and indigenised across Southeast Asia. Its principal Southeast Asian versions — the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa, the Thai Rāmakien, the Khmer Reamker, the Lao Phra Lak Phra Lam, the Burmese Yama Zatdaw, the Malay Hikayat Seri Rama and the Maranao Maharadia Lawana of Mindanao in the southern Philippines — are surveyed in Section 12.2, and their literary sources in Section 12.2.4.

Scholarly Note: The Prambanan Temple Reliefs

The ninth-century Prambanan temple complex in Central Java carries Rāmāyaṇa narrative reliefs on the balustrades of its Śiva temple, continued on the Brahmā temple. They are among the most extensive and accomplished visual narratives of the Rāma story outside India, and they differ in several details from the Old Javanese Kakawin, suggesting that more than one version of the story circulated in Java.

docs.title: 2.17 The Rāmāyaṇa in Music, Art and Nature Writing
2.17.1 The Rāmāyaṇa and Music Traditions
docs.text:
The Rāmāyaṇa describes itself as a song: Vālmīki teaches the poem to Lava and Kuśa, who sing it to the lute at Rāma’s horse sacrifice. The connection between the Rāma story and musical performance has remained close ever since (Table 2.6).

Table 2.6. The Rāmāyaṇa in Indian Musical Traditions Musical Tradition Region Rāmāyaṇa Content and Style Tyāgarāja’s kīrtanas South India Several hundred songs, most addressed to Rāma, by Tyāgarāja (1767–1847), central to the Karnatak repertoire Tulsīdās’s Mānas North India Recitation and singing of the Rāmacaritamānas, in homes, temples and public mānas gatherings Rāmanām saṅkīrtana All India Collective chanting of Rāma’s name, popularised by the sant and bhakti traditions Harikathā / kīrtan South India, Maharashtra Narrative musical discourse combining storytelling, song and exposition of Rāmāyaṇa episodes

The annual Tyāgarāja Ārādhana at Tiruvaiyāru, where musicians gather to sing his compositions together, remains one of the major events of the Karnatak music calendar.

docs.title: 2.17.2 The Rāmāyaṇa in Visual Arts Traditions
docs.text:
From the Gupta-period reliefs at Deogarh to modern calendar art, the Rāma story has been among the subjects most often depicted in South and Southeast Asian art. Besides the traditions in Table 2.7, there are the illustrated Persian Rāmāyaṇas made for the Mughal court and its nobles (Section 12.1.6) and the Mysore school of painting; temple sculpture is discussed further in Section 12.3.

Table 2.7. Major Visual Art Traditions Depicting the Rāmāyaṇa Art Form Region / Period Distinctive Features Pahari miniatures Punjab Hills, 17th–19th c. Lyrical colours, intimate scale, emphasis on Śrīṅgāra and Karuṇa rasas Kalamkari textiles Andhra Pradesh Hand-painted cloth narratives using natural dyes; temple hangings depicting complete Kāṇḍas Pata-chitra scrolls Odisha Long narrative scrolls unrolled during oral recitation; bold outlines, vivid colours Temple sculptures South and Southeast Asia, c. 500–1500 Stone relief panels narrating sequential episodes, from Deogarh (Gupta period) to Prambanan, Angkor Wat and Hampi Tanjore paintings Tamil Nadu, 18th–19th c. Gold-leaf embellishment, jewel inlay, iconic devotional images of Rāma and Sītā Shadow puppetry Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh Leather puppets creating projected narratives; Togalu Gombeyāta tradition

docs.title: 2.17.3 Nature in the Rāmāyaṇa and Ecocritical Readings
docs.text:
Recent “ecocritical” readings have drawn attention to the Rāmāyaṇa’s portrayal of nature. Rivers, forests and mountains are vividly described and often addressed as living beings: Sītā prays to the Gaṅgā, and Rāma, searching for her, questions the trees and animals of the forest. The forests (vana) are the setting of the hermitages of sages, and the Rākṣasas’ attacks on these hermitages provide the epic’s justification for Rāma’s campaign. Such readings are modern interpretations; the epic’s own concern is with dharma and kingship rather than with ecology in the modern sense.

The Vānaras — Hanumān, Sugrīva, Aṅgada and their army — are full participants in Rāma’s struggle. The much-loved story of the squirrel that helped build the bridge by carrying grains of sand, and whom Rāma blessed by stroking its back (leaving the stripes on Indian palm squirrels), is a later folk addition, popular especially in the south.

docs.title: 2.18 Conclusion
docs.text:
For the tradition the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa is the life of the ideal human being, a teaching on dharma embedded in narrative, and a celebration of devotion in the figures of Lakṣmaṇa, Hanumān and Bharata. For literary history it is the ādikāvya, the source of a large family of retellings in many languages and religions. For modern readers it is also a text whose treatment of women, of the forest peoples and of the low-born Śambūka raises questions that its retellers have answered in very different ways. It continues to be retold in every Indian language and art form, and argued over in public, more than two millennia after its composition.

The following chapter examines each of the seven Kāṇḍas in detail, following Rāma’s journey from the palace of Ayodhyā to the banks of the Sarayū, from the joy of birth to the supreme test of kingship.

docs.title: Chapter 3: The Seven Kāṇḍas of the Rāmāyaṇa
docs.text:
rāmo vigrahavān dharmaḥ sādhuḥ satyaparākramaḥ / rājā sarvasya lokasya devānām iva vāsavaḥ // “Rāma is dharma embodied, good, of true valour; king of all the world, as Vāsava (Indra) is of the gods.”

— Mārīca to Rāvaṇa, Rāmāyaṇa 3.35.13 (Critical Edition)

The journey of Rāma as narrated in the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa unfolds across seven books called Kāṇḍas. The word kāṇḍa means “section,” “chapter,” or more literally “stalk” or “joint” — suggesting that each Kāṇḍa is a distinct joint in the larger bamboo stalk of the narrative. Together, these seven Kāṇḍas trace an arc from cosmic joy (the birth of Rāma) through the depths of sorrow (the abduction of Sītā) to the triumph of dharma (the defeat of Rāvaṇa) and the complex aftermath of return (Figure 3.1).

Figure 3.1. The Seven Kāṇḍas of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa: A Narrative Timeline

docs.title: 3.1 Bāla Kāṇḍa: The Book of Childhood
3.1.1 Overview
docs.text: The Bāla Kāṇḍa (“Book of the Child”) has 77 sargas in the southern vulgate (76 in the Critical Edition). It functions both as a prologue to the main narrative and as an account of Rāma’s birth and youth. It also contains the krauñcavadha episode that occasions the composition of the poem — placing the act of creation within the created work itself. Together with the Uttarakāṇḍa, it is generally regarded by scholars as a later frame added to the older core (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 3.1.2 Principal Episodes
docs.text:
• The Sacrifice for Sons: King Daśaratha, longing for sons, performs a horse sacrifice and a rite for progeny with the help of the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. A great being emerges from the sacrificial fire bearing a golden vessel of pāyasa (rice cooked in milk), which Daśaratha distributes among his three queens, Kausalyā, Kaikeyī and Sumitrā.

  • The Birth of the Four Princes: Rāma (born to Kausalyā on the ninth day of the month of Caitra, under the asterism Punarvasu), Bharata (to Kaikeyī), and the twins Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna (to Sumitrā).

  • Viśvāmitra’s Request: The sage Viśvāmitra takes Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to protect his sacrifice from the Rākṣasas. Rāma kills the Rākṣasī Tāṭakā, overcoming his reluctance to kill a woman at the sage’s insistence, and drives off Mārīca.

  • Ahalyā’s Release: In Vālmīki, Ahalyā, cursed by her husband Gautama for her union with Indra, lives invisible in the hermitage, fasting and lying on ashes, until Rāma’s arrival releases her; she receives the princes as guests. The familiar version in which she has been turned to stone and is restored by the touch of Rāma’s foot belongs to later tradition (the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, Tulsīdās). Ahalyā is one of the five women (pañcakanyā) remembered in a popular morning prayer.

  • The Bow at Mithilā: King Janaka has declared that his daughter Sītā, found in a furrow while the field was being ploughed, will be given only to a man who can string the great bow of Śiva — a “bride-price of valour” (vīryaśulka) rather than a choice by the bride. Rāma not only strings but breaks the bow, and the four brothers are married to Sītā, her sister Ūrmilā and their cousins.

docs.title: 3.2 Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa: The Book of Exile
3.2.1 Overview
docs.text: The Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa (“Book of Ayodhyā”, 119 sargas in the southern vulgate, 111 in the Critical Edition) is the second-longest book of the poem and is widely regarded as its most searching treatment of dharma. It confronts the reader with conflicts of duty, loyalty and love within a royal family, and contains some of the epic’s most powerful speeches.

docs.title: 3.2.2 Principal Episodes and Dharmic Themes
docs.text:
• Coronation Preparations: King Daśaratha, growing old, prepares to crown Rāma as Yuvarāja (heir-apparent). The city of Ayodhyā celebrates with great joy.

  • Kaikeyī’s Fatal Demands: Influenced by her scheming maid Mantharā, Queen Kaikeyī invokes two boons Daśaratha had long ago promised her: (1) Bharata to be crowned king, and (2) Rāma to be exiled for fourteen years.

  • Rāma’s Acceptance: Rāma, upon hearing the decree, accepts without a moment’s hesitation. This acceptance encapsulates the Rāmāyaṇa’s understanding of Dharma: a son’s duty to his father’s word supersedes personal happiness.

  • Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā Accompany Rāma: Despite Rāma’s protests, both Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā insist on accompanying him.

  • Bharata’s Devotion: Returning from his maternal grandfather’s home, Bharata discovers his father Daśaratha has died of grief. He refuses the throne and places Rāma’s pādukās (sandals) upon it, ruling as regent until Rāma’s return.

docs.title: 3.3 Araṇya Kāṇḍa: The Book of the Forest
3.3.1 Overview
docs.text: The Araṇya Kāṇḍa (“Book of the Forest”, 75 sargas in the southern vulgate, 71 in the Critical Edition) covers Rāma’s life in the Daṇḍaka forest, his encounters with sages and Rākṣasas, and culminates in the central crisis of the epic: the abduction of Sītā by Rāvaṇa.

docs.title: 3.3.2 Principal Episodes
docs.text:
• Among the Sages of Daṇḍaka: Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa visit the hermitages of the sages Śarabhaṅga, Sutīkṣṇa and Agastya, and Rāma promises to protect the ascetics from the Rākṣasas — a promise Sītā questions, warning him against violence towards those who have not wronged him. After ten years they settle at Pañcavaṭī on the Godavarī.

  • Śūrpaṇakhā: Rāvaṇa’s sister Śūrpaṇakhā approaches Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa amorously and is mocked by both; when she attacks Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, at Rāma’s command, cuts off her nose and ears. The episode, with its mockery and mutilation of a woman of the forest, has been sharply criticised by modern feminist and Dravidian readers.

  • Rāvaṇa’s Conspiracy: Rāvaṇa, after his armies under Khara and Dūṣaṇa have been destroyed, conspires with Mārīca, who takes the form of a golden deer to lure Rāma away.

  • The Abduction of Sītā: With Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa lured away, Rāvaṇa appears as a wandering ascetic and carries Sītā off. The old vulture Jaṭāyu fights Rāvaṇa to protect her and is mortally wounded. (The “line” drawn by Lakṣmaṇa around the hut, the Lakṣmaṇa rekhā, is a later addition not found in Vālmīki.)

  • Rāma’s Grief: Rāma laments Sītā’s absence and questions the trees and animals of the forest — a passage much imitated by later poets.

  • Kabandha and Śabarī: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa free the monster Kabandha from a curse, and he directs them to Sugrīva. At the lake Pampā they are received by Śabarī, an aged female ascetic (śramaṇī) who had served the sages of Mataṅga’s hermitage; she honours Rāma with forest fruits and then ascends to heaven.

In Vālmīki, Śabarī is an ascetic whose name suggests origin among the Śabara forest people. Later devotional versions made her an exemplar of bhakti that transcends caste: the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa and Tulsīdās have Rāma declare that he values devotion above birth, and popular North Indian tradition adds the story that she tasted each berry before offering only the sweetest to Rāma — an act of ritual “pollution” that Rāma accepts with joy. The detail is not found in Vālmīki. Bhakti poets cited Śabarī as proof that love of God outweighs ritual purity, even as the same tradition left the social order largely intact.

docs.title: 3.4 Kiṣkindhā Kāṇḍa: The Book of Alliance
3.4.1 Overview
docs.text: The Kiṣkindhā Kāṇḍa (67 sargas in the southern vulgate, 66 in the Critical Edition) is named after the Vānara kingdom of Kiṣkindhā, traditionally identified with the Hampi region of Karnataka. It narrates Rāma’s alliance with Sugrīva and sets in motion the search for Sītā.

docs.title: 3.4.2 Principal Episodes
docs.text:
• Meeting Hanumān: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa meet Hanumān, minister of the exiled Vānara prince Sugrīva. Rāma is struck by the correctness and eloquence of his speech.

  • Vālin and Sugrīva: Sugrīva had been driven from the kingdom by his elder brother Vālin, who had also taken Sugrīva’s wife Rumā. Rāma helps Sugrīva by shooting Vālin from hiding while the brothers fight (see below).

  • Sugrīva’s Pledge: In return, Sugrīva, now king, pledges his armies to the search for Sītā, though he delays until Lakṣmaṇa angrily reminds him of his promise.

  • The Rainy Season: Rāma spends the rains on Mount Prasravaṇa; his grief is set against celebrated descriptions of the monsoon and of autumn.

  • The Search Parties: Sugrīva dispatches search parties in the four directions, describing the geography of each quarter. The southern party, led by Aṅgada and including Hanumān and Jāmbavat, learns from the vulture Sampāti that Sītā is in Laṅkā.

The Killing of Vālin

The killing of Vālin from hiding has been debated since the commentators. The dying Vālin denounces Rāma at length for attacking a warrior engaged with another, who had done him no wrong. Rāma replies that the land belongs to the Ikṣvākus, so that he, acting for Bharata, may punish wrongdoers; that Vālin had taken his younger brother’s wife, a sin as grave as incest; and that, as a monkey, Vālin could be killed from concealment as kings hunt animals. Commentators such as Govindarāja elaborate these arguments and treat the episode as an instance of the “subtlety of dharma” (dharmasūkṣmatā), and theologians who regard Rāma as the Supreme Being hold that his acts are just by definition. Many readers, ancient and modern, have found the justifications unconvincing; they see in Vālin’s eloquent protest the poem’s own acknowledgment of moral ambiguity, a quality the Mahābhārata develops much further.

docs.title: 3.5.1 Overview
docs.text:
The Sundara Kāṇḍa (“Beautiful Book”, 68 sargas in the southern vulgate, 66 in the Critical Edition) is the most popular book of the Rāmāyaṇa for devotional recitation. It is devoted to Hanumān’s mission to Laṅkā: his leap across the ocean, his search for Sītā, his discovery of her in the Aśoka grove, his conversation with her, and his destruction of the grove and burning of the city.

The meaning of the title, “beautiful,” is uncertain. Popular explanations refer it to Hanumān’s deeds, to the long descriptions of Laṅkā and of the Aśoka grove where Sītā is held, or to the first good news after Sītā’s abduction, which makes the book auspicious to recite.

docs.title: 3.5.2 Principal Episodes
docs.text:
• The Leap: Hanumān leaps across the ocean to Laṅkā, overcoming the tests of Surasā, mother of serpents, and the demoness Siṃhikā.

  • Searching Laṅkā: Hanumān searches the city of Laṅkā at night, and the poet describes its palaces, its women and its defences at length.

  • Finding Sītā: Hanumān locates Sītā in the Aśokavanikā, surrounded by guards and under tremendous pressure to accept Rāvaṇa’s advances. Her steadfast loyalty to Rāma in this extreme trial became, for the tradition, the supreme expression of the ideal of wifely devotion (pātivratya).

  • The Sign of Recognition: Hanumān presents Rāma’s ring as proof of his identity. Sītā gives Hanumān her cūḍāmaṇi (crest jewel) to carry back.

  • Destruction of the Grove: Hanumān wrecks the Aśoka grove and kills many of Rāvaṇa’s warriors, including his son Akṣa, before allowing himself to be captured by Indrajit.

  • Before Rāvaṇa: Brought before Rāvaṇa, Hanumān serves as an ambassador for Rāma, advising the demon king to return Sītā. His tail is set on fire as punishment.

  • Burning of Laṅkā: Hanumān sets the golden city of Laṅkā ablaze with his burning tail — the famous Laṅkā Dahan episode.

docs.title: 3.6 Yuddha Kāṇḍa: The Book of War
3.6.1 Overview
docs.text: The Yuddha Kāṇḍa (“Book of War”, called Laṅkā Kāṇḍa in some versions) is the longest book (128 sargas in the southern vulgate, 116 in the Critical Edition). It narrates the war between Rāma’s Vānara army and Rāvaṇa’s Rākṣasas, culminating in the death of Rāvaṇa, Sītā’s ordeal and the return to Ayodhyā. See Table 3.1.

docs.title: 3.6.2 Major Episodes
docs.text: Table 3.1. Key Episodes of the Yuddha Kāṇḍa Episode Dharmic Significance Vibhīṣaṇa’s Surrender Rāma accepts the enemy’s own brother as an ally despite his counsellors’ doubts; the model of protecting one who seeks refuge (śaraṇāgati) Building of the Setu The Vānaras, directed by Nala, build a causeway across the ocean after Rāma threatens the Ocean, who then appears and advises him Vibhīṣaṇa’s Consecration Rāma consecrates Vibhīṣaṇa as king of Laṅkā as soon as he accepts him Death of Kumbhakarṇa Rāvaṇa’s gigantic brother rebukes him for abducting Sītā but fights for him out of loyalty Indrajit’s Sorcery Rāvaṇa’s son Indrajit (Meghanāda) uses magical weapons to strike down Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who are revived by Garuḍa and by Hanumān’s mountain of herbs; Lakṣmaṇa finally kills him Death of Rāvaṇa After a long duel in which Rāvaṇa’s heads grow back as fast as they are cut off, Rāma kills him with a divine weapon given by Agastya Sītā’s Ordeal Rāma publicly repudiates Sītā; she enters a fire, and Agni restores her unharmed Return to Ayodhyā The return in the aerial car Puṣpaka; reunion with Bharata; coronation

docs.title: 3.6.3 Sītā’s Ordeal by Fire
docs.text:
The episode of Sītā’s ordeal by fire (later called the agniparīkṣā) is among the most debated in the epic. In Vālmīki’s account, Rāma receives Sītā after Rāvaṇa’s death in front of the assembled army and tells her that he fought to avenge the insult to his own honour and lineage, not for her sake; that a woman who has lived in another man’s house cannot be taken back; and that she is free to go wherever she likes, even to Lakṣmaṇa or Vibhīṣaṇa. Sītā answers him with dignity and reproach — he speaks, she says, like a common man to a common woman — and asks Lakṣmaṇa to build a pyre. She enters the fire, the gods appear and reveal Rāma’s divinity, and Agni returns Sītā unharmed, declaring her innocence. Rāma then says that he had never doubted her, but that the test was needed to convince the world.

Interpretations divide sharply:

  • Traditional justifications: Rāma as king was bound by public opinion (lokāpavāda); the ordeal was meant to prove Sītā’s purity beyond doubt for her own sake; and, in devotional readings, the whole episode is divine play. The Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa and Tulsīdās remove much of the sting by having the real Sītā enter the fire for safekeeping before the abduction, so that the ordeal merely retrieves her from Agni and dismisses an illusory double.

  • Literary and textual readings: Several scholars regard the scene, with its revelation of Rāma’s divinity, as belonging to a later layer of the Yuddhakāṇḍa, and many later poets softened or omitted it. Bhavabhūti’s Uttararāmacarita (8th century) is among the earliest works to place Sītā’s suffering, and Rāma’s guilt, at the centre.

  • Feminist and popular criticism: Modern feminist scholars have read the ordeal and the later banishment as expressions of the epic’s control of female sexuality, and studies of audiences show that ordinary listeners, too, have long been troubled by them. Linda Hess has documented the range of Indian responses to “the ideal man’s cruel treatment of his ideal wife,” from defensive explanation to outright rejection; women’s songs in many languages take Sītā’s side against Rāma (Hess 1999; Sutherland 1989; Narayana Rao 1991).
