Table 5.3. Day-by-Day Summary of the Kurukṣetra War Day Kaurava Commander Key Event Notes 1 Bhīṣma Bhagavad Gītā; battle begins Arjuna’s despondency resolved by Kṛṣṇa’s teaching 2–9 Bhīṣma Escalating combat; heavy losses Bhīṣma proves unbeatable; Kṛṣṇa twice threatens to break his vow not to fight 10 Bhīṣma Bhīṣma falls on bed of arrows Brought down by placing Śikhaṇḍin before Arjuna 11–12 Droṇa Droṇa assumes command; attempt to capture Yudhiṣṭhira The teacher fights his own students 13 Droṇa Abhimanyu’s death in the circular formation Several warriors attack one youth 14 Droṇa Arjuna kills Jayadratha; night battle; Ghaṭotkaca killed Fighting continues after dark 15 Droṇa Droṇa killed through deception “Aśvatthāman is dead” — truth used as a weapon 16 Karṇa Karṇa assumes command Inconclusive fighting; Karṇa asks for Śalya as his charioteer 17 Karṇa Karṇa killed by Arjuna Bhīma kills Duśśāsana; Karṇa is shot while freeing his chariot wheel 18 Śalya Śalya killed; Duryodhana defeated The mace duel; the night massacre follows

docs.title: 5.21 The Post-War Parvas: The Price of Victory
docs.text:
The narrative books that follow the war (Sauptika and Strī, and, after the didactic Śānti and Anuśāsana and the Āśvamedhika, the last four books) dwell on its consequences. Victory brings no joy; the victors are left with grief, guilt and a ruined world (Figure 5.3).

Figure 5.3. The Post-War Parvas: From Destruction to Transcendence (the narrative books; the didactic Śānti and Anuśāsana, books 12–13, and the Āśvamedhika, book 14, intervene)

The epic thus ends not with a celebration of triumph but with the transience of worldly glory, which is why Ānandavardhana judged its dominant mood to be tranquillity born of disillusion (Section 1.7).

docs.title: 5.22 Threads and Teachings Across the Parvas
5.22.1 Interconnections Between the Parvas: Narrative Threads
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata is not a linear narrative but a web of themes, prophecies and consequences that span many books. The sage Kiṃdama’s curse on Pāṇḍu in the Ādi Parva determines the divine paternity of the Pāṇḍavas. Draupadī’s humiliation in the Sabhā Parva becomes a driving force behind the war. Śikhaṇḍin’s change of sex, rooted in the story of Ambā told in the Udyoga Parva, determines the fall of Bhīṣma; and Gāndhārī’s curse on Kṛṣṇa after the war (Strī Parva) brings about the destruction of the Yādavas (Mausala Parva).

These threads function as a system of causation in which vows, curses and boons shape later events. They express the epic’s concern with the consequences of action (karman), though the text also leaves much to fate (daiva) and time (kāla), whose relation to human effort its characters repeatedly debate.

docs.title: 5.22.2 The Didactic Parvas: An Encyclopaedia Within an Epic
docs.text:
The Śānti and Anuśāsana Parvas together make up roughly a quarter of the critical text. Bhīṣma, lying on his bed of arrows, discourses on the duties of kings, conduct in times of distress, the nature of the self and the paths to liberation, gifts and observances, and the duties of the social classes and of women (Table 5.4).

Table 5.4. Major Didactic Topics in the Śānti and Anuśāsana Parvas Topic Scope of Discussion Rājadharma Duties of the king, taxation, justice, protection of subjects, appointment of ministers Āpaddharma Conduct during emergencies, when ordinary rules may be modified Mokṣadharma Paths to liberation; early forms of Sāṅkhya, Yoga and Vedāntic thought (Chapter 11) Dānadharma The ethics and merit of gifts, especially to brahmins Strīdharma The duties of wives, notably in the dialogue of Śiva and Umā in the Anuśāsana Parva Varṇadharma The duties of the social classes. Some passages define a brahmin by conduct rather than birth (for example Yudhiṣṭhira’s answer to Nahuṣa in the Āraṇyaka Parva), while many others affirm hereditary hierarchy and the subordination of Śūdras

The didactic books carry out the epic’s claim to be a complete guide to life, and they are also the main evidence for the brahmanical social thought of the period in which it took shape (Sutton 2000; Fitzgerald 2004).

docs.title: Chapter 6: The Bhagavad Gītā
docs.text:
sarvopaniṣado gāvo dogdhā gopālanandanaḥ / pārtho vatsaḥ sudhīr bhoktā dugdhaṃ gītāmṛtaṃ mahat //

— Gītādhyāna 4 (traditional)

The Bhagavad Gītā — the “Song of the Lord” — is the best-known philosophical text of the Hindu tradition and has been translated more often than any other Sanskrit work. Comprising 700 ślokas in 18 chapters in the vulgate, it forms chapters 23–40 of the Bhīṣma Parva of the Mahābhārata in the Critical Edition (25–42 in the vulgate). It records the dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and the warrior Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra, at the moment when the war is about to begin, as reported by Sañjaya to the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra (van Buitenen 1981; Malinar 2007).

A verse of the traditional meditation recited before the Gītā (Gītādhyāna) describes its relation to the Upaniṣads: “All the Upaniṣads are the cows; the milker is Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd’s son; Arjuna is the calf; the wise are the drinkers; the milk is the great nectar of the Gītā.”

docs.title: 6.1 Date and Composition
docs.text: The Gītā is part of the Mahābhārata and cannot be dated independently of it. Most scholars place its composition between the second century BCE and the first century CE, though estimates range from the fifth century BCE to the second century CE (see Table 1.5). It presupposes the major Upaniṣads, early Sāṅkhya and Yoga, and the debates between ritualists and renouncers, and it shares vocabulary with early Buddhism (brahmanirvāṇa, 2.72). Whether it is a single composition has long been debated. From Richard Garbe onwards, some scholars have distinguished an older theistic Sāṅkhya–Yoga core from later Vedāntic and devotional additions (Garbe 1905); Franklin Edgerton defended its unity as a work that deliberately combines several religious approaches; and Angelika Malinar has read it as a carefully constructed argument, developed in stages, that responds to debates about kingship, violence and devotion to a supreme god within the epic itself (Edgerton 1944; Malinar 2007). The tradition, by contrast, regards it as the very words of Kṛṣṇa spoken on the battlefield.

docs.title: 6.2 Context: The Crisis on the Battlefield
docs.text:
As the two armies stand arrayed on the field of Kurukṣetra, Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa, his charioteer, to drive his chariot between the two armies. Seeing his own grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, and friends on the opposing side, Arjuna is overwhelmed by grief and confusion. He puts down his bow, the legendary Gāṇḍīva, and declares that he will not fight.

Arjuna’s Despair — Gītā 1.47

Sanskrit: sañjaya uvāca — evam uktvārjunaḥ saṅkhye rathopastha upāviśat visṛjya saśaraṃ cāpaṃ śokasaṃvignamānasaḥ Translation: “Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna cast aside his bow and arrows, and sat down on the seat of the chariot, his mind overwhelmed with grief.”

This crisis becomes the occasion for Kṛṣṇa’s teaching — a teaching that addresses not only Arjuna’s immediate dilemma (whether a warrior may kill his kin for a just cause) but also broader questions: the nature of the self, the meaning of action, the path to liberation, and the relationship between the individual and the supreme God.

docs.title: 6.3 Structure of the Bhagavad Gītā
docs.text:
A later traditional scheme, popularised by commentators such as Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (16th century), groups the eighteen chapters into three sections of six (ṣaṭkas), associated respectively with action, devotion and knowledge. The scheme is a convenient guide rather than a feature of the text, in which all three themes recur throughout (Figure 6.1):

Figure 6.1. The Three Ṣaṭkas (Hexads) of the Bhagavad Gītā (later traditional scheme)

docs.title: 6.4 The Course of the Argument
docs.text:
Each chapter of the Gītā carries, in the colophons of the manuscripts, a title naming it as a “yoga”; the titles are later than the text and vary slightly between editions. Table 6.1 gives them with the main content of each chapter. The argument itself does not move in straight lines, and the paragraphs below follow its main themes rather than the chapters one by one.

Table 6.1. The Eighteen Chapters of the Bhagavad Gītā Ch. Traditional title Main content 1 Arjunaviṣādayoga Arjuna’s despondency at the sight of his kin 2 Sāṅkhyayoga The immortal self; action without attachment; the person of steady wisdom 3 Karmayoga Action is unavoidable; sacrifice; acting for the welfare of the world 4 Jñānakarmasaṃnyāsayoga The teaching’s lineage; divine descent; inaction in action 5 Karmasaṃnyāsayoga Renunciation as inner detachment 6 Ātmasaṃyamayoga Meditation and the discipline of the mind 7 Jñānavijñānayoga Kṛṣṇa’s lower and higher nature 8 Akṣarabrahmayoga The imperishable; remembering Kṛṣṇa at death 9 Rājavidyārājaguhyayoga The “royal secret”: devotion open to all 10 Vibhūtiyoga Kṛṣṇa’s manifestations in the world 11 Viśvarūpadarśanayoga The vision of the cosmic form 12 Bhaktiyoga Worship of the manifest and the unmanifest; the devotee dear to Kṛṣṇa 13 Kṣetrakṣetrajñavibhāgayoga The field (body and nature) and its knower 14 Guṇatrayavibhāgayoga The three guṇas 15 Puruṣottamayoga The cosmic fig tree; the supreme person 16 Daivāsurasampadvibhāgayoga Divine and demonic dispositions 17 Śraddhātrayavibhāgayoga Faith, food, sacrifice, austerity and gifts by the three guṇas; oṃ tat sat 18 Mokṣasaṃnyāsayoga Renunciation; the duties of the varṇas; surrender

docs.title: 6.4.1 Grief and the Self (Chapters 1–2)
docs.text:
Arjuna’s objections in the first chapter are themselves arguments from dharma: killing kinsmen destroys families, the destruction of families ruins their traditions and their women, and the “mixing of varṇas” that follows sends the ancestors to hell. Kṛṣṇa’s first answer is metaphysical. The self that Arjuna fears to kill cannot be killed:

The Immortal Ātman — Gītā 2.20

Sanskrit: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācit nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ ajo nityaḥ śāśvato ’yaṃ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre Translation: “The Ātman is never born, nor does it ever die. Having once existed, it does not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, changeless, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.”

To this he adds an argument from Arjuna’s station — for a warrior nothing is better than a righteous war (2.31) — and an argument from honour. The second chapter then introduces the two ideas that the rest of the poem develops: action performed without attachment to its results, and the person of “steady wisdom” (sthitaprajña) who has achieved it (Section 6.8).

docs.title: 6.4.2 Action without Attachment (Chapters 3–6)
docs.text:
No one can remain without acting, Kṛṣṇa argues in the third chapter, and even the body cannot be maintained without action; the question is how to act without being bound (Section 6.12). Action offered as sacrifice, done because it ought to be done and without desire for its fruit, does not bind, and the wise act “for the holding together of the world” (lokasaṅgraha). In the fourth chapter Kṛṣṇa reveals that he taught this discipline long ago, and that he himself takes birth in age after age:

The Avatāra Declaration — Gītā 4.7–8

Sanskrit: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṃ sṛjāmy aham paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṃ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām dharma-saṃsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge Translation: “Whenever Dharma declines and Adharma prevails, O Bhārata, I manifest Myself. For the protection of the righteous, the destruction of the wicked, and the establishment of Dharma, I appear in every age.”

The fifth chapter reconciles action and renunciation: true renunciation is inner detachment, not abstention from activity. The sixth describes the practice of meditation — the seat, the posture, the control of a mind that Arjuna finds as hard to restrain as the wind (6.34) — and assures Arjuna that no sincere effort is lost.

docs.title: 6.4.3 God and Devotion (Chapters 7–12)
docs.text:
The middle chapters turn from the self to God. Kṛṣṇa describes his lower nature, the material world, and his higher nature, the life within it; he is the taste in water, the light of sun and moon, the syllable Oṃ in the Vedas (7.8). Those who remember him at death go to him (chapter 8). The ninth chapter offers what it calls the royal secret, a devotion that requires no learning or wealth:

The Universal Offering — Gītā 9.26

Sanskrit: patraṃ puṣpaṃ phalaṃ toyaṃ yo me bhaktyā prayacchati tad ahaṃ bhakty-upahṛtam aśnāmi prayatātmanaḥ Translation: “Whoever offers Me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water with devotion — that offering of the pure-hearted, I accept.”

After listing his manifestations in the world (chapter 10), Kṛṣṇa grants Arjuna a divine eye and shows him his cosmic form (chapter 11; Section 6.11; Figure 6.2). In the twelfth chapter Arjuna asks whether those who worship Kṛṣṇa in manifest form or those who meditate on the unmanifest Imperishable are the better yogis; both reach him, Kṛṣṇa answers, but the path of the unmanifest is harder for embodied beings, and he describes the devotee who is dear to him (12.13–20).

Figure 6.2. Arjuna before Kṛṣṇa’s cosmic form (viśvarūpa, Gītā 11): an Indian miniature painting. The school, date and collection of the original are not recorded in the source of this reproduction Anonymous miniature painting, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 6.4.4 Knowledge, the Guṇas and Surrender (Chapters 13–18)
docs.text:
The last six chapters return to analysis. The thirteenth distinguishes the “field” — body, mind and the whole of material nature — from its “knower,” the self. The fourteenth explains how the three guṇas of nature, sattva (clarity), rajas (passion) and tamas (inertia), bind the self, and chapters 16–18 classify faith, food, sacrifice, austerity, gifts, knowledge, action and happiness by the same three qualities (Table 6.2). Between them, the fifteenth chapter uses the image of the cosmic fig tree (aśvattha), with roots above and branches below, for the world from which the self must cut itself free, and names Kṛṣṇa the supreme person beyond both the perishable and the imperishable.

Table 6.2. The Three Guṇas and Their Manifestations Aspect Sattva Rajas Tamas Nature Illumination, purity Activity, passion Inertia, darkness Binds through Attachment to happiness, knowledge Attachment to action, desire Negligence, sleep, indolence Knowledge Sees the One in all Sees multiplicity Clings to one partial view Action Duty without attachment Driven by desire for results Undertaken from delusion Food Fresh, wholesome, nourishing Excessively spicy, sour, hot Stale, impure, leftover Charity Given without expectation Given with expectation of return Given with contempt Worship Of the gods (devas) Of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas Of ghosts and spirits (17.4) Destiny Ascent (ūrdhva) Middle regions Descent (adho)

The eighteenth chapter recapitulates: true renunciation is the renunciation of the fruits of action, the four varṇas have their duties by nature (18.41–48), and the poem closes with what many commentators regard as its final message:

The Supreme Message — Gītā 18.66

Sanskrit: sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja ahaṃ tvā sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ Translation: “Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in Me alone. I shall free you from all sins; do not grieve.”

What “abandoning all dharmas” means has been among the most debated questions in the commentaries: Śaṅkara takes it as the renunciation of all action in favour of knowledge, while Rāmānuja and the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition read the verse as the charter of surrender (prapatti) to God. Arjuna, at any rate, declares his confusion gone and takes up his bow.

docs.title: 6.5 The Gītā and the Social Order
docs.text:
The Gītā’s teaching on action is framed by the social order of varṇa. Kṛṣṇa declares that he created the four varṇas “according to the division of qualities and actions” (guṇakarmavibhāgaśaḥ, 4.13), urges Arjuna that “one’s own duty (svadharma), even imperfectly done, is better than another’s duty well performed” (3.35, 18.47), and in Chapter 1 has Arjuna fear that war will cause the “mixing of varṇas” through the corruption of women. At the same time the Gītā opens the path of devotion to all: “even those of sinful birth, women, Vaiśyas and Śūdras” reach the highest goal by taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa (9.32).

These passages have been read in sharply different ways. Modern Hindu interpreters such as Gandhi and Radhakrishnan emphasised “qualities and actions” and argued that the Gītā grounds varṇa in aptitude rather than birth; the classical commentators, however, generally understood svadharma as the duty of one’s hereditary station. B. R. Ambedkar, in his unfinished essay “Krishna and His Gita,” read the text as a defence of the four-varṇa order (Ambedkar 1987), and the phrase “of sinful birth” in 9.32 shows the hierarchical assumptions within which its universalism operates. A balanced reading recognises both the text’s offer of liberation through devotion to all, and its affirmation of a social order that most modern readers reject (Davis 2015; Minor 1986).

docs.title: 6.6 The Three Yogas: Ranked or Integrated?
docs.text:
Modern readers often take the Gītā to teach three paths — action (karma), devotion (bhakti) and knowledge (jñāna) — and to combine them in a single discipline, in which each person, according to temperament (svabhāva), emphasises one path while practising the others (Figure 6.3). This synthesising reading became widespread through modern interpreters from Vivekananda and Aurobindo onwards, and it has a basis in the text’s habit of moving between the three themes. It is, however, one interpretation among several. The classical commentators ranked the paths. Śaṅkara held that knowledge alone liberates, and that action purifies the mind only as a preparation for it; Rāmānuja made devotion, culminating in surrender, the supreme means, with knowledge and action as its auxiliaries; and Tilak argued in the twentieth century that the Gītā’s real teaching is energetic action, which knowledge and devotion serve (Section 6.13). The text itself speaks in 3.3 of two disciplines, knowledge for the Sāṅkhyas and action for the yogins, and in 13.24 of meditation, Sāṅkhya and action; it nowhere sets out three paths as a scheme, and the division of its chapters into three hexads is likewise later (Figure 6.1) (Sharma 1986; Malinar 2007).

Figure 6.3. The three yogas of the Bhagavad Gītā as a modern synthesising reading presents them. Classical commentators ranked the paths differently (see text)

docs.title: 6.7 Commentarial Traditions
docs.text:
The Bhagavad Gītā has attracted more commentaries than any other Sanskrit text. Because the Vedānta schools counted it among their three foundational texts (prasthānatraya), with the Upaniṣads and the Brahmasūtra, each school’s founder or leading teacher wrote on it, interpreting it through the lens of his own philosophy. The commentaries reveal not a single “correct” reading but a spectrum of perspectives (Sharma 1986). Table 6.3 lists the principal classical commentaries; the modern interpretations of Tilak, Aurobindo and Gandhi are discussed in Section 6.13.

Table 6.3. Major Commentaries and Interpretations of the Bhagavad Gītā Commentator School Period Key Emphasis Śaṅkara Advaita Vedānta c. 8th c. CE Earliest surviving commentary; knowledge of the non-dual Self as the means of liberation; action as preparatory Abhinavagupta Kashmir Śaivism late 10th–early 11th c. Gītārtha­saṅgraha, a Śaiva non-dual reading of the Kashmir recension Rāmānuja Viśiṣṭādvaita 11th–12th c. Devotion (bhakti) and surrender as the supreme means; God both transcendent and immanent Madhva Dvaita 13th c. Eternal distinction between God and souls; devotion to Viṣṇu Jñāneśvara (Jñānadeva) Vārkarī sant tradition 1290 Jñāneśvarī, a Marathi verse commentary that made the Gītā accessible to non-Sanskrit audiences Śrīdhara Svāmin Advaita with devotion c. 14th c. Subodhinī, widely read Madhusūdana Sarasvatī Advaita with devotion 16th c. Gūḍhārtha­dīpikā; reconciles knowledge and devotion

docs.title: 6.8 Key Philosophical Concepts of the Gītā
docs.text: The Bhagavad Gītā introduces and develops several foundational philosophical concepts that have shaped Indian thought for over two millennia.

docs.title: 6.8.1 The Concept of Sthitaprajña (One of Steady Wisdom)
docs.text:
Among the Gītā’s most influential passages is its portrait of the sthitaprajña, the person of steady wisdom. Arjuna asks (2.54) what the marks of such a person are: how does he speak, sit and walk? Kṛṣṇa’s answer (2.55–72) became a classic portrait of the liberated person, much loved by Gandhi, who had these verses recited daily at his ashram prayers (Table 6.4).

The Sthitaprajña — Gītā 2.55

prajahāti yadā kāmān sarvān pārtha manogatān / ātmany evātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthitaprajñas tadocyate // Translation: “When a person abandons all desires that enter the mind, Pārtha, and is content in the self by the self alone, then he is said to be of steady wisdom.”

Table 6.4. Characteristics of the Sthitaprajña (Gītā 2.54–72) Quality Description from the Gītā Freedom from desire When all desires of the heart are abandoned, the self finds satisfaction in the Self alone (2.55) Equanimity Undisturbed by sorrow, free from longing for pleasure, beyond attachment, fear and anger (2.56) Non-attachment Neither welcoming good fortune nor resenting bad (2.57) Withdrawal of senses Like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs, he withdraws the senses from their objects (2.58) Inner stability Like the ocean, which remains unmoved though rivers constantly flow into it (2.70)

Gītā 2.70 — The Ocean Metaphor

āpūryamāṇam acalapratiṣṭhaṃ samudram āpaḥ praviśanti yadvat / tadvat kāmā yaṃ praviśanti sarve sa śāntim āpnoti na kāmakāmī // Translation: “As waters enter the ocean, which is ever being filled yet stays unmoved in its place, so the one whom all desires enter attains peace — not the one who desires desires.”

docs.title: 6.8.2 The Concept of Yoga in the Gītā
docs.text:
The Gītā uses the term yoga in a broad sense. While the word literally means “union” or “yoking,” the Gītā employs it to mean any disciplined path that leads to spiritual realisation. Each chapter is called a “Yoga” — indicating that every teaching, from action to devotion to knowledge, is a complete path of spiritual discipline.

Kṛṣṇa’s Definition of Yoga — Gītā 2.48

Sanskrit: yogasthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā dhanañjaya siddhy-asiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṃ yoga ucyate Translation: “Established in Yoga, perform actions, O Dhanañjaya, abandoning attachment, remaining the same in success and failure. This evenness of mind is called Yoga.”

docs.title: 6.8.3 The Doctrine of Avatāra (Divine Descent)
docs.text: The Gītā’s teaching (4.7–8) that Kṛṣṇa takes birth “in age after age” whenever dharma declines became the charter of the doctrine of divine descent. The Gītā does not itself use the noun avatāra, which becomes standard in the Purāṇas, where lists of ten or more descents of Viṣṇu develop (Chapter 7). The idea of recurring descent distinguishes this theology from those, such as Christianity, that speak of a single incarnation.

docs.title: 6.9 The Gītā’s Influence on World Thought
docs.text:
The Bhagavad Gītā is the most widely translated text of the Indian tradition. Its global career began with Charles Wilkins’s English translation of 1785, and its modern prominence owes much to colonial-era translators, Indian nationalists and Western seekers alike (Davis 2015). See Table 6.5.

Table 6.5. Global Reception of the Bhagavad Gītā Thinker / Movement Period Key Engagement with the Gītā Charles Wilkins 1785 First English translation; opened the Gītā to the Western world August Wilhelm Schlegel 1823 Edition with Latin translation; important for German Indology Ralph Waldo Emerson 1840s Praised it in his journals; shaped American Transcendentalism Henry David Thoreau 1854 In Walden: “In the morning I bathe my intellect in the stupendous and cosmogonal philosophy of the Bhagvat Geeta” T. S. Eliot 1941 Allusion to Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna in “The Dry Salvages” (Four Quartets) J. Robert Oppenheimer 1965 Recalled in a television interview that Gītā 11.32 (“Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds”) came to his mind at the 1945 Trinity test Aldous Huxley 1944–45 Introduction to the Prabhavananda–Isherwood translation; The Perennial Philosophy Christopher Isherwood 1944 Translation with Swami Prabhavananda

docs.title: 6.10 The Gītā and Other Gītās in the Mahābhārata
docs.text:
The Bhagavad Gītā is not the only “Gītā.” The Śānti Parva itself contains several short “songs” (the Piṅgalā, Bodhya, Hārīta, Vṛtra and Haṃsa Gītās), and later Purāṇas and independent works imitated the form (Table 6.6):

Table 6.6. The Gītā Tradition: Other Gītās in Indian Literature Gītā Source Speaker Primary Teaching Bhagavad Gītā Bhīṣma Parva Kṛṣṇa Karma, Bhakti, Jñāna; integral liberation Anu Gītā Aśvamedhika Parva Kṛṣṇa Yoga, meditation, Brahman knowledge Uddhava Gītā Bhāgavatam 11 Kṛṣṇa Final teachings before departure; renunciation Īśvara Gītā Kūrma Purāṇa Śiva Knowledge of the self and yoga; Śiva as supreme Brahman Devī Gītā Devī Bhāgavata Devī Śākta philosophy; feminine divine Gaṇeśa Gītā Gaṇeśa Purāṇa Gaṇeśa Gaṇeśa as supreme reality Avadhūta Gītā Independent Dattātreya Radical Advaita; formless realisation Aṣṭāvakra Gītā Independent Aṣṭāvakra Pure non-dual consciousness

docs.title: 6.11 The Viśvarūpa Darśana: Analysis of the Cosmic Vision
docs.text:
In chapter 11 Arjuna, granted a “divine eye,” sees the whole universe within the body of God: all beings and worlds, creation and destruction at once, and the warriors of both armies rushing into Kṛṣṇa’s flaming mouths. Theologians have drawn several lessons from the vision (Figure 6.4). It presents the supreme reality as a personal being of terrifying power and beauty rather than an abstract principle. Arjuna sees the other gods — Brahmā, Śiva, the Ādityas, the Rudras — within Kṛṣṇa’s form, which readers took as a statement of the unity of the divine. Kṛṣṇa identifies himself with time as the destroyer of worlds (11.32). And Arjuna, unable to bear the vision, begs him to return to his familiar human form, a confession of the limits of human understanding.

Kṛṣṇa as Time — Gītā 11.32

Sanskrit: kālo ’smi lokakṣayakṛt pravṛddho lokān samāhartum iha pravṛttaḥ / ṛte ’pi tvā na bhaviṣyanti sarve ye ’vasthitāḥ pratyanīkeṣu yodhāḥ // Translation: “I am Time, grown mature, the destroyer of worlds, engaged here in annihilating the worlds. Even without you, all these warriors arrayed in the opposing ranks shall cease to be.”

Figure 6.4. Three Levels of Divine Revelation in the Bhagavad Gītā (a Vedāntic reading)

docs.title: 6.12 The Gītā’s Theory of Action: Karma Yoga in Detail
docs.text:
The Gītā’s treatment of action is often considered its most important philosophical contribution. Chapter 3 establishes that action is inescapable — even the maintenance of the body requires it (3.8). The Vedic ritualists held that ritual action brings its rewards; the renouncers held that all action binds and must be abandoned for liberation. The Gītā proposes a third way: action performed as duty, offered to God, without attachment to its fruits, does not bind.

Later commentators systematised this teaching with the terms sakāma karma (action driven by desire for results) and niṣkāma karma (action without such desire); the Gītā itself speaks of action (karman), wrong action (vikarman) and non-action (akarman), and says that the wise see non-action in action (4.17–18). See Table 6.7.

Table 6.7. The Gītā’s Classification of Action Type Sanskrit Term Characteristics and Outcome Desire-driven Action Sakāma Karma Performed for personal gain; binds the soul to the cycle of Saṃsāra Selfless Action Niṣkāma Karma Performed as duty without attachment to results; purifies the mind and leads to liberation Inaction in Action Akarma The enlightened state where the wise perceive non-action even in the midst of action (4.18) Prohibited Action Vikarma Action contrary to Dharma; produces negative karmic consequences

Kṛṣṇa’s teaching that “your right is to action alone, never to its fruits” (karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana, 2.47) is the most frequently quoted line of the Gītā. It does not counsel indifference to outcomes so much as freedom from the anxiety and bondage that attachment to results creates.

Lokasaṅgraha: Action for the Welfare of the World

In Chapter 3, Kṛṣṇa introduces the concept of lokasaṅgraha — action for the holding together of the world (3.20, 3.25). He himself, though he has nothing to gain in the three worlds, continues to act, because if he ceased to act people would follow his example and the world would fall into confusion (3.22–24). The concept turns the discipline of action into a social ethic, and modern interpreters from Tilak onwards made it central to their readings.

docs.title: 6.13 The Gītā in the Indian Freedom Movement
docs.text:
The Bhagavad Gītā played a large part in India’s struggle for independence, serving as a source of moral strength and philosophical justification for leaders across the political spectrum. B. G. Tilak’s Gītā Rahasya (1915) interpreted the Gītā as a call to selfless action in the service of the nation, arguing that Kṛṣṇa’s message was not one of world-renunciation but of active engagement. Revolutionary nationalists in Bengal and Maharashtra also drew on the Gītā, sometimes to justify political violence.

Gandhi, who first read the Gītā in Edwin Arnold’s English translation as a law student in London, made it the centre of his daily religious practice. His interpretation emphasised non-attachment (anāsakti) and read the battle of Kurukṣetra as an allegory of the inner struggle between good and evil — a reading that allowed him to derive non-violence from a text set on a battlefield. Aurobindo’s Essays on the Gita, serialised in his journal Arya between 1916 and 1920, presented a synthetic reading integrating action, knowledge and devotion into a philosophy of spiritual evolution. Gandhi set out his own reading in Anāsaktiyoga (written 1929, published 1930) and called the Gītā his “mother.” Vinoba Bhave’s Talks on the Gita, given in prison in 1932, drew from it a practical ethic of simplicity and service, and S. Radhakrishnan’s translation and commentary (1948) presented it as a work of universal philosophical significance (Minor 1986; Davis 2015).

docs.title: 6.13.1 The Gītā and Comparative Philosophy
docs.text: The Bhagavad Gītā’s content invites comparison with other philosophical traditions. Its treatment of duty has been compared with Kant’s ethics, though it grounds duty not in abstract reason but in the nature of the self and its relation to God and to the social order. Its psychology of desire and attachment parallels Buddhist analysis while offering a theistic framework that Buddhism rejects. Its counsel to act without attachment to results has been compared to Stoic philosophy, particularly Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius. Such comparisons are modern analogies, useful for readers but not evidence of historical influence.

docs.title: Chapter 7: The Eighteen Mahāpurāṇas
docs.text:
The Purāṇas form a very large and varied body of Sanskrit literature. The word purāṇa means “ancient” (from purā, “formerly”), and these texts gather cosmological, genealogical, mythological, ritual, philosophical and devotional lore. Recited by professional paurāṇikas to mixed audiences, they became the main vehicle of Hindu religious teaching for people who had no access to the Veda. Their inclusiveness had limits — they frequently reaffirm the hierarchy of varṇa and the subordination of women and Śūdras — but they also preserved, in their māhātmyas, the gods and holy places of communities far beyond the brahmanical elite (Rocher 1986).

The tradition assigns the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas (Great Purāṇas) a combined total of 400,000 ślokas (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.13), four times the traditional size of the Mahābhārata. The printed texts do not always match the traditional figures: the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, for example, claims 23,000 verses but has about 6,000–7,000.

docs.title: 7.1 Definition and Pañca Lakṣaṇa
docs.text:
As discussed in Chapter 1, a Purāṇa is defined by its five characteristics (Pañca Lakṣaṇa):

  1. Sarga — Primary creation (cosmogony)

  2. Pratisarga — Secondary creation, dissolution, and re-creation

  3. Vaṃśa — Genealogies of gods, sages, and Prajāpatis

  4. Manvantara — Cosmic epochs presided over by Manus

  5. Vaṃśānucarita — Genealogical histories of royal dynasties (Sūrya Vaṃśa and Candra Vaṃśa)

However, the actual content of the Mahāpurāṇas far exceeds these five topics. They also contain:

  • Dharmaśāstra: Law, ethics, duties of different stages of life

  • Tīrtha Māhātmya: Glorification of sacred places

  • Vrata Kathā: Stories and methods of religious observances

  • Dāna Vidhi: Methods and merits of charitable giving

  • Stotras and Prayers: Hymns to various deities

  • Yoga and Meditation: Spiritual practices

  • Jyotiṣa and Kalpa: Astrology and rituals

  • Technical subjects: Architecture, medicine, music, iconography

docs.title: 7.2 Dating and Formation of the Purāṇas
docs.text:
Purāṇa as a category of lore is old: the Atharvaveda, the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and the Chāndogya Upaniṣad mention itihāsa and purāṇa as subjects of recitation, and the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra (3rd–2nd century BCE) cites a “Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.” None of the extant Purāṇas, however, survives in a form that can be dated to that period. The most influential attempt to date them was made by R. C. Hazra, whose Studies in the Purāṇic Records on Hindu Rites and Customs (1940) and Studies in the Upapurāṇas (1958–63) analysed the chapters on ritual and law that the Purāṇas share with the Dharmaśāstras. Hazra placed the oldest layers of the Mārkaṇḍeya, Vāyu, Brahmāṇḍa, Viṣṇu and Matsya Purāṇas in roughly the 3rd–5th centuries CE, and most others later, some well into the second millennium (Hazra 1940, 1958–1963).

One useful anchor is the account of the “future” kings of the Kali age, which several Purāṇas narrate as prophecy. Pargiter showed that these lists are reasonably accurate for the Nandas, Mauryas, Śuṅgas, Kāṇvas and Āndhras (Sātavāhanas), and that they end with the early Guptas ruling along the Gaṅgā — which suggests that this material was given its form in about the fourth century CE (Pargiter 1913). The much longer genealogies of the Solar and Lunar dynasties for the earlier ages are another matter: historians regard them as legendary constructions that cannot be used to build a chronology (Thapar 2013).

Ludo Rocher’s survey stresses a more fundamental point. The Purāṇas were never fixed texts. Each was recited, expanded, abridged and reworked over centuries, so that a date can be given only for a particular version or section, not for “the” Purāṇa; the same Purāṇa may exist in quite different recensions, and the classical definition of five characteristics describes an ideal rather than the actual contents (Rocher 1986). Two examples illustrate this fluidity. A Nepalese manuscript of a Skandapurāṇa dated 810 CE contains a text quite unlike the vast printed Skanda Purāṇa, much of whose material is later (Adriaensen et al. 1998); and the Pratisargaparvan of the printed Bhaviṣya Purāṇa contains “prophecies” of medieval and even British rule, added in the early modern period.

Within this history, scholars distinguish an older layer concerned with cosmology, genealogy and smārta ritual from later sectarian reworkings that exalt Viṣṇu, Śiva or the Goddess, and a steady incorporation of local deities, pilgrimage places and festivals through māhātmya chapters. The Purāṇas were thus one of the principal means by which brahmanical religion absorbed and reshaped regional traditions. Jains, too, wrote their own purāṇas — notably Jinasena’s Ādipurāṇa (9th century) — presenting a Jain universal history (Doniger 1993).

The Nepalese Skandapurāṇa shows what the earliest sectarian Purāṇas looked like before later expansion. Probably composed in the sixth or seventh century, it is a Śaiva text that tells the myths of Śiva and Pārvatī and of their son Skanda, and it maps a network of Śaiva holy places across northern India, with Vārāṇasī prominent among them. Peter Bisschop’s study of its sacred geography connects these sites with the Śaiva ascetic communities, above all the Pāśupatas, who were active at them, and so shows a Purāṇa recording the institutions of a particular religious movement at a particular time (Adriaensen et al. 1998; Bisschop 2006). The same approach to the Goddess Purāṇas and to the Upapurāṇas of the regions is described in Chapter 8.

docs.title: 7.3 The Tripartite Classification
docs.text:
The eighteen Mahāpurāṇas are classified in the Padma Purāṇa (a Vaiṣṇava text) into three groups of six according to the three guṇas: sāttvika (associated with Viṣṇu), rājasa (associated with Brahmā) and tāmasa (associated with Śiva). The scheme reflects its Vaiṣṇava origin: the Śaiva Purāṇas are ranked lowest (Figure 7.1).

Figure 7.1. The Padma Purāṇa’s Classification of the Eighteen Mahāpurāṇas

Scholarly Note: On Classification

The assignment of Purāṇas to groups varies across sources, and so does the list of eighteen itself: some lists include the Vāyu Purāṇa and others the Śiva Purāṇa, and several texts claim Mahāpurāṇa status. Moreover, every Purāṇa contains hymns and teachings related to several deities. The classification should therefore be understood as indicating predominant emphasis, not exclusive focus.

docs.title: 7.4 The Eighteen Mahāpurāṇas: A Mnemonic Verse
docs.text:
A traditional mnemonic verse lists all eighteen:

Mnemonic for the 18 Mahāpurāṇas (Devībhāgavata 1.3.2)

Sanskrit: ma-dvayaṃ bha-dvayaṃ caiva bra-trayaṃ va-catuṣṭayam a-nā-pa-liṅ-ga-kū-skāni purāṇāni pṛthak pṛthak Expansion: Ma(tsya), Mā(rkaṇḍeya); Bha(viṣya), Bhā(gavata); Bra(hma), Bra(hmāṇḍa), Bra(hmavaivarta); Vā(mana), Va(rāha), Vi(ṣṇu), Vā(yu) (other lists have Śiva in place of Vāyu); A(gni), Nā(radīya), Pa(dma), Liṅ(ga), Ga(ruḍa), Kū(rma), Ska(nda)

docs.title: 7.5 Detailed Study of Each Mahāpurāṇa
docs.text: The figures for ślokas given below are the traditional counts (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.13); printed texts often differ considerably.

docs.title: 7.5.1 Brahma Purāṇa
docs.text: Traditionally assigned 10,000 ślokas and placed first in most lists, the Brahma Purāṇa is also called the Ādi Purāṇa, “the first Purāṇa.” The printed text (some 245 chapters) opens with cosmogony and genealogy but consists largely of māhātmyas of Puruṣottama (Jagannātha at Purī), of Koṇārka and of the Godāvarī; despite its traditional primacy it is a late compilation that draws heavily on other Purāṇas.

docs.title: 7.5.2 Padma Purāṇa
docs.text: The Padma Purāṇa (traditionally 55,000 ślokas) is a Vaiṣṇava work whose division into five or six books (khaṇḍas) differs between recensions (one arrangement has Sṛṣṭi, Bhūmi, Svarga, Pātāla and Uttara Khaṇḍas). It is rich in tīrtha māhātmyas and contains the classification of the Purāṇas by the three guṇas discussed above.

docs.title: 7.5.3 Viṣṇu Purāṇa
docs.text: The Viṣṇu Purāṇa is often regarded as the most “model” Purāṇa — the one that most closely follows the five-characteristic scheme. Its core is usually placed in the mid-first millennium CE (Hazra suggested c. 4th century CE), making it one of the oldest extant Purāṇas (Hazra 1940). Narrated by Parāśara to his disciple Maitreya in six books (aṃśas), it gives a systematic account of creation, cosmography, cyclic time and the royal genealogies, and in its fifth book a life of Kṛṣṇa that builds on the Harivaṃśa. Tradition assigns it 23,000 ślokas; the printed text has about 6,000–7,000.

docs.title: 7.5.4 Śrīmad Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Bhāgavatam)
docs.text:
The Bhāgavata Purāṇa is the most widely read and most often commented upon of the Purāṇas. Most current scholarship dates it to c. 9th–10th century CE and locates its composition in South India, where its intense, emotional devotion to Kṛṣṇa shows the influence of the Tamil Āḻvār poets; Hazra had earlier argued for the 6th century (Hardy 1983; Bryant 2003). Traditionally of 18,000 ślokas in twelve books (skandhas; Section 7.9), it is narrated by Śuka to King Parīkṣit in the seven days before his death, and describes itself as the ripened fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree of the Veda:

The Ripened Fruit — Bhāgavata 1.1.3

Sanskrit: nigamakalpataror galitaṃ phalaṃ śukamukhād amṛtadravasaṃyutam pibata bhāgavataṃ rasam ālayaṃ muhur aho rasikā bhuvi bhāvukāḥ Translation: “O connoisseurs of spiritual bliss! Drink again and again the nectar of the Bhāgavatam — the ripened fruit fallen from the wish-fulfilling tree of Vedic literature, made sweeter by flowing from the lips of Śukadeva.”

docs.title: 7.5.5 Śiva Purāṇa
docs.text: The Śiva Purāṇa (traditionally 24,000 ślokas), which some lists name in place of the Vāyu Purāṇa, is in its printed form divided into seven collections (saṃhitās): Vidyeśvara, Rudra, Śatarudra, Koṭirudra, Umā, Kailāsa and Vāyavīya. It narrates the myths of Śiva and Pārvatī, the origin of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas (Section 8.4) and the forms of Śaiva worship and practice.

docs.title: 7.5.6 Skanda Purāṇa
docs.text:
The largest of all Purāṇas by traditional count (81,100 ślokas). The printed text, divided into seven khaṇḍas (Māheśvara, Vaiṣṇava, Brahma, Kāśī, Āvantya, Nāgara and Prabhāsa) or into saṃhitās in another arrangement, is a vast and late collection of tīrtha māhātmyas, among them the Kāśī Khaṇḍa, the Revā Khaṇḍa and the Setu Māhātmya. An earlier and very different Skandapurāṇa survives in Nepalese manuscripts, one of them dated 810 CE (Section 7.2). All eighteen are summarised in Table 7.1; the remaining Mahāpurāṇas are described after it.

Table 7.1. Summary of All Eighteen Mahāpurāṇas Purāṇa Ślokas (trad.) Group Distinctive Content Brahma 10,000 Rājasa Creation, Puruṣottama (Jagannātha) Māhātmya Padma 55,000 Sāttvika Tīrthas, classification of Purāṇas Viṣṇu 23,000 Sāttvika Model Purāṇa, cyclic cosmology Śiva (or Vāyu) 24,000 Tāmasa Śiva myths, Jyotirliṅgas Bhāgavata 18,000 Sāttvika Kṛṣṇa’s life, devotion, philosophy Nāradīya 25,000 Sāttvika Vratas, tīrthas, summaries of the other Purāṇas Mārkaṇḍeya 9,000 Rājasa Devī Māhātmya; Hariścandra; Madalasā Agni 15,400 Tāmasa Encyclopaedic: grammar, medicine, law, architecture Bhaviṣya 14,500 Rājasa “Prophecies” (many very late), vratas, sun worship Brahmavaivarta 18,000 Rājasa Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa; a late text Liṅga 11,000 Tāmasa Origin of the liṅga, Śiva worship Varāha 24,000 Sāttvika Rescue of the earth, Vaiṣṇava rites Skanda 81,100 Tāmasa Largest; tīrtha māhātmyas Vāmana 10,000 Rājasa Vāmana avatāra; Śiva and Viṣṇu Kūrma 17,000 Tāmasa Kūrma avatāra, Īśvara Gītā Matsya 14,000 Tāmasa Matsya avatāra, dynasties, iconography and temples Garuḍa 19,000 Sāttvika After-death rites (Pretakalpa), gems, medicine Brahmāṇḍa 12,000 Rājasa Lalitā cult; cosmic egg; the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa is attributed to it Total 400,000

docs.title: 7.5.7 Vāyu and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas
docs.text: The Vāyu and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas share long passages, often word for word, in their accounts of creation, cosmography, the Manvantaras and the royal genealogies, and most scholars regard them as two later recensions of what was once a single text. Willibald Kirfel used this shared material, together with parallels in the Viṣṇu, Matsya and other Purāṇas, to reconstruct an early common core that corresponded closely to the five characteristics, and the Vāyu is usually counted among the oldest of the extant Purāṇas (Kirfel 1927; Rocher 1986). Both texts were later expanded in different directions. The Vāyu acquired, among other additions, a Gayāmāhātmya on the ancestral rites at Gayā; the Brahmāṇḍa came to include the Lalitopākhyāna, the charter narrative of the Śrīvidyā cult of the goddess Lalitā, from which the widely recited Lalitāsahasranāma is taken, as well as the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (Table 7.1).

docs.title: 7.5.8 Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa
docs.text: The Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (traditionally 9,000 ślokas) is among the most varied of the Purāṇas, and it begins with the Mahābhārata. Jaimini, a pupil of Vyāsa, has puzzled over four questions that the epic leaves unanswered: why the Lord took a human birth; how Draupadī came to be the wife of five husbands; how Balarāma atoned for killing a brahmin; and why Draupadī’s five sons died young and unmarried. The sage Mārkaṇḍeya sends him to four wise birds in the Vindhya mountains, and their answers, which lead from one story to another, make up the first part of the text. Among them is the story of King Hariścandra, who for the sake of truthfulness loses his kingdom, sells his wife and son and serves at a cremation ground. Another is the story of Queen Madālasā, who sings to her infant sons lullabies teaching that the self is pure and untouched by the body, so that they grow up to renounce the world, until her husband asks her to raise the last as a king. The later chapters, cast as a dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and a pupil, cover the Manvantaras and include the Devī Māhātmya (Section 7.7). Because it lacks a strong sectarian bias and shows little of the later tīrtha literature, the Mārkaṇḍeya is generally placed, at least in its earlier parts, among the older Purāṇas (Hazra 1940).

docs.title: 7.5.9 Matsya and Kūrma Purāṇas
docs.text:
The Matsya Purāṇa (traditionally 14,000 ślokas) is narrated by the fish incarnation of Viṣṇu to Manu, whom it rescues from the flood; the story first appears in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, and the Purāṇa makes it the frame of an encyclopaedic text. Its account of the dynasties of the Kali age is one of the fullest, and Pargiter relied on it heavily (Pargiter 1913). It also contains extended chapters on iconography and temple building (Section 7.15), on vows and gifts, and on the sanctity of Prayāga and Vārāṇasī.

The Kūrma Purāṇa (traditionally 17,000 ślokas) takes its name from Viṣṇu’s tortoise incarnation, but in its present form it is largely a Śaiva text, teaching the Pāśupata form of Śaiva devotion and yoga. Its best-known section, the Īśvara Gītā, is a dialogue in which Śiva instructs the sages in a manner closely modelled on the Bhagavad Gītā (Section 6.10). Hazra argued that the text was originally a Vaiṣṇava work of the Pāñcarātra tradition and was later reworked by Pāśupata redactors, which would explain the tension between its title and its teaching (Hazra 1940).

docs.title: 7.5.10 Liṅga, Vāmana and Varāha Purāṇas
docs.text: The Liṅga Purāṇa (traditionally 11,000 ślokas) is a Śaiva manual of myth, cosmology and ritual organised around the liṅga as the form of Śiva beyond form. It tells the myth of the column of fire whose top Brahmā and whose base Viṣṇu cannot find, which establishes Śiva’s supremacy over both and which became a favourite subject of temple sculpture as Liṅgodbhava; it also contains Pāśupata teachings on yoga and on the worship of the liṅga. The Vāmana Purāṇa (traditionally 10,000 ślokas), despite its Vaiṣṇava name, gives as much space to Śiva and the Goddess as to Viṣṇu, and is rich in the sacred geography of Kurukṣetra and the Sarasvatī. The Varāha Purāṇa (traditionally 24,000 ślokas) is narrated by Viṣṇu as the boar to the Earth he has raised from the waters; it is concerned largely with Vaiṣṇava ritual and vows, and includes a long glorification of Mathurā.

docs.title: 7.5.11 Garuḍa, Bhaviṣya, Nāradīya and Brahmavaivarta Purāṇas
docs.text:
The Garuḍa Purāṇa (traditionally 19,000 ślokas) is the Purāṇa most often heard in Hindu homes today, though only in part. Its Pretakalpa or Pretakhaṇḍa, in which Viṣṇu tells Garuḍa what befalls the dead, describes the journey of the departed through the realm of Yama, the hells awaiting particular sins and the rites that sustain the dead person until he joins the ancestors; in much of North India it is recited during the days of mourning after a death. The rest of the text is a compendium, with sections on gems, medicine, law and polity.

The Bhaviṣya Purāṇa (traditionally 14,500 ślokas) is an extreme example of Purāṇic fluidity. Its oldest parts deal with vows and with the worship of the sun, and they preserve the legend of Kṛṣṇa’s son Sāmba, who is cured of leprosy by the sun and brings Maga priests from Śākadvīpa to serve the sun temple he founds, an account that reflects the arrival of Iranian sun priests in northern India. Its later sections, especially the Pratisargaparvan, contain “prophecies” of medieval and colonial history added in the early modern period (Section 7.2).

The Nāradīya (Nārada) Purāṇa (traditionally 25,000 ślokas) is chiefly a Vaiṣṇava manual of vows and pilgrimage, but it is also valuable to historians for its table of contents of the eighteen Purāṇas, which summarises the topics each was believed to contain and so allows comparison with the texts as printed. The Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa (traditionally 18,000 ślokas), in four books (Brahma, Prakṛti, Gaṇeśa and Kṛṣṇajanma), is in its present form a late text, perhaps of eastern India, which presents Kṛṣṇa as the supreme being dwelling in his heaven of Goloka and Rādhā as his eternal power and consort (Section 7.10) (Rocher 1986).

docs.title: 7.6 The Purāṇas as a Knowledge Repository
docs.text: Besides cosmology, genealogy and law, the Purāṇas preserve material from many fields of traditional learning, often in digest form: the geography of the continents (dvīpas) and of the pilgrimage places, the building of temples and the making of images, medicine, astronomy and the calendar, music, dance and poetics, and summaries of Sāṅkhya, Yoga and Vedānta. The Agni Purāṇa (Section 7.13) is the extreme case of this encyclopaedism.

docs.title: 7.7 The Devī Māhātmya
docs.text:
The Devī Māhātmya (also known as the Durgā Saptaśatī or Caṇḍī Pāṭha), embedded in chapters 81–93 of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa and usually dated c. 6th century CE, is the foundational text of Śākta theology. Its thirteen chapters are traditionally reckoned as seven hundred mantras, hence the name Saptaśatī, “the seven hundred”; the printed text has substantially fewer full verses, and the traditional total is reached by counting the units of recitation in a particular way (Coburn 1984, 1991). The text presents the Goddess as the supreme power underlying all reality, who takes form to destroy the demons that threaten the gods. Its place in Śākta and Tantric worship is discussed in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama. It narrates three great victories:

  1. Madhu and Kaiṭabha: The Goddess as Yoganidrā withdraws from Viṣṇu so that he can wake and slay the two demons

  2. Mahiṣāsura: The Goddess, formed from the combined energies of the gods, slays the buffalo demon

  3. Śumbha and Niśumbha: The Goddess and her emanations, including Kālī and the Seven Mothers, destroy the demon brothers and their generals

docs.title: 7.7.1 The Three Episodes of the Devī Māhātmya
docs.text:
Later tradition associates the three episodes with three forms of the Goddess and with the three guṇas (Table 7.2):

Table 7.2. The Three Caritas of the Devī Māhātmya Carita Chapters Battle Traditional association Prathama 1 Madhu and Kaiṭabha Mahākālī; tamas Madhyama 2–4 Mahiṣāsura Mahālakṣmī; rajas Uttama 5–13 Śumbha and Niśumbha Mahāsarasvatī; sattva

Devī Māhātmya 11.10 (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 91.9)

sarvamaṅgalamāṅgalye śive sarvārthasādhike / śaraṇye tryambake gauri nārāyaṇi namo ’stu te // Translation: “Auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, benevolent one, accomplisher of every aim, giver of refuge, three-eyed Gaurī, Nārāyaṇī, homage to you.”

docs.title: 7.7.2 The Commentarial Tradition on the Devī Māhātmya
docs.text:
The Devī Māhātmya has inspired a rich commentarial tradition, reflecting its importance across multiple Śākta lineages:

  1. Bhāskararāya (18th century): the Guptavatī, which interprets the text in the light of Śrīvidyā Tantric practice.

  2. Other commentaries printed in traditional editions include the Śāntanavī and the Nāgojībhaṭṭī.

  3. The text is also accompanied in ritual recitation by ancillary hymns and mantras (the kavaca, argalā and kīlaka), which reflect its use in Tantric worship.

docs.title: 7.8 Daśāvatāra — The Ten Avatāras in the Purāṇas
docs.text:
The Purāṇas present the doctrine of divine descent (avatāra) in several forms. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (1.3) lists twenty-two descents of Viṣṇu and adds that they are innumerable; the familiar list of ten (daśāvatāra) became standard in the later first millennium and is celebrated in Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda (12th century). Lists differ, notably in including either Balarāma or the Buddha (Table 7.3; Figure 7.2):

Table 7.3. The Ten Descents of Viṣṇu (Daśāvatāra) in the Common List No. Avatāra Form Purpose 1 Matsya Fish Rescue of the Vedas during the great flood 2 Kūrma Tortoise Support for Mount Mandara during Samudra Manthana 3 Varāha Boar Rescue of the Earth from the cosmic ocean 4 Narasiṃha Man-Lion Protection of Prahlāda, destruction of Hiraṇyakaśipu 5 Vāmana Dwarf Brāhmaṇa Subduing of Bali’s sovereignty through three steps 6 Paraśurāma Warrior sage Restraining the Kṣatriya power 7 Rāma Prince of Ayodhyā Destruction of Rāvaṇa; the ideal reign 8 Kṛṣṇa Cowherd and Yādava prince Destruction of Kaṃsa and the oppressive kings; the Gītā 9 Buddha (or Balarāma) Teacher In some Purāṇas Viṣṇu takes the form of the Buddha to mislead the demons with false doctrine; Jayadeva praises him for compassion and for ending animal sacrifice 10 Kalki Future warrior Destruction of Adharma at end of Kali Yuga Figure 7.2. Relief panels on the outer wall of the Vidyāśaṅkara temple at Śṛṅgeri, Karnataka, built in the mid-fourteenth century under the early Vijayanagara kings. The fish avatāra (Matsya) occupies the second niche from the left, among other Vaiṣṇava figures; the photograph shows only part of the temple’s series of avatāras Photo: Mashalti, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 7.9 The Bhāgavata Purāṇa: Literary Excellence and Commentarial Tradition
docs.text: The literary quality and the theology of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa made it the most commented-upon Purāṇic text and the scriptural foundation of the Kṛṣṇa devotion of Vallabha, Caitanya and many others. Its twelve books are summarised in Table 7.4.

docs.title: 7.9.1 The Twelve Skandhas: Structure and Content
docs.text: Table 7.4. The Twelve Skandhas of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam Skandha Theme Chapters Key Content 1 The setting 19 Vyāsa’s despondency; Nārada’s instruction; Parīkṣit’s curse and preparation for death 2 Meditation and creation 10 Meditation on the cosmic form; outline of creation 3 Creation 33 Vidura and Maitreya; Kapila’s teaching to his mother Devahūti; Varāha 4 Creation continued 31 Dakṣa’s sacrifice; Dhruva; Pṛthu 5 Cosmography 26 Ṛṣabha; Jaḍa Bharata; the structure of the universe 6 Devotion and sin 19 Ajāmila; Vṛtra 7 Devotion 15 Prahlāda; Narasiṃha 8 Manvantaras 24 Gajendra’s release; churning of the ocean; Vāmana 9 Dynasties 24 Solar and Lunar dynasties; the story of Rāma 10 Kṛṣṇa 90 Kṛṣṇa’s life in Vraja, Mathurā and Dvārakā — the heart of the text 11 Departure 31 Uddhava Gītā; destruction of the Yādavas 12 The Kali age 13 Kali Yuga prophecies; summary; phalaśruti

docs.title: 7.9.2 The Commentarial Tradition on the Bhāgavatam
docs.text:
The Bhāgavata Purāṇa has attracted more commentaries than perhaps any other Purāṇic text. Each major Vaiṣṇava ācārya has written a commentary interpreting the text through his own philosophical lens (Table 7.5):

Table 7.5. Major Commentaries on the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam Commentator Period School Commentary Name & Approach Śrīdhara Svāmin c. 14th c. Advaita with devotion Bhāvārtha­dīpikā — harmonises devotion with Advaita; the most influential commentary Madhva 13th c. Dvaita Bhāgavata­tātparya­nirṇaya — dualist theology Vallabha late 15th–early 16th c. Śuddhādvaita Subodhinī — Puṣṭimārga interpretation Jīva Gosvāmin 16th c. Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava Kramasandarbha and the Ṣaṭsandarbha — Caitanyite theology Viśvanātha Cakravartin c. 1700 Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava Sārārtha­darśinī — rasa-centred analysis

Scholarly Note: The Authorship and Date of the Bhāgavata

The tradition holds the Bhāgavata to be Vyāsa’s crowning work, composed after the Mahābhārata to resolve the dissatisfaction he still felt — a frame the text itself supplies (1.4–7). In early modern Indian polemics some critics, objecting to its authority, claimed that the thirteenth-century grammarian Vopadeva, who wrote digests of the Bhāgavata, was its real author; that claim is not accepted by modern scholars, since the text is clearly older, and the academic dating rests instead on its language, theology and relation to Tamil devotion (see above) (Hardy 1983; Rocher 1986).

docs.title: 7.9.3 The Tenth Skandha: The Heart of the Bhāgavatam
docs.text:
The Tenth Skandha, comprising 90 chapters and nearly 4,000 ślokas, narrates the life of Kṛṣṇa — from his birth in Kaṃsa’s prison to his life as a cowherd in Vraja, his slaying of Kaṃsa and his rule at Dvārakā. Its account of Kṛṣṇa’s childhood and of his love-play with the cowherd women (gopīs), above all the rāsalīlā (10.29–33), has inspired a vast body of art, music, dance, poetry and devotional practice (Bryant 2003). Its theology and its treatment of the cowherd women are discussed in Section 7.10.

The Rāsa Līlā — Bhāgavatam 10.33.39

Sanskrit: vikrīḍitaṃ vrajavadhūbhir idaṃ ca viṣṇoḥ śraddhānvito ’nuśṛṇuyād atha varṇayed yaḥ bhaktiṃ parāṃ bhagavati pratilabhya kāmaṃ hṛd-rogaṃ āśv apahinoty acireṇa dhīraḥ Translation: “One who faithfully hears or describes the divine play of Viṣṇu with the young women of Vraja attains supreme devotion to the Lord. Being sober-hearted, such a person quickly drives away the heart’s disease of lust.”

docs.title: 7.10 The Bhāgavata as Literature and Theology
docs.text: The previous section described the Bhāgavata’s structure and its commentators. This section considers the text itself: where and when it was composed, how it is written, what it teaches about God and devotion, and how it treats the cowherd women whose love for Kṛṣṇa became the model of devotion for much of India.

docs.title: 7.10.1 Date, Place and Language
docs.text:
Most scholars place the Bhāgavata in the ninth or tenth century CE, in South India. The case for a southern origin, set out most fully by Friedhelm Hardy, rests on three kinds of evidence. The text knows the Tamil country well and gives it a special place: in the eleventh book (11.5.38–40) it says that in the Kali age devotees of Nārāyaṇa will be found here and there, but in great numbers in the Draviḍa land, where the Tāmraparṇī, the Kṛtamālā (Vaigai), the Payasvinī, the Kāverī and “the great river that flows west” run, and that those who drink their waters are mostly devotees of Vāsudeva. Its devotion has the emotional intensity, and especially the theme of the beloved’s absence, that Tamil Vaiṣṇava poetry had developed from the sixth century onwards in the hymns of the Āḻvārs (Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā). And several episodes have close parallels in Tamil devotional poetry and ritual: the vow that the herders’ daughters keep to the goddess Kātyāyanī in the hope of winning Kṛṣṇa as husband (10.22), for example, resembles the girls’ vow (pāvai nōṉpu) of the Tamil month of Mārkaḻi celebrated in Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai. Hardy concluded that the Bhāgavata was the work of brahmin Vaiṣṇavas who rendered the devotion of the Āḻvārs into the prestige language of Sanskrit and the authoritative form of a Purāṇa (Hardy 1983).

Other scholars argue for an earlier date. Dennis Hudson read the sculptural programme of the Vaikuṇṭha Perumāḷ temple at Kāñcīpuram, built under the Pallava king Nandivarman II in the later eighth century, as following the Bhāgavata closely, which would require the text to have existed by then (Hudson 2008); Edwin Bryant reviewed this evidence and suggested that the text may be older still and need not be southern at all (Bryant 2002). Critics reply that sculptors could draw on narratives without a written text before them. The latest possible date is firmer: by the thirteenth century Vopadeva was writing digests of the Bhāgavata and Madhva was commenting on it as scripture.

Whatever its date, the Bhāgavata is written in a deliberately old-fashioned Sanskrit. It uses Vedic verb forms and vocabulary that had long fallen out of use, and its first verse, which begins by defining the absolute as “that from which the birth and so on of this world proceed” (janmādy asya yataḥ), echoes both the second aphorism of the Brahmasūtra and the meditative formula of the Gāyatrī. J. A. B. van Buitenen called this its “archaism”: a conscious claim to Vedic authority by a text that presents itself as the ripened fruit of the Veda (1.1.3; Section 7.5) (van Buitenen 1966). The language is also unusually rich in poetic ornament, especially in the tenth book, which reads in places like court poetry (kāvya) rather than Purāṇic narrative.

docs.title: 7.10.2 Kṛṣṇa Himself and Devotion beyond Liberation
docs.text:
The Bhāgavata’s theology can be stated in two of its own propositions. The first comes at the end of its list of Viṣṇu’s descents (1.3): “these are portions or partial manifestations of the Supreme Person, but Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself” (kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam, 1.3.28). Where the Viṣṇu Purāṇa had made Kṛṣṇa a descent of Viṣṇu (Section 4.9), the Bhāgavata inverts the relation: Kṛṣṇa is the source, and the other descents derive from him. Later Kṛṣṇa-centred schools, above all the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas of Bengal, made this verse the cornerstone of their theology.

The second proposition is that devotion (bhakti) is the highest goal, higher even than liberation. The supreme dharma, the text declares in its opening book, is that from which devotion to the Lord arises, devotion “without motive and without interruption” (ahaituky apratihatā, 1.2.6). In Kapila’s teaching to his mother (3.29.13), the Lord says that his devotees will not accept any of the forms of liberation — residence in his world, equal power, proximity, likeness of form, or even union — if it is offered without the opportunity to serve him. Prahlāda, the child devotee of the seventh book, lists nine forms of devotion that later manuals adopted as a standard scheme: hearing about Viṣṇu, singing his praise, remembering him, serving his feet, worship, salutation, servitude, friendship and self-surrender (7.5.23–24).

The Bhāgavata does not reject the non-dualist language of the Upaniṣads; it frequently describes the Lord as the one consciousness in which the world appears, and Śrīdhara Svāmin could read it as compatible with Advaita (Table 7.5). But it subordinates knowledge to love. In the tenth book Uddhava, Kṛṣṇa’s learned friend, is sent from Mathurā to console the cowherd women with a teaching on the self; he ends by praising them, and wishes he might be born as a shrub or creeper in Vṛndāvana touched by the dust of their feet (10.47.61), having found in their longing a devotion that his learning lacked.

docs.title: 7.10.3 The Cowherd Women and the Rāsa
docs.text:
The episode that made the Bhāgavata the scripture of Kṛṣṇa devotion is the rāsapañcādhyāyī, the “five chapters on the rāsa dance” (10.29–33). On an autumn night Kṛṣṇa plays his flute in the forest, and the women of Vraja leave their husbands, children and household tasks to go to him. He first tells them to go home, since a woman’s duty lies with her husband; they reply that he is the self of all beings and the true object of every duty. He dances with them, but when they become proud of his favour he vanishes, taking one of them with him; when she too becomes proud, he leaves her. The women search the forest, ask the trees and creepers whether they have seen him, act out his exploits in their distraction, and finally sing the lament known as the Gopīgīta (10.31). When he reappears he forms the circle of the rāsa, multiplying himself so that each woman finds him at her side (10.33.3).

The text anticipates the moral objection. King Parīkṣit asks how Kṛṣṇa, who came to protect dharma, could consort with other men’s wives (10.33.26–28). Śuka answers that the transgressions of the powerful do not taint them, as fire is not polluted by what it consumes, and that others must never imitate such conduct, even in thought (10.33.29–30); he adds that the herders felt no resentment, for by Kṛṣṇa’s power each believed his wife had remained at his side (10.33.37). The theologians who followed went further. The women’s love, they argued, was free of selfish desire, because it sought only Kṛṣṇa’s pleasure, and its very defiance of social rules showed that it surpassed every other obligation. Gauḍīya theologians long debated whether the women should be understood as Kṛṣṇa’s own (svakīyā) or as belonging to others (parakīyā), and the second, more daring view prevailed in later Bengal. Modern readers have also noted the limits of this freedom: the women’s agency is real within the story, but it is defined entirely by their longing for a male god, and the text insists that it is not a model for social conduct (Schweig 2005; Gupta and Valpey 2013).

The theme of separation (viraha) is at least as important as union. The women’s search in the forest, their lament, and above all the “song to the bee” (bhramaragīta) of the forty-seventh chapter, in which a woman takes a bee for a messenger from the absent Kṛṣṇa and rebukes it, make longing itself the highest form of love. This is the point at which Hardy located the Tamil inheritance most clearly, for Āḻvār poets such as Nammāḻvār and Āṇṭāḷ had already sung of God in the voice of a woman waiting for an absent lover (Hardy 1983).

docs.title: 7.10.4 Rādhā’s Absence
docs.text:
Readers who know Kṛṣṇa through later poetry, painting and dance are often surprised that the Bhāgavata never names Rādhā. Nor do the Harivaṃśa or the Viṣṇu Purāṇa. The favoured woman whom Kṛṣṇa leads away in the rāsa chapters is anonymous; the other women say of her that she must have worshipped the Lord well, since he has left them all for her (10.30.28). Later commentators, especially in the Gauḍīya tradition, heard in the word ārādhitaḥ (“worshipped”) a hidden reference to Rādhā, and identified her with this unnamed favourite.

Rādhā is known outside the Purāṇas well before she appears in them. A verse of the Prakrit anthology attributed to Hāla, the Gāhāsattasaī, already mentions her, and verses on Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa are quoted in Sanskrit works on poetics from about the ninth century. In Tamil the Āḻvārs celebrate a favourite cowherd girl of their own, Nappiṉṉai, whom Kṛṣṇa wins by subduing seven bulls; Hardy argued that she belongs to the same pastoral tradition, though the two figures cannot simply be identified. Rādhā becomes central in Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda (12th century) and in the later Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa, and through the theologies of Nimbārka, Caitanya and their followers she came to be worshipped as Kṛṣṇa’s own power and eternal consort (Hardy 1983). The Gītagovinda and the vernacular Rādhā poetry are treated in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

docs.title: 7.10.5 The Bhāgavata in the Regional Languages
docs.text: No other Purāṇa was so widely retold. The tenth book in particular was rendered or adapted in almost every Indian language: by Pōtana in Telugu (15th century), by Śaṅkaradeva and his circle in Assamese, by Jagannātha Dāsa in Odia (16th century), and in the Braj songs of Sūrdās; Eknāth’s Marathi commentary on the eleventh book and Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri’s Sanskrit Nārāyaṇīyam (1586), a condensation of the whole text in about a thousand verses, are only the best known of many works devoted to it. These retellings, discussed in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā, made the Bhāgavata the common source of Kṛṣṇa devotion from Assam to Kerala, and its seven-day public recitation (Section 8.14) remains a widespread form of Purāṇic performance.

docs.title: 7.11 The Purāṇic Cosmological Framework
docs.text: The Mahāpurāṇas, particularly the Viṣṇu, Bhāgavata and Vāyu Purāṇas, describe the structure, origin, maintenance and dissolution of the universe in great detail.

docs.title: 7.11.1 The Cosmic Cycles: Sarga and Pratisarga
docs.text:
The Purāṇic cosmology is fundamentally cyclic. The universe undergoes repeated cycles of creation (Sarga), maintenance (Sthiti), and dissolution (Pralaya). These cycles operate at multiple scales:

Table 7.6. Purāṇic Time Scales Unit Duration (human years) Description Kṛta (Satya) Yuga 1,728,000 Dharma stands on four feet Tretā Yuga 1,296,000 Dharma on three feet; age of Rāma in tradition Dvāpara Yuga 864,000 Dharma on two feet; age of the Bhārata war in tradition Kali Yuga 432,000 Dharma on one foot; the present age Mahāyuga 4,320,000 One cycle of four Yugas Manvantara 306,720,000 Reign of one Manu (71 Mahāyugas) Kalpa 4,320,000,000 One day of Brahmā (1,000 Mahāyugas; 14 Manvantaras with their junctions) Brahmā’s life 311,040,000,000,000 100 years of Brahmā (each year of 360 days and nights)

The yuga figures are in “divine years” in the oldest sources and were later converted into human years by multiplying by 360; the scheme is a theological and cosmological framework, not an empirical chronology.

docs.title: 7.11.2 The Structure of the Cosmos: Brahmāṇḍa
docs.text:
Figure 7.3. The Fourteen Lokas of the Purāṇic Cosmos (in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa’s scheme the three worlds perish at each dissolution, the upper three endure and Maharloka lies between)

The Mahāpurāṇas present a cosmological vision of great scale. The Purāṇic earth is a disc with Mount Meru at its centre, surrounded by seven concentric continents (dvīpas) separated by seven oceans, each of a different substance (salt water, sugar-cane juice, wine, clarified butter, curds, milk and fresh water); India (Bhāratavarṣa) lies in the southern part of the innermost continent, Jambūdvīpa. Above the earth rise the upper worlds to Satyaloka, below it the seven nether regions down to Pātāla. Time, as described above, is measured in vast cycles of yugas, manvantaras and kalpas. Indian astronomers from Āryabhaṭa onward retained the yuga framework for calculation while quietly abandoning much of the Purāṇic geography; the tension between the two cosmologies is itself an important chapter in Indian intellectual history. Purāṇic cosmography and its relation to astronomical geography are treated in detail in Volume 21, Bhūgola. See Figure 7.3.

docs.title: 7.11.3 The Manvantara System
docs.text:
The Purāṇas describe fourteen Manvantaras in each Kalpa, each presided over by a Manu, along with specific Devas, Saptarṣis, and an Avatāra of Viṣṇu. The present Manvantara is the seventh, presided over by Vaivasvata Manu (also called Śrāddhadeva), son of Vivasvān (the Sun).

The Fourteen Manus

The fourteen Manus of the present Kalpa are: Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, Vaivasvata (the current Manu), Sāvarṇi, Dakṣa-sāvarṇi, Brahma-sāvarṇi, Dharma-sāvarṇi, Rudra-sāvarṇi, Raucya (Deva-sāvarṇi), and Bhautya (Indra-sāvarṇi). Each Manu establishes Dharma anew for the beings of his epoch.

docs.title: 7.12 Comparative Study of Purāṇic Narratives
docs.text: The same narrative often appears in several Purāṇas with significant variations, which reflect different theological perspectives and devotional emphases (Table 7.7).

docs.title: 7.12.1 The Creation Narrative Across Purāṇas
docs.text: Table 7.7. Variations in the Creation Narrative Purāṇa Creation Narrative Emphasis Viṣṇu Purāṇa Viṣṇu as the supreme cause; creation through Nārāyaṇa’s will; systematic Pañca Lakṣaṇa Bhāgavata Purāṇa Creation as divine līlā; lists of Viṣṇu’s descents (1.3); emphasis on Bhakti as the purpose of creation Śiva Purāṇa Śiva as the uncaused cause; creation through Śakti and Śiva’s will Brahmavaivarta Kṛṣṇa as the supreme cause; creation through Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa’s combined power Brahmāṇḍa The cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) as the primary metaphor; detailed Kalpa cycles Devī Bhāgavata Devī as the ultimate reality; creation proceeds from the Goddess

docs.title: 7.12.2 The Samudra Manthana: A Multi-Purāṇic Comparison
docs.text: The churning of the ocean (samudramanthana) is first told in the Ādiparvan of the Mahābhārata and briefly in the Bālakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa, and is retold in several Purāṇas, including the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (Book 1) and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Book 8). The core narrative is consistent — gods and demons churn the ocean using Mount Mandara as the churning stick and the serpent Vāsuki as the rope, Viṣṇu as a tortoise supports the mountain, Śiva drinks the poison that first emerges, and Viṣṇu, as the enchantress Mohinī, cheats the demons of the nectar — but the occasion, the list of treasures that emerge (often fourteen) and the theological emphasis vary. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa frames the churning as a consequence of the sage Durvāsas’s curse on Indra and gives prominence to the emergence of Śrī-Lakṣmī; the Bhāgavata stresses Viṣṇu’s grace and his several forms in the episode.

docs.title: 7.13 The Agni Purāṇa: An Encyclopaedia of Knowledge
docs.text:
The Agni Purāṇa, a compilation of the later first millennium CE, is less a narrative than a compendium of digests on a wide range of subjects:

  1. Vyākaraṇa (Grammar): A digest of Sanskrit grammar

  2. Chandaḥśāstra (Prosody): All major Sanskrit metres

  3. Alaṅkāra Śāstra (Poetics): Theories of literary composition

  4. Dharmaśāstra (Law): Inheritance, property, marriage, judicial procedure

  5. Āyurveda (Medicine): Diseases and remedies, including the treatment of horses and elephants

  6. Jyotiṣa (Astronomy/Astrology): Planetary movements, horoscopy

  7. Dhanur Veda (Military Science): Weapons, formations, fortification

  8. Śilpa Śāstra (Architecture & Iconography): Temple construction, image-making

  9. Rāja Nīti (Political Science): Governance, diplomacy, statecraft

  10. Kośa (Lexicography): Synonyms and technical terminology

docs.title: 7.14 Modern Scholarly Engagement with the Mahāpurāṇas
docs.text: The modern academic study of the Purāṇas began in the nineteenth century with European Indologists and has since grown into a major field of research encompassing textual criticism, literary analysis, historical reconstruction, and comparative religion.

docs.title: 7.14.1 The Critical Edition Projects
docs.text: The All-India Kashiraj Trust (Varanasi) has published critical editions of several Purāṇas (among them the Vāmana, Kūrma and Varāha), and a Groningen team has been editing the early Skandapurāṇa. The Ancient Indian Tradition and Mythology series (Motilal Banarsidass) has published English translations of most of the Mahāpurāṇas (Table 7.8).

docs.title: 7.14.2 Key Scholarly Contributions
docs.text: Table 7.8. Major Scholars and Their Contributions to Purāṇa Studies Scholar Contribution F. E. Pargiter The Purāṇic lists of the Kali-age dynasties (The Purāṇa Text of the Dynasties of the Kali Age, 1913) and Ancient Indian Historical Tradition (1922) R. C. Hazra Dating and interrelation of the Purāṇas through their ritual and legal chapters (1940; Studies in the Upapurāṇas, 1958–63) Ludo Rocher The Purāṇas (1986) in A History of Indian Literature — the standard survey, stressing the fluidity of the texts Cornelia Dimmitt and J. A. B. van Buitenen Classical Hindu Mythology: A Reader in the Sanskrit Purāṇas (1978) (Dimmitt and Buitenen 1978) Peter Bisschop Early Śaivism and the Skandapurāṇa (2006): the early Skandapurāṇa and Śaiva sacred geography C. Mackenzie Brown The Triumph of the Goddess (1990): the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa Kunal Chakrabarti Religious Process (2001): the Bengal Upapurāṇas and regional tradition Friedhelm Hardy Viraha-Bhakti (1983): the South Indian background of the Bhāgavata Thomas B. Coburn Devī-Māhātmya: The Crystallization of the Goddess Tradition (1984)

docs.title: 7.15 The Purāṇas and Temple Culture
docs.text:
The Mahāpurāṇas, particularly the Agni and Matsya Purāṇas, contain prescriptions for temple architecture, iconography (pratimālakṣaṇa) and ritual procedure (pūjāvidhi), including the consecration of images (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), that overlap with the Śilpaśāstras and Āgamas. The Matsya Purāṇa provides one of the earlier systematic Purāṇic treatments of image-making, specifying iconographic attributes, proportions and materials.

This connection between Purāṇic literature and temple building is reflected in the symbolism attributed to Hindu temples: the tower (śikhara or vimāna) is often said to represent Mount Meru, and the sanctum (garbhagṛha) the “womb” or cave where the deity dwells. The temples’ sculptural programmes, in turn, are largely illustrations of Purāṇic myths (Table 7.9).

Table 7.9. Purāṇic Sources for Temple Arts and Sciences Purāṇa Contribution to Temple Culture Agni Purāṇa Temple architecture, Vāstu principles, consecration rituals, iconographic standards Matsya Purāṇa Image-making, temple types, proportional systems for sculpture Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa Painting (the Citrasūtra), music, dance and the theory of rasa Skanda Purāṇa Sthala Māhātmyas (glorification of sacred places), temple legends

docs.title: 7.16 The Purāṇas and Indian Historical Consciousness
docs.text:
Colonial scholars often dismissed the Purāṇas as mere mythology, but their genealogical sections (vaṃśānucarita) have long been used as historical sources. Pargiter’s Ancient Indian Historical Tradition (1922) argued that the king-lists preserved genuine memories reaching back into the early first millennium BCE (Pargiter 1922); as noted above (Section 7.2), historians now accept the Kali-age lists from the Nandas to the early Guptas as broadly corroborated but regard the earlier genealogies as legendary constructions shaped by the brahmins who compiled them (see also Section 1.1).

The lists of peoples (janapadas) in the geographical chapters correspond broadly to known historical geography, and the laments of the Kali-age chapters about Śūdra kings, heretics and the breakdown of varṇa have been read as reflecting brahmin anxieties in periods of foreign and non-brahmanical rule. Above all, the Purāṇas document the religious history of their own times: the rise of image worship, temple religion, pilgrimage and devotional theism.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Upapurāṇas and Sthala Purāṇas — Minor Purāṇas and Sacred Place Histories
docs.text: Beyond the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas lies a vast secondary layer of Purāṇic literature: the Upapurāṇas (subsidiary Purāṇas) and the Sthala Purāṇas or Māhātmyas (accounts of the sanctity of particular places). These texts, long neglected in academic scholarship, are of great importance for understanding the lived religious landscape of South Asia — its sacred geography, local cults, temple histories and regional traditions (Hazra 1958–1963; Rocher 1986).

docs.title: 8.1 The Upapurāṇas — An Overview
docs.text: The term upapurāṇa means “subsidiary Purāṇa.” Tradition holds that there are eighteen Upapurāṇas, mirroring the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, but the lists given in different texts disagree, and well over a hundred works call themselves Upapurāṇas. R. C. Hazra’s Studies in the Upapurāṇas (1958–63) remains the basic survey; he showed that many of these texts are late (often from the second millennium CE), regional, and closely tied to particular sects or cults (Hazra 1958–1963).
