Kunal Chakrabarti’s study of the Upapurāṇas composed in Bengal treats them as the record of a “religious process”: brahmin authors absorbed local goddesses, rites and social groups into a Purāṇic framework, and in doing so produced a regional tradition that was at once local and recognisably brahmanical (Chakrabarti 2001).

docs.title: 8.1.1 A Traditional List of Eighteen Upapurāṇas
docs.text:
One frequently cited list, found in the Kūrma Purāṇa, runs as follows (Table 8.1; other lists substitute other titles):

Table 8.1. The Eighteen Upapurāṇas according to the Kūrma Purāṇa (lists vary) No. Upapurāṇa Remarks 1 Sanatkumāra 2 Nārasiṃha Narasiṃha avatāra; an early and comparatively well-preserved Upapurāṇa 3 Skanda Distinct from the Mahāpurāṇa of that name 4 Śivadharma Early Śaiva ritual and ethical teaching 5 Daurvāsasa 6 Nāradīya 7 Kāpila 8 Vāmana 9 Auśanasa 10 Brahmāṇḍa 11 Vāruṇa 12 Kālikā Goddess worship in Kāmarūpa (Assam) 13 Māheśvara 14 Sāmba Sun worship and the Śākadvīpī brahmins 15 Saura Sun worship 16 Pārāśara 17 Mārīca 18 Bhārgava

Scholarly Note: The Devī Bhāgavata Controversy

The Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa occupies a unique position. Śākta traditions consider it a Mahāpurāṇa, identifying it as the true “Bhāgavata” of the list of eighteen and relegating the Vaiṣṇava Bhāgavata to the Upapurāṇas; Vaiṣṇava traditions reverse the classification. Modern scholars generally date the Devī Bhāgavata to the first half of the second millennium CE, later than the Vaiṣṇava Bhāgavata, on which its structure is modelled; C. Mackenzie Brown has shown how it takes over the Bhāgavata’s form and much of its narrative in order to proclaim the supremacy of the Goddess (Brown 1990). Similar claims to Mahāpurāṇa status were made for other works, such as the Gaṇeśa and Mudgala Purāṇas of the Gāṇapatyas.

docs.title: 8.1.2 Characteristics of Upapurāṇas
docs.text:
The Upapurāṇas share many features with the Mahāpurāṇas but tend to:

  • Focus more intensely on a specific deity or devotional path

  • Contain more detailed descriptions of specific vratas (observances) and rituals

  • Preserve regional and local traditions more prominently

  • Include more māhātmya material tied to particular regions

docs.title: 8.2 Sthala Purāṇas — Sacred Place Histories
docs.text:
The Sthala Purāṇas (sthala, “place”) form a distinct genre within Purāṇic literature. They narrate the sacred history (māhātmya) of specific temples, pilgrimage centres (tīrthas), cities, rivers, and geographical features. They typically explain (Figure 8.1; Table 8.2):

  1. How the sacred site originated: Often involving divine manifestation (prākaṭya)

  2. Who established the temple or worship: Usually a deity, sage, or ancient king

  3. Miracles and divine interventions associated with the site

  4. Rituals, festivals, and procedures specific to the site

  5. The spiritual merit (puṇya) obtained by visiting, worshipping, or bathing there

docs.title: 8.2.1 Major Categories of Sthala Purāṇas
docs.text: Figure 8.1. Categories of Sthala Purāṇas

docs.title: 8.2.2 Notable Sthala Purāṇas
docs.text: Table 8.2. Select Notable Sthala Purāṇas Sthala Purāṇa Sacred Place Description Kāśī Khaṇḍa Varanasi Viśvanātha temple, Gaṅgā Māhātmya Setu Māhātmya Rāmeśvaram Rāma Setu, Jyotirliṅga Puruṣottama Māhātmya Purī Jagannātha temple, Ratha Yātrā Kāñcī Māhātmya Kāñcīpuram Sacred city of thousand temples Śrīraṅga Māhātmya Śrīraṅgam Raṅganātha temple, island temple Tirupati Sthala Purāṇa Tirumala Veṅkaṭeśvara, Padmāvatī Dvārakā Māhātmya Dvārakā Kṛṣṇa’s capital city Badarikāśrama Māhātmya Badrīnāth Himalayan shrine of Nārāyaṇa Gayā Māhātmya Gayā Piṇḍadāna, ancestral rites Narmadā Māhātmya Narmadā river Merits of the river; the parikramā (circumambulation) tradition

docs.title: 8.3 The Concept of Sacred Geography (Puṇya Bhūmi)
docs.text:
The māhātmyas collectively construct a sacred geography of South Asia — a landscape in which rivers, mountains, forests and cities are charged with religious significance, and in which pilgrimage (tīrthayātrā) links distant regions. Diana Eck has described this as a “sacred geography” that long preceded, and later fed into, modern ideas of India as a single land (Eck 2012).

The best-known expression of this geography is the list of seven cities that grant liberation (sapta purī): the birthplaces of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa at Ayodhyā and Mathurā, Haridvāra (Māyā) where the Gaṅgā leaves the mountains, Śiva’s city of Kāśī, Kāñcī in the south, Ujjain (Avantikā) with its temple of Mahākāla, and Kṛṣṇa’s western capital Dvārakā:

The Seven Sacred Cities (traditional verse)

ayodhyā mathurā māyā kāśī kāñcī avantikā / purī dvāravatī caiva saptaitā mokṣadāyikāḥ // Translation: “Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā (Haridvāra), Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā and the city of Dvāravatī — these seven bestow liberation.”

docs.title: 8.4 The Dvādaśa Jyotirliṅga Tradition
docs.text:
The twelve Jyotirliṅgas (“liṅgas of light”) are the most celebrated set of Śiva shrines. The list is given in the Śiva Purāṇa and in a popular hymn (the Dvādaśajyotirliṅgastotra); for several of the twelve, more than one site claims the title. Each has its own sthala narrative — for instance, Somanātha is where the Moon worshipped Śiva to be freed from Dakṣa’s curse, and Kedārnātha where Śiva, hiding as a bull from the Pāṇḍavas, left his hump (Table 8.3).

Table 8.3. The Dvādaśa Jyotirliṅgas No. Jyotirliṅga Location 1 Somanātha Prabhāsa, Gujarat 2 Mallikārjuna Śrīśailam, Andhra Pradesh 3 Mahākāleśvara Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh 4 Oṃkāreśvara Oṃkāreśvara, Madhya Pradesh 5 Kedāreśvara Kedārnāth, Uttarakhand 6 Bhīmaśaṅkara Maharashtra (also claimed in Assam) 7 Viśveśvara Kāśī, Uttar Pradesh 8 Tryaṃbakeśvara Nāsik, Maharashtra 9 Vaidyanātha Deoghar, Jharkhand (also claimed at Parli, Maharashtra) 10 Nāgeśvara Near Dvārakā, Gujarat (other sites also claim it) 11 Rāmeśvara Rāmeśvaram, Tamil Nadu 12 Ghṛṣṇeśvara Ellora, Maharashtra

docs.title: 8.5 Significance and Contemporary Relevance
docs.text: The Upapurāṇas and Sthala Purāṇas remain part of living religious practice. Temple priests (arcakas) draw on them for ritual procedures and festival calendars; pilgrims undertake tīrthayātrā on the authority of their promises; and regional māhātmyas tie local identity to the pan-Indian tradition. For historians they preserve, usually in mythologised form, temple foundation legends, royal patronage, local cults and social history (Section 8.13). The sacred status that they give to rivers such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is often invoked by modern campaigns against pollution, although sacredness has not in itself prevented the rivers’ degradation.

docs.title: 8.6 Detailed Study of Select Upapurāṇas
docs.text: The Upapurāṇas as a class have received less scholarly attention than the Mahāpurāṇas, but several of them are major sources for the theology, ritual and regional traditions of particular sects.

docs.title: 8.6.1 The Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa
docs.text: The Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa, comprising traditionally 18,000 ślokas in twelve books (skandhas), is the most extensive Śākta Purāṇa. It deliberately parallels the structure of the Vaiṣṇava Bhāgavata but replaces the primacy of Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa with the supreme Goddess (parā śakti). It retells the myths of the Devī Māhātmya, describes the Goddess’s jewelled island (Maṇidvīpa), and includes in its seventh book the Devī Gītā, in which the Goddess teaches Himālaya a Śākta form of Vedānta and yoga, modelled on the Bhagavad Gītā.

docs.title: 8.6.2 The Gaṇeśa Purāṇa
docs.text: The Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, divided into two parts (Upāsanā Khaṇḍa and Krīḍā Khaṇḍa), is, with the Mudgala Purāṇa, the principal scriptural authority for the Gāṇapatya tradition, which worships Gaṇeśa as the supreme deity. A relatively late text, probably of the first half of the second millennium CE, it describes four descents of Gaṇeśa in the four ages — Mahotkaṭa (Kṛta), Mayureśvara (Tretā), Gajānana (Dvāpara) and Dhūmraketu (Kali) — and contains the Gaṇeśa Gītā. The Mudgala Purāṇa describes eight incarnations of Gaṇeśa.

docs.title: 8.6.3 The Kālikā Purāṇa
docs.text: The Kālikā Purāṇa, composed in the Kāmarūpa region (Assam), probably around the tenth or eleventh century, is a key source for the Śākta traditions of eastern India. It describes the Kāmākhyā temple and its goddess in detail, prescribes elaborate rituals of goddess worship — including a notorious chapter on blood sacrifice — and preserves regional myths, such as the story of the river Brahmaputra, not found elsewhere.

docs.title: 8.7 The Nadī Māhātmyas: River Glorifications
docs.text: Among the most popular kinds of māhātmya are those glorifying the sacred rivers (Table 8.4).

docs.title: 8.7.1 The Seven Sacred Rivers
docs.text:
Invocation of the Seven Rivers (traditional, used in ritual)

Sanskrit: gaṅge ca yamune caiva godāvari sarasvati narmade sindhu kāveri jale ’smin sannidhiṃ kuru Translation: “O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī — be present in this water!”

Table 8.4. Sacred Rivers and Their Purāṇic Significance River Divine Association Purāṇic Māhātmya Gaṅgā Viṣṇu’s feet; Śiva’s locks Descended from heaven through Bhagīratha’s tapas; purifies all sins Yamunā Daughter of Sūrya; sister of Yama Kṛṣṇa’s river in Vraja Sarasvatī Vāg Devī The “invisible” river, believed to join the Gaṅgā and Yamunā underground at Prayāga Narmadā Born, in one legend, from Śiva’s body Its stones are worshipped as Śiva liṅgas; the parikramā tradition (Revākhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa) Godāvarī Gautama’s tapas “Dakṣiṇa Gaṅgā” — the Gaṅgā of the South Kāverī Sage Agastya “Ponni” (the golden one) in Tamil tradition Sindhu The Indus Praised above all other rivers in the Ṛgveda’s hymn to the rivers (10.75)

docs.title: 8.7.2 The Narmadā Parikramā
docs.text: The Narmadā Parikramā — the circumambulation of the Narmadā on foot, from its source at Amarkaṇṭak to its mouth near Bharuch and back along the opposite bank — is one of the most demanding pilgrimages in India. The journey covers roughly 2,600 kilometres; tradition prescribes a period of three years, three months and thirteen days. The Revākhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa describes the merit of the pilgrimage and the sacred sites along both banks.

docs.title: 8.8 The Śakti Pīṭha Tradition
docs.text:
The Śakti Pīṭhas — sites where, according to a myth developed in the Purāṇas and Tantras, parts of the goddess Satī’s body fell when Viṣṇu’s discus dismembered the corpse carried by the grieving Śiva — form one of the most important pilgrimage networks of the Śākta tradition. Different texts enumerate different numbers of Pīṭhas, from four to 108; the figure of fifty-one is the most popular. The Śākta pīṭhas and their Tantric context are treated more fully in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama. See Figure 8.2.

Figure 8.2. Select Śakti Pīṭhas and the Body Parts Associated with Them in Popular Tradition (attributions vary between lists, and several sites claim the same relic)

The Four Early Pīṭhas

The earliest Tantric texts that speak of pīṭhas, Hindu and Buddhist, name four: Oḍḍiyāna (probably in the Swat valley, Pakistan), Jālandhara (associated with Jvālāmukhī in Himachal Pradesh), Pūrṇagiri (of uncertain location) and Kāmarūpa (Kāmākhyā, Assam). The larger lists of fifty-one or more pīṭhas developed later.

docs.title: 8.9 The Cār Dhām and Pilgrimage Networks
docs.text:
The Cār Dhām (Four Abodes) frame the whole subcontinent as a sacred geography oriented to the four cardinal directions (Table 8.5):

Table 8.5. The Cār Dhām Pilgrimage Framework Dhām Direction Deity Sthala Purāṇa Tradition Badrīnāth North Viṣṇu (Badrī Nārāyaṇa) Śaṅkarācārya’s restoration; Tapta Kuṇḍa Rāmeśvaram South Śiva (Rāmanātha) Rāma established the Liṅga before crossing to Laṅkā Dvārakā West Kṛṣṇa (Dvārakādhīśa) Kṛṣṇa’s capital Purī (Jagannātha) East Jagannātha Puruṣottama Kṣetra; the Ratha Yātrā

Tradition attributes this four-fold pilgrimage, together with the four monasteries (maṭhas) at or near the same places, to Śaṅkara. The attribution belongs to later hagiography and the institutionalised circuit is probably much later than Śaṅkara, but the idea expresses a vision of the subcontinent as a single sacred space bounded by its four quarters.

docs.title: 8.10 The Sthala Purāṇas of South Bhārata: A Special Tradition
docs.text:
South Bhārata possesses an exceptionally rich tradition of Sthala Purāṇas, many composed in regional languages (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) alongside Sanskrit. The Tēvāram hymns of the Nāyaṉmārs and the Divya Prabandham of the Āḻvārs function as Tamil Sthala Purāṇas, glorifying specific temples visited by these saint-poets.

Tamil also developed its own purāṇam literature. Cēkkiḻār’s Periya Purāṇam (12th century), composed at the Cōḻa court, tells the lives of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmār saints and became the twelfth book of the Śaiva canon (Tirumuṟai). Later works such as the Kanta Purāṇam of Kacciyappa Civācāriyar, a Tamil retelling of the Skanda myth, and the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam of Parañcōti Muṉivar, on the sixty-four “sacred sports” of Śiva at Madurai, show how Sanskrit Purāṇic material was recast in Tamil around particular temples and cities. Hundreds of later Tamil talapurāṇams (from Sanskrit sthala) were composed for individual shrines.

docs.title: 8.10.1 The Pañcārāma Kṣetras
docs.text: The five Śiva temples of the Andhra region — Amarārāma (Amarāvatī), Drākṣārāma, Somārāma (Bhīmavaram), Kumārārāma (Sāmarlakoṭa) and Kṣīrārāma (Pālakollu) — form a pilgrimage circuit with individual Sthala Purāṇas describing the circumstances of each Liṅga’s manifestation.

docs.title: 8.10.2 The Divya Deśas
docs.text:
The 108 Divya Deśas — temples glorified in the 4,000 verses of the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham by the twelve Āḻvār saints — constitute the most important Viṣṇu temple pilgrimage network in South Bhārata. Each Divya Deśa has its own Sthala Purāṇa, its own processional deity (Utsava Mūrti), and its own festival calendar (Table 8.6).

Table 8.6. Distribution of the 108 Divya Deśas Region Number Notable Temples Cōḻa Nāḍu (Tamil Nadu) 40 Śrīraṅgam, Kumbakoṇam, Chidambaram Pāṇḍya Nāḍu (Tamil Nadu) 18 Śrīvilliputtūr, Tirukkuṟuṅkuṭi Naṭu Nāḍu (Tamil Nadu) 2 Tirukkōvalūr Toṇṭai Nāḍu (Tamil Nadu) 22 Kāñcīpuram temples Malai Nāḍu (Kerala) 13 Tiruvanantapuram Vaṭa Nāḍu (the North) 11 Tirumala, Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Badrīnāth Celestial 2 Vaikuṇṭha, the Ocean of Milk

docs.title: 8.11 The Pañcabhūta Sthalas
docs.text:
A distinctive group of Śaiva sites, the Pañcabhūta Sthalas, comprises five South Indian temples where Śiva is worshipped as the embodiment of each of the five elements (Table 8.7):

Table 8.7. The Pañcabhūta Sthalas Element Temple Location Significance Pṛthvī (Earth) Ekāmbareśvara Kāñcīpuram Liṅga of earth (sand); the sacred mango tree Jala (Water) Jambūkeśvara Tiruvānāikka Water springs around the Liṅga Agni (Fire) Aruṇācaleśvara Tiruvaṇṇāmalai Hill itself is the Liṅga of fire; Kārttikai Dīpam Vāyu (Air) Kāḷaha­stīśvara Śrīkāḷahasti Air liṅga; a lamp before it is said to flicker without draught Ākāśa (Space) Naṭarāja Chidambaram The Citsabhā — the space where Śiva dances

docs.title: 8.12 Reading a Sthala Purāṇa: Authority, Structure and Motifs
docs.text: The sections above list the major networks of sacred places. This section turns to the texts themselves and asks how a māhātmya works: how it claims authority, how it is put together, what stories it habitually tells, and how such texts were composed and made public.

docs.title: 8.12.1 How a Māhātmya Claims Authority
docs.text:
Most Sanskrit māhātmyas present themselves as part of a Mahāpurāṇa, most often the Skanda, but also the Padma, Brahmāṇḍa and others. Their colophons place them in a named section (khaṇḍa) of that Purāṇa. Some were absorbed into the printed vulgates, which is why the printed Skanda Purāṇa is in large part a collection of such texts (Section 7.2 and the profile of the Skanda in Chapter 7). Many more circulate as independent manuscripts and appear in no edition of the Purāṇa they claim to belong to. The attribution is less a statement of textual history than a claim of standing. By placing a local story inside a work ascribed to Vyāsa, the māhātmya makes the shrine part of the all-India tradition. The title of the Skanda Purāṇa in particular came to serve almost as a general home for such texts, a problem discussed in Rocher’s survey (Rocher 1986).

The narration is framed as a dialogue between an authoritative speaker and a questioner: Sūta and the sages of the Naimiṣa forest, Śiva and Pārvatī, or Skanda and a sage. In the Kāśīkhaṇḍa the listener is Agastya. He has left Kāśī for the south on the gods’ errand of humbling the Vindhya mountain, and he hears the glory of the city he cannot return to. The frame thus enacts the longing for the place that the text means to arouse. The body of a typical māhātmya follows a recognisable order:

  • an account of how the deity came to be present at the site, often in a former age;

  • a tour of the subsidiary tīrthas within the sacred zone (kṣetra), each with its own story;

  • rules for bathing, worship and gifts, and a festival calendar;

  • a phalaśruti promising rewards to those who visit, or who merely hear the text.

A favourite device is the sinner saved by accident. A thief, a hunter or an animal does something at the site without meaning to, such as dying within its bounds, being splashed by its water or staying awake on a holy night, and earns the full reward. The device makes the point that the power belongs to the place, not to the worshipper’s merit. The topography of Kāśī as the māhātmyas describe it is treated in Volume 21, Bhūgola.

Because māhātmyas were revised as their shrines grew, comparing their versions can show a sacred landscape taking shape. Hans Bakker’s study of Ayodhyā edited the Ayodhyāmāhātmya, which claims to belong to the Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa, in its different recensions, and read them against inscriptions and other evidence. In Bakker’s reconstruction the earlier layers centre on bathing places along the Sarayū and on older Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva shrines. Sites tied to episodes of Rāma’s life gain importance in later recensions, in step with the growth of Rāma devotion in the second millennium CE (Bakker 1986). The method does not prove or disprove the beliefs the text expresses. It shows, as the scholarly note below says of the genre generally, that a māhātmya is a historical document of the period in which each layer was written.

docs.title: 8.12.2 Tamil Talapurāṇams and the Logic of the Shrine Myth
docs.text:
The Tamil talapurāṇams (Section 8.10) were the subject of David Shulman’s Tamil Temple Myths, which surveyed a large corpus of them and argued that beneath their variety lies a small number of recurrent patterns (Shulman 1980). Four are especially prominent.

The shrine that survives the flood.

Many shrines claim to have outlasted the dissolution of the world (pralaya) and to be the place where creation began again. Cīkāḻi (Sirkazhi) is said to have floated on the waters like a boat, hence its name Tōṇipuram, “boat city”. Kumpakōṇam takes its name from the pot (kumbha) holding the seed of creation, which the flood carried there and Śiva broke with an arrow. On Shulman’s reading such myths make the shrine a self-sufficient world, older than the cosmic cycle and closed within its own boundaries, so that whoever dies within them is freed.

The discovery of the hidden god.

The god is often said to have been found rather than installed. A cow lets her milk flow onto an anthill and the liṅga is uncovered beneath it, or a hunter’s arrow or a woodcutter’s axe strikes a hidden liṅga, which bleeds. The scar may still be shown to pilgrims. The self-manifest (svayaṃbhū) liṅga thus enters the human world through an act of violence, and Shulman connects this to a wider theme of sacrifice in the myths.

The divine marriage.

A local goddess, frequently a powerful virgin, is married to Śiva, and the marriage brings her dangerous power into the order of the temple. At Madurai, Mīnākṣī is born to the Pāṇḍya king with three breasts. She grows up a warrior and conquers the world until she meets Śiva, at which point the third breast disappears and she becomes his bride. The Cittirai festival re-enacts the wedding every year. Viṣṇu, as the goddess’s brother, gives the bride away; in the popular telling his form as Aḻakar sets out from his hill shrine to attend the wedding, arrives too late and turns back at the Vaikai river. At Kāñcī, the goddess Kāmākṣī does penance under a mango tree, and when a flood threatens she clasps her sand liṅga to save it. That liṅga is worshipped at the Ekāmbareśvara temple (Table 8.7).

The localisation of universal myth.

Pan-Indian stories such as the churning of the ocean, Dakṣa’s sacrifice and the appearance of Śiva as a column of fire (liṅgodbhava) are relocated to the shrine. Each major temple thus becomes the place where the universal event actually happened.

Shulman’s interpretations, especially of the erotic and violent symbolism surrounding the goddess, have been debated, but his typology remains the starting point for the study of the genre. It also explains why the same motif can be met at shrine after shrine: the talapurāṇam is less a record of a single place than a local performance of a shared religious grammar.

docs.title: 8.12.3 Composing and Premiering a Talapurāṇam
docs.text:
A talapurāṇam often began as a Sanskrit māhātmya, itself claiming to come from the Skanda or another Purāṇa. A poet then rendered it into Tamil verse, frequently with the support of the temple, a local patron or one of the Śaiva monasteries (ātīṉam). A few talapurāṇams are older, but most surviving works were composed between roughly the sixteenth and the nineteenth centuries. Its last great practitioner was Mīṉāṭcicuntaram Piḷḷai (1815–1876), poet of the Tiruvāvaṭutuṟai monastery, who wrote a large number of them; his pupil U. Vē. Cāminātaiyar, later famous as the editor of the Caṅkam classics, wrote his biography. A new work was made public through an araṅkēṟṟam (“ascent to the stage”). The poet read and expounded it before the assembled scholars and patrons, usually in the temple itself, and had to answer objections. Tradition tells the same of Kampaṉ’s Rāmāyaṇa at Śrīraṅgam. The genre thus moved between Sanskrit and Tamil, and between text and public performance.

Telugu has a parallel tradition, including Śrīnātha’s Kāśī­khaṇḍamu and his Bhīma­khaṇḍamu on Drākṣārāma, one of the Pañcārāma shrines (Section 8.10), and Dhūrjaṭi’s Śrīkāḷahastīśvara Māhātmyamu; these are discussed as literature in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā. The genre is still productive. Prose booklets on the history of a temple (Tamil talavarāḻāṟu) are sold at most South Indian shrines. They retell the talapurāṇam, add the temple’s recent history and its festival calendar, and are now joined by temple websites that do the same.

docs.title: 8.13 The Sthala Purāṇas and Architectural Tradition
docs.text:
The Sthala Purāṇas also preserve, in mythologised form, traditions about the foundation and rebuilding of temples, the origin of festivals and processional routes, and the rights of particular communities in temple service. The concept underlying them is that of the kṣetra (“field”): a place where the boundary between the human and divine realms is believed to be especially permeable, whose sanctity the māhātmya explains by narrating the divine events that occurred there and the benefits that await the pilgrim.

Scholarly Note: Māhātmyas and Temple Chronicles as Historical Sources

While the Sthala Purāṇas are primarily devotional, historians increasingly use them, together with temple chronicles and inscriptions, as sources for local history. Diana Eck’s study of Banaras, for example, draws extensively on the Kāśīkhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa to reconstruct the sacred topography of the medieval city (Eck 1982). Temple chronicles such as the Kōyil Oḻugu of Śrīraṅgam, which records the removal of the temple’s image to safety during the raids of the fourteenth century, belong to a related genre. Such texts must be read critically: they frequently project later arrangements back into a mythic past.

The Vrata Literature: Women’s Religious Agency

The Purāṇas and Upapurāṇas contain extensive vrata (vow) literature describing observances practised especially by women. Vows such as Hartalikā and Vaṭa Sāvitrī, the latter modelled on the Sāvitrī story of the Mahābhārata, are kept mainly by women, often at home and without a priest. The vrata texts supply the stories (kathās), procedures and promised rewards for these observances. Scholars have read them in two ways: as a domain in which women exercised religious agency and transmitted their own narratives, and as a means of reinforcing the ideal of the devoted wife (pativratā), since so many vows are undertaken for a husband’s long life.

docs.title: 8.13.1 Sthala Purāṇas and the Creation of Sacred Landscapes
docs.text: Through the māhātmya narratives, ordinary geographical locations are transformed into tīrthas (“crossings” between the human and divine worlds). The site is identified as the location of a divine event — a god’s appearance, a sage’s austerity, a cosmic battle; it is declared to possess particular powers of purification, healing or liberation; and ritual prescriptions connect the pilgrim’s physical journey to an inner transformation. The same strategies allowed brahmanical tradition to incorporate local and tribal deities into the Purāṇic pantheon, as in the case of Jagannātha at Purī, whose cult has long been thought to have tribal roots.

docs.title: 8.14 Living Traditions: Purāṇic Oral Performance
docs.text:
The Purāṇas were never merely written texts; they were — and remain — performance traditions. Purāṇic discourse (purāṇa pravacana) remains a vibrant tradition across India, with trained expositors (kathāvācakas) narrating Purāṇic stories to audiences over periods ranging from a single evening to the traditional seven days (saptāha).

The Bhāgavata Saptāha, a seven-day recitation of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, remains a popular religious event in Hindu culture. The expositor combines textual recitation with commentary, song, dramatic performance, and philosophical exposition. This oral tradition keeps the Purāṇas accessible to those who cannot read Sanskrit, in keeping with their traditional role as a “fifth Veda” open to audiences excluded from the Veda itself (Section 1.2).

The Harikathā and Kathā Kālakṣepam Traditions

The performance traditions of Harikathā (in Karnataka, Andhra and Maharashtra, where the related form is called kīrtan) and Kathā Kālakṣepam (in Tamil Nadu) combine Purāṇic storytelling with classical music, gesture and commentary. The performer typically narrates a story from the Bhāgavata or Rāmāyaṇa, interspersing it with devotional songs (Marathi abhaṅgas, Karnatak kīrtanas) and interpretive commentary.

The saptāha’s seven days come from the Bhāgavata’s own frame story. King Parīkṣit, cursed to die within seven days, spends them listening to the Purāṇa from the sage Śuka. A separate text, the Bhāgavata Māhātmya, turns this frame into a rite. The version in general use claims to belong to the Padma Purāṇa (a shorter one claims the Skanda); it is usually printed at the head of editions of the Bhāgavata and recited at the opening of a saptāha. It tells how Bhakti, personified as a young woman, found her sons Jñāna and Vairāgya (knowledge and detachment) grown old and feeble in the Kali age, and how they were revived by hearing the Bhāgavata recited. It then tells of the brahmin Gokarṇa, whose dissolute brother Dhundhukārī died a violent death and became a ghost. Gokarṇa freed him by a seven-day recitation: the ghost sat in a bamboo of seven joints, one of which split on each day of the reading. The text ends with rules for the reciter, the sponsor and the listeners. It is a clear case of a māhātmya doing for a text what the sthala māhātmyas do for a place (Section 8.12). It supplies a charter story, a ritual procedure and a promise of reward, and so gives the performance its form.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Dharma in the Epics — Hard Cases, Distress and Limits
docs.text:
dharma eva hato hanti dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ / tasmād dharmo na hantavyo mā no dharmo hato ’vadhīt //

— Manusmṛti 8.15

The verse of the Manusmṛti quoted above states the traditional conviction about dharma: “Dharma, when violated, destroys; dharma, when protected, protects. Therefore dharma must not be violated, lest violated dharma destroy us.” The narrative chapters of this volume have described the epics’ teachings episode by episode. This chapter asks a different question: what kind of moral thinking do the epics do? It looks at the cases in which duties conflict, at the doctrine of conduct in distress, at the rules of war and their breach, and at the limits that caste and gender set to the epic ethic.

docs.title: 9.1 What Dharma Means in the Epics
docs.text:
The Sanskrit concept of dharma — at once cosmic order, religious duty, law, custom and virtue — has no single English equivalent. Alf Hiltebeitel has argued that the word, relatively uncommon and specialised in the Vedic texts, became a central term of brahmanical thought only in the centuries around Mauryan rule, partly in response to its use by Aśoka and the Buddhists, and that the epics, together with the Dharmasūtras and the Manusmṛti, worked out its meaning in narrative (Hiltebeitel 2011). In the epics dharma is not a single code. There is a dharma common to all (sādhāraṇa dharma) — truthfulness, non-injury, compassion; the Mahābhārata repeatedly calls non-cruelty (ānṛśaṃsya) the highest dharma. Beside it stand the duties of one’s class and stage of life (varṇāśrama dharma), the duty of one’s own station (svadharma), as when Kṛṣṇa tells Arjuna that for a warrior nothing is better than a righteous war (Gītā 2.31), the duties of the king (rājadharma), of the lineage (kuladharma) and of women (strīdharma), and the special rules of distress (āpaddharma). These obligations vary with person and circumstance, and they can conflict, so that dharma must often be discerned afresh: the epic’s own term is “the subtlety of dharma” (Section 4.14).

The Purāṇas teach dharma differently. Instead of a single narrative full of dilemmas, they offer exemplary stories of devotees, sinners, kings and sages, tales attached to particular vows (vrata kathās) and places (tīrtha māhātmyas; Section 8.12), and direct instruction in dialogue. The hard cases are mostly the epics’.

docs.title: 9.2 Ideal and Hard Case: The Two Epics Compared
docs.text:
The tradition reads the Rāmāyaṇa as a poem of ideals and the Mahābhārata as a poem of dilemmas. The contrast is useful if it is not pressed too hard. Rāma’s acceptance of exile is the Rāmāyaṇa’s model of truth-keeping (satya), and the tradition reads it as a conscious choice to honour his father’s word at great cost; but Lakṣmaṇa’s angry objection that the promise was extorted, and Rāma’s reply, show that the poem itself recognised the question. Rāma’s compassion towards the vulture Jaṭāyu, whom he cremates with his own hands, towards Śabarī and towards Vibhīṣaṇa is equally part of the ideal. The ideal kingdom of Rāma, Rāmarājya, was invoked by Gandhi as a model of just and non-violent self-rule, and modern interpreters have drawn from it the principles that the king exists for the people and must heed the humblest subject. The Rāmāyaṇa’s own ideal kingdom, however, was one of hierarchical order: the Rāma who banishes Sītā because of a subject’s gossip is the Rāma who executes the Śūdra Śambūka (Sections 3.6.3 and 3.7.4).

The Mahābhārata makes the conflict of duties its subject. Arjuna’s refusal to fight his kin, Draupadī’s question in the dicing hall, Karṇa’s loyalty to Duryodhana, Bhīṣma’s silence and Yudhiṣṭhira’s half-truth are described in Section 4.12; the sections below take up the epic’s explicit reflection on such cases.

docs.title: 9.3 The Subtlety of Truth
docs.text:
Truth-telling is the virtue for which Yudhiṣṭhira is famous, and the Mahābhārata examines it most closely. In the Karṇa Parva, Arjuna, who has vowed to kill anyone who tells him to give his bow to another, is about to kill Yudhiṣṭhira for having done so in a moment of anger. Kṛṣṇa stops him with a discourse on the subtlety of truth: speaking the truth is good, but there are circumstances — to save a life, for instance — in which untruth is not wrong, and a truth that leads to the death of the innocent is not dharma. He illustrates the point with the story of the ascetic Kauśika, who had vowed always to speak the truth. When robbers pursuing some travellers asked him where they had gone, he told them, and the travellers were killed; Kṛṣṇa declares that Kauśika went to hell for it. Truth divorced from compassion and judgement is, on this view, not dharma but its perversion.

The same tension runs through the episode of Yudhiṣṭhira’s half-truth. Persuaded by Kṛṣṇa, he confirms to Droṇa that “Aśvatthāman is dead,” meaning the elephant of that name, and Droṇa lays down his arms. The epic does not let the deed pass: Yudhiṣṭhira’s chariot, which had always floated above the ground, touches the earth, and at the end of the poem he must glimpse hell before he enters heaven (Sections 5.7 and 5.18). The episode raises questions about the limits of truthfulness, the weight of consequences and the moral cost of victory that the epic leaves unresolved.

docs.title: 9.4 Vidura Nīti — The Wisdom of Vidura
docs.text:
Vidura, the wise counsellor born of Vyāsa and a servant woman (dāsī), is the voice of practical wisdom in the Mahābhārata. His counsel to Dhṛtarāṣṭra on a sleepless night before the war (Udyoga Parva, chapters 33–40 in the CE), part of the Prajāgaraparvan or “Book of the Vigil,” is a classic collection of maxims on nīti, the science of wise conduct. Its themes include the marks of the wise and the foolish, the choice of counsellors, the vices that ruin kings (gambling, drink, women and hunting), the dangers of greed and anger, the duty of a king to protect his subjects, the grounding of prosperity in dharma, and the folly of favouring a wicked son — a pointed lesson for its royal listener. One of its best-known verses lists the faults to be abandoned by anyone who seeks prosperity:

Vidura’s Six Faults — Udyoga Parva 5.33.66 (Critical Edition)

ṣaḍ doṣāḥ puruṣeṇeha hātavyā bhūtim icchatā / nidrā tandrī bhayaṃ krodha ālasyaṃ dīrghasūtratā // Translation: “Six faults should be abandoned by a man who desires prosperity here: sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, idleness and procrastination.”

The vigil continues with the more metaphysical teaching of the Sanatsujātīya (Section 11.3).

docs.title: 9.5 The Doctrine of Āpad Dharma: Ethics in Extremity
docs.text:
A distinctive contribution of the Mahābhārata to ethical thought is the doctrine of āpaddharma, conduct appropriate in times of extreme distress. Elaborated in the second section of the Śānti Parva (Section 5.12), it addresses what happens when normal rules conflict with survival itself, for kings in danger of losing their kingdoms and for individuals facing famine (Table 9.1).

Table 9.1. Normal Rules and Their Modification in Times of Distress (Āpad) Normal Rule Modification in Distress Illustration Brahmins live by teaching and sacrifice May take up the occupations of other classes Droṇa and Aśvatthāman live as warriors Rules of diet and purity May be suspended to preserve life Viśvāmitra, starving in a famine, steals dog’s meat from an outcaste (caṇḍāla) and argues with him about dharma A king must act openly and honestly May use stratagems and alliances of convenience to survive Bhīṣma’s teachings on the king in distress, such as the parable of the cat and the mouse

The Viśvāmitra story is the sharpest. The outcaste, not the sage, defends the rules of purity, and the sage answers that a man must first stay alive in order to practise dharma at all; the text lets the argument stand. The āpaddharma teaching, like the cases of truth above, illustrates the principle that dharma is “subtle” (sūkṣma) and must be discerned rather than read off from rules.

docs.title: 9.5.1 The Yakṣa Praśna
docs.text:
The Yakṣa Praśna (“Questions of the Yakṣa”; Āraṇyaka Parva 3.295–299 in the CE, 3.311–315 in the vulgate) gathers the epic’s ethical wisdom in the form of riddles. A Yakṣa, who is Dharma himself in disguise, has killed four of the brothers at a forest pool, and Yudhiṣṭhira wins them back by answering his questions (Table 9.2). Offered the life of one brother, he chooses Nakula, the son of his father’s other wife, so that each of Pāṇḍu’s queens should have a living son — an answer that the Yakṣa rewards by reviving them all.

Table 9.2. Selected Questions and Answers from the Yakṣa Praśna (rows marked * are found only in the vulgate) Yakṣa’s Question Yudhiṣṭhira’s Answer What is swifter than the wind? The mind (Manas) What is the greatest wonder in the world?* That men see others dying daily, yet believe themselves immortal What is the path?* The path is that which the great have walked; argument and scripture alone lead to no conclusion What must one renounce to become beloved? Pride What must one renounce to become wealthy? Desire What makes a person a Brāhmaṇa?* Conduct, not birth or learning alone

Yudhiṣṭhira’s answer that conduct, not birth, makes a brahmin — repeated in his dialogue with the serpent Nahuṣa — is often quoted as evidence of the epic’s liberality. It must be read alongside the many passages that affirm hereditary hierarchy (Section 9.8).

docs.title: 9.6 The Ethics of War: Yuddha Dharma
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata examines at length when war is justified and how it may be fought. The Udyoga Parva debates whether war can be avoided, and Kṛṣṇa’s embassy dramatises the principle that peaceful means should be exhausted first. The conventions that the two sides agree at the start of the war (Section 4.15) require warriors to fight their equals, and forbid striking those who withdraw, surrender or are disarmed, those engaged with another, and charioteers and attendants; the rules of the mace duel forbid blows below the navel.

The narrative of the eighteen days then records how these conventions give way, on both sides. Abhimanyu is surrounded and killed by several great warriors at once. Fighting, which normally ceased at sunset, continues through the fourteenth night by torchlight. Bhīṣma falls because the Pāṇḍavas, on his own advice, place Śikhaṇḍin before Arjuna: Bhīṣma has vowed not to fight one who was born a woman, lowers his weapons, and is shot down from behind Śikhaṇḍin — a stratagem that turns the old warrior’s own code against him. Droṇa is deceived by the half-truth about his son and beheaded after he has laid down his arms; Karṇa is shot while he struggles to free his chariot wheel; Bhīma breaks Duryodhana’s thighs with a blow below the navel, to the fury of Balarāma. On the Kaurava side, Aśvatthāman’s massacre of the sleeping camp breaks every rule at once. Several of the Pāṇḍava breaches are made on Kṛṣṇa’s advice, and when they are denounced he defends them on the ground that the Kaurava champions could not have been killed in fair fight and had themselves broken the rules first. The epic records the defence without quite endorsing it: the victory is real, and so is its moral cost.

docs.title: 9.7 Forgiveness and Compassion: Kṣamā
docs.text: The epics also praise forgiveness (kṣamā) as one of the highest virtues. In the Āraṇyaka Parva, Draupadī and Bhīma argue passionately that the Pāṇḍavas should take revenge on the Kauravas; Draupadī cites the teaching of Prahlāda to his grandson Bali that there is a time for forbearance and a time for force. Yudhiṣṭhira replies by praising forgiveness, quoting verses that declare forgiveness to be dharma, sacrifice and truth itself (kṣamā dharmaḥ kṣamā yajñaḥ, 3.30.36). The text gives both sides their full weight, and the war that follows shows the costs of both justice and mercy.

docs.title: 9.8 Dharma, Caste and Gender: The Limits of the Epic Ethic
docs.text:
An honest account of the epics’ moral teaching must acknowledge that their dharma is the dharma of a hierarchical society. The duties they prescribe are differentiated by varṇa and by gender, and the narratives often enforce those differences.

  • Ekalavya: In the Ādi Parva, a Niṣāda (tribal) youth who has taught himself archery before a clay image of Droṇa is asked by Droṇa for his right thumb as the teacher’s fee, so that Arjuna may remain the greatest archer. Ekalavya gives it.

  • Karṇa: At the tournament of the princes, Karṇa is mocked as a charioteer’s son and told he may not compete with princes; his humiliation drives him into Duryodhana’s camp.

  • Śambūka: In the Rāmāyaṇa’s Uttarakāṇḍa, the ideal king executes a Śūdra for practising austerities (Section 3.7.4).

  • Women: The Anuśāsana Parva’s teachings on the duties of women (strīdharma) present the wife’s devotion to her husband as her highest religious duty, and Sītā’s and Draupadī’s sufferings are framed by a patriarchal order — even as both women challenge it in speech (Chapter 10).

At the same time, the epics contain voices that question the hierarchy: Yudhiṣṭhira’s answers to the Yakṣa and to Nahuṣa, the Gītā’s promise of liberation to women and Śūdras (9.32), Draupadī’s challenge in the assembly, and the devotional traditions that made Śabarī and other low-born devotees into exemplars. Modern readers have responded in different ways: B. R. Ambedkar treated the epics as charters of caste; Dalit writers have adopted Ekalavya and Śambūka as emblems of the denial of knowledge to the oppressed; and feminist historians such as Uma Chakravarti have analysed how epic and Dharmaśāstra norms linked the control of women’s sexuality to the maintenance of caste (Ambedkar 1987; Chakravarti 2003). Recognising these limits does not cancel the epics’ ethical depth; it situates it historically.

docs.title: 9.9 Modern Uses of the Epics’ Ethics
docs.text: The epics’ teachings on dharma are widely invoked in modern public life, and the ways in which they are used are themselves part of their history. Gandhi made Rāmarājya the name of his ideal of self-rule and anāsakti, non-attachment, the key to the Gītā; Tilak read the same text as a call to selfless political action (Section 6.13). Writers on public administration cite Bhīṣma’s teachings on royal duty, and writers on negotiation the Udyoga Parva’s account of Kṛṣṇa’s embassy. Environmental campaigns invoke the sacredness of rivers and forests in the epics and Purāṇas (Section 12.7). A large popular and management literature presents the Gītā’s svadharma and action without attachment as an ethic for professional life. That use reinterprets the texts: the classical commentators understood svadharma as the duty of one’s hereditary station (Section 6.5), and its modern reading as individual vocation is a twentieth-century development. Against all these stand the Dalit and feminist readings described above, for which the same texts are evidence of what modern India must leave behind. The epics continue, in short, to provide the vocabulary in which Indians argue about right action, whichever side of the argument they take.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Women in the Epics — Role, Agency, and Significance
docs.text:
yatra nāryas tu pūjyante ramante tatra devatāḥ / yatraitās tu na pūjyante sarvās tatrāphalāḥ kriyāḥ //

— Manusmṛti 3.56

The women of the Sanskrit epics are not background figures. Sītā, Draupadī, Kuntī, Gāndhārī, Mandodarī, Sāvitrī, Damayantī, Tārā, Ambā and many others speak, argue, choose and suffer, and their choices drive the narratives at decisive points. Yet they act within a patriarchal social order that the epics, like the Dharmaśāstras of the same period, largely take for granted, and that frequently subjects them to humiliation, abandonment and tests of chastity. Both facts need to be held together. This chapter presents the major women of the epics as the tradition has honoured them, and also the feminist and other critical readings that have questioned the ideals they were made to embody (Sutherland 1989; Hess 1999; Chakravarti 2003).

The Manusmṛti verse quoted above — “where women are honoured, there the gods rejoice; where they are not honoured, all rites are fruitless” — is often cited to show the high status of women in the tradition. The same text also declares that “her father protects her in childhood, her husband in youth, her sons in old age; a woman is not fit for independence” (na strī svātantryam arhati, 9.3). The epics’ portrayal of women moves between these poles.

docs.title: 10.1 Sītā
docs.text: Sītā, the daughter of King Janaka, found in a furrow of the earth (hence ayonijā, “not born from a womb”), is the central female figure of the Rāmāyaṇa. For the tradition she is the model wife; for modern readers she is also an independent moral agent whose speech and endurance are integral to the epic, and whose treatment by Rāma is its most contested theme.

docs.title: 10.1.1 Key Dimensions of Sītā’s Character
docs.text:
1. Intelligence and eloquence: Sītā is articulate and versed in dharma. In the Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa she insists on sharing the exile, and in the Araṇya Kāṇḍa she warns Rāma against violence towards those who have not wronged him.

  2. Courage in captivity: In the Aśoka grove she withstands Rāvaṇa’s threats and blandishments, speaking to him only after placing a blade of grass between them, and refuses Hanumān’s offer to carry her away, saying that Rāma himself must rescue her.

  3. The ordeal by fire: When Rāma publicly repudiates her, Sītā answers him with reproach and enters the fire; the episode and its readings are discussed in Section 3.6.3.

  4. The final refusal: In the Uttara Kāṇḍa, summoned to swear her purity again before the assembly, Sītā instead calls on the Earth, her mother, to receive her — a refusal of a second test that many readers regard as the most powerful act in the epic.

docs.title: 10.1.2 Sītā’s Argument for the Exile
docs.text:
Sītā’s decision to follow Rāma into exile is presented not merely as wifely devotion but as a reasoned claim. When Rāma tells her to stay behind, she argues with him at length, and when he still refuses, she taunts him: did her father, she asks, take him for a man when he was only a woman in a man’s form?

Sītā’s Arguments for Accompanying Rāma (Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa)

  • A wife shares her husband’s fortune, good or bad

  • The forest holds no terrors for one who walks with Rāma

  • Separation from her husband would be worse than death

  • Brahmins had foretold that she would one day live in the forest

Sītā does not merely ask permission; she prevails through argument and conviction — though the content of her argument is the ideal of the devoted wife.

docs.title: 10.2 Draupadī — The Fire-Born Queen
docs.text: Draupadī (also called Kṛṣṇā, Pāñcālī and Yājñasenī) is the most complex and outspoken woman of the Mahābhārata. Born from Drupada’s sacrificial fire and married to all five Pāṇḍavas, she is a catalyst of the epic’s central conflict and a relentless voice for justice (Hiltebeitel 1988).

docs.title: 10.2.1 Draupadī’s Key Roles
docs.text:
1. The cause of the war: Her humiliation in the Kaurava assembly becomes the irrevocable cause of the war. Bhīma vows to drink Duśśāsana’s blood and to break Duryodhana’s thigh, and both vows are fulfilled.

  2. The questioner of dharma: Her question in the Sabhā Parva — whether Yudhiṣṭhira, having first lost himself, still had the right to stake her — is a moral and legal question that goes to the heart of the epic. Bhīṣma replies only that dharma is subtle; the young Kaurava Vikarṇa and Vidura support her, but the assembly gives no clear answer, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra finally grants her boons out of fear.

  3. The unbound hair: Dragged into the assembly by her hair, Draupadī becomes in later tradition the woman who keeps her hair unbound until it can be washed in Duśśāsana’s blood — a motif developed especially in Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa’s play Veṇīsaṃhāra and in regional retellings.

  4. Political judgment: In the forest she challenges Yudhiṣṭhira’s passivity, arguing for vengeance and questioning divine justice (see below).

  5. Devotion to Kṛṣṇa: Later devotional tradition celebrates her surrender to Kṛṣṇa during the attempted disrobing as supreme bhakti; on the absence of her prayer from the critical text, see Section 4.8.

In parts of South India Draupadī is worshipped as a goddess, and the Draupadī cult of Tamil Nadu, with its fire-walking festivals and dramatic performances of the epic, has been studied in detail by Alf Hiltebeitel (Hiltebeitel 1988).

docs.title: 10.3 Kuntī
docs.text: Kuntī (also called Pṛthā) is the mother of the three elder Pāṇḍavas and the secret mother of Karṇa, and her secret shapes the whole epic.

docs.title: 10.3.1 Key Aspects of Kuntī’s Character
docs.text:
• Unmarried motherhood: Using a mantra given her by the sage Durvāsas, she summons the Sun god before her marriage and bears Karṇa, whom she sets adrift in a basket.

  • Resilience: She raises her three sons and Mādrī’s twins through exile and danger.

  • The shared marriage: When her sons return with Draupadī and announce the “alms” they have won, Kuntī, without looking, tells them to share it equally — words that cannot be revoked and lead to the polyandrous marriage.

  • Counsel to fight: Before the war Kuntī sends Yudhiṣṭhira, through Kṛṣṇa, the story of Vidulā, a queen who goaded her defeated son back into battle — a fierce call to Kṣatriya duty.

  • The meeting with Karṇa: Kuntī reveals to Karṇa that she is his mother, seeking to turn him from the Kaurava side; he refuses, but promises to spare all her sons except Arjuna.

  • Her final choice: After the war she chooses to accompany Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī to the forest, where she dies with them in a forest fire.

docs.title: 10.4 Gāndhārī — The Blindfolded Queen
docs.text:
Gāndhārī, the princess of Gāndhāra who binds her eyes on learning that her husband Dhṛtarāṣṭra is blind, is a figure of great austerity (tapas) and tragic dimension.

  1. Her self-imposed blindness is presented as supreme wifely devotion; modern readers have also seen it as a symbol of the moral blindness of the Kaurava household, and even as a protest.

  2. She repeatedly warns Duryodhana against his course and urges him to make peace; when he asked for her blessing in the war, it was famously conditional: “where dharma is, there is victory” (yato dharmas tato jayaḥ, 11.17.6).

  3. In the Strī Parva she reproaches Kṛṣṇa for allowing the slaughter when he could have prevented it, and curses him: his own clan will destroy itself, as hers has. Kṛṣṇa accepts the curse calmly, and it is fulfilled in the Mausala Parva; the epic thus concedes to a grieving mother the moral authority to curse a god.

  4. Her lament over the bodies of her sons on the battlefield is the centre of the Strī Parva. (The popular story that she made Duryodhana’s body invulnerable by unbinding her eyes to look at him belongs to later retellings.)

docs.title: 10.5 Mandodarī
docs.text: Mandodarī, the chief queen of Rāvaṇa, repeatedly urges her husband to return Sītā and avoid destruction. Her lament over his body in the Yuddha Kāṇḍa, in which (in the vulgate) she recognises Rāma as more than human and blames Rāvaṇa’s lust for his ruin, is admired by the tradition as an example of pathos (karuṇa); for the tradition she shows that even in the household of adharma the voice of dharma is heard.

docs.title: 10.6 Sāvitrī and Damayantī — Heroines of the Upākhyānas
10.6.1 Sāvitrī — She Who Won Back Her Husband from Death
docs.text:
The story of Sāvitrī is told to Yudhiṣṭhira by Mārkaṇḍeya in the Āraṇyaka Parva (the Pativratāmāhātmya). Sāvitrī chooses Satyavat as her husband despite Nārada’s warning that he will die within a year. When Yama, the god of death, comes for Satyavat, she follows him, and through a series of eloquent speeches on dharma wins boons from him, until he restores her husband’s life (Table 10.1).

Table 10.1. The Boons Won by Sāvitrī from Yama Boon Request Effect First Restoration of her blind father-in-law Dyumatsena’s sight She asks for another, not for herself Second Restoration of Dyumatsena’s lost kingdom Yama’s respect grows Third A hundred sons for her own father Piety toward her natal family Fourth A hundred sons for herself by Satyavat The decisive move: the boon implies that Satyavat must live Fifth Satyavat’s life itself Yama, praising her, releases him

Sāvitrī’s victory comes through speech and persistence rather than force, and she became the model wife invoked in the women’s vow of Vaṭa Sāvitrī, observed for a husband’s long life.

docs.title: 10.6.2 Damayantī — Intelligence and Devotion
docs.text: Damayantī, in the story of Nala and Damayantī in the Āraṇyaka Parva, recognises the true Nala at her svayaṃvara among four gods who have taken his form and chooses him over them. When Nala, possessed by Kali, abandons her in the forest, she survives by her own courage, and it is she who finally contrives their reunion by setting a second svayaṃvara as a trap for her disguised husband.

docs.title: 10.7 Other Women of the Epics
docs.text:
Beside the great heroines stand women whose stories are shorter but often more revealing of the social world the epics take for granted. Several of them show, more plainly than Sītā or Draupadī, how women could be given, exchanged and used to secure a lineage (Brodbeck 2009; Brodbeck and Black 2007).

Satyavatī is the daughter of a fisher chief (dāśa). Before her marriage she bears the sage Parāśara a son, Vyāsa, on an island in the Yamunā. King Śāntanu wishes to marry her, and her father agrees only if her sons inherit the throne, the condition that produces Bhīṣma’s vow (Table 10.2). She is not only her father’s instrument. When both her sons die without heirs, it is Satyavatī who directs the dynasty’s policy: she first asks Bhīṣma to beget sons on her widowed daughters-in-law, and when he refuses she summons her first-born, Vyāsa, whose niyoga produces Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and Vidura (Figure 4.1). After Pāṇḍu’s death she withdraws to the forest with Ambikā and Ambālikā, foreseeing the evil to come. The Kuru line on which the whole epic turns is thus continued through a woman of low birth and a son born before her marriage.

The most striking case in the epic of a woman exchanged among men is that of Mādhavī, whose story Nārada tells Duryodhana in the Udyoga Parva as a warning against obstinacy. The young brahmin Gālava insists on paying his teacher Viśvāmitra a fee, and the exasperated teacher demands eight hundred white horses, each with one black ear. Unable to find them, Gālava goes with the bird Garuḍa to King Yayāti, who has no horses to spare and gives him instead his daughter Mādhavī, who has the boon of regaining her virginity after each childbirth. Gālava gives her in turn to three kings — Haryaśva of Ayodhyā, Divodāsa of Kāśī and Uśīnara — each of whom pays two hundred horses for the right to beget one son on her; since no more such horses exist, he hands her to Viśvāmitra himself in place of the last two hundred, and she bears him a fourth son. Returned to her father, Mādhavī is offered a svayaṃvara, and instead chooses the forest, where she lives as an ascetic among the deer. Her sons’ merit later saves Yayāti when he falls from heaven. The story treats her as a means of exchange, and it also lets her make, at the end, the one choice that is hers.

Three women of Arjuna’s and Bhīma’s wanderings come from outside the Aryan kingdoms. Hiḍimbā, a Rākṣasī of the forest, falls in love with Bhīma after he kills her brother; with Kuntī’s consent she lives with him until she bears a son, Ghaṭotkaca, and then returns to the forest, while her son comes back to fight for his father’s family and dies in the war (Section 5.7). She is worshipped as a goddess in the western Himalaya, where the epic’s “demoness” is a local deity. Ulūpī, a Nāga princess, carries Arjuna off to her underwater realm during his exile and bears him Irāvat, the Aravāṉ of the Tamil Draupadī cult (Section 12.5); in the Āśvamedhika Parva she revives Arjuna with a magic jewel after he has been killed in battle by his own son. That son is Babhruvāhana, born to Citrāṅgadā, princess of Maṇipūra, whose father allowed the marriage only on condition that her son continue his own line rather than Arjuna’s — the arrangement of the “appointed daughter” (putrikā) that the lawbooks recognise for a man without sons. Rabindranath Tagore’s play Citrāṅgadā (1892) reimagined her as a princess raised as a warrior.

In the Rāmāyaṇa, Tārā, Vālin’s wife, warns him not to fight Sugrīva again, perceiving that he must have found a powerful ally; ignored, she laments him with great eloquence and later calms an angry Lakṣmaṇa on Sugrīva’s behalf. Kausalyā blesses her son as he leaves for exile even as she grieves, and Sumitrā sends Lakṣmaṇa to serve him. Lakṣmaṇa’s wife Ūrmilā, who stays behind for fourteen years, is barely mentioned by Vālmīki; modern writers took her silence as their subject, among them Tagore in an essay on the women whom poetry has neglected and Maithilīśaraṇ Gupta in his Hindi epic Sāket (1931). Ahalyā, Tārā and Mandodarī, together with Draupadī and Kuntī (Sītā in some versions), make up the five “maidens” (pañcakanyā) of a popular morning prayer — a list that, as many readers have noticed, honours women whose marriages were anything but conventional.

docs.title: 10.8 Women as Catalysts of Narrative Transformation
docs.text:
Both epics turn on the actions, choices or sufferings of women. It should be noted, however, that the tradition’s habit of locating the cause of disaster in women — Kaikeyī’s demand, Śūrpaṇakhā’s desire, Sītā’s insistence that Lakṣmaṇa leave her — has itself been criticised as a misogynist pattern (Table 10.2):

Table 10.2. Women as Narrative Catalysts in the Epics Woman Action Narrative Consequence Kaikeyī Demands Rāma’s exile Sets the entire Rāmāyaṇa in motion Sītā Sends Lakṣmaṇa after Rāma, accusing him of designs on her Leaves her alone when Rāvaṇa comes Śūrpaṇakhā Approaches Rāma in desire Precipitates the Rākṣasa conflict Draupadī The vastraharaṇa Generates the moral imperative for the Mahābhārata war Kuntī Reveals Karṇa’s identity Creates the tragic dimension of the great war Satyavatī Marries Śāntanu on condition that her sons inherit; later summons Vyāsa to continue the line Bhīṣma’s vow; the birth of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu (Section 10.7) Gāndhārī Curses the Yādavas Brings about the destruction of Kṛṣṇa’s clan Ambā/Śikhaṇḍinī Vows revenge on Bhīṣma Causes Bhīṣma’s fall in battle

docs.title: 10.9 The Ambā-Śikhaṇḍinī Narrative: Gender, Agency, and Cosmic Justice
docs.text:
The story of Ambā is one of the most complex in the Mahābhārata. Ambā, princess of Kāśī, is abducted by Bhīṣma together with her sisters as brides for his half-brother Vicitravīrya. When she reveals that she had chosen King Śālva, Bhīṣma releases her — but Śālva rejects her as another man’s prize, and Bhīṣma cannot marry her because of his vow. Caught between the honour codes of men, Ambā is left with nothing.

Her response is not resignation but fierce determination. After even Paraśurāma fails to defeat Bhīṣma on her behalf, she performs terrible austerities, obtains Śiva’s promise that she will kill Bhīṣma in another life, and is reborn as Śikhaṇḍinī, daughter of Drupada, raised as a son and later changed into a man through an exchange of sex with a Yakṣa. As Śikhaṇḍin, she becomes the instrument of Bhīṣma’s fall. The story raises questions about gender, the persistence of a grievance across births, and the injustice done to women by men’s vows and alliances.

docs.title: 10.10 Beyond the “Ideal Woman” Narrative
docs.text: The women of the epics cannot be reduced to a single “ideal woman” template. Sītā endures with dignity but does not submit, and ends by refusing a second ordeal; Draupadī demands justice and refuses to forgive; Kuntī makes hard decisions with a long view; Gāndhārī’s curse shows the force of a restraint long kept; Sāvitrī defeats Death by argument; Tārā gives political counsel; and Śabarī is remembered for simple devotion. Without Sītā there is no Rāmāyaṇa and without Draupadī no Mahābhārata; their sufferings are also the epics’ sharpest questions about their own moral order.

docs.title: 10.10.1 Women as Intellectual and Spiritual Authorities
docs.text:
The epics and Purāṇas include women who hold spiritual knowledge and philosophical authority. In the Śānti Parva, Sulabhā, a wandering female ascetic, engages King Janaka in debate on the nature of the self and of liberation, and exposes the limits of his claim to be liberated while still a king. The Yogavāsiṣṭha presents Cūḍālā as a queen who attains realisation before her husband and then guides him. In the Devī Gītā, the Goddess herself is the supreme teacher.

These figures continue the Upaniṣadic memory of Gārgī and Maitreyī. They are, however, exceptional: the normative texts generally exclude women from Vedic study and from the ascetic path, and Sulabhā herself is attacked by Janaka for her presumption (Table 10.3).

Table 10.3. Women as Spiritual and Intellectual Authorities in the Epics Woman Text Role and Achievement Sulabhā Mahābhārata (Śānti Parva) Defeated King Janaka in philosophical debate on Ātman Cūḍālā Yogavāsiṣṭha Attained Mokṣa before her husband; served as his Guru Devī Devī Bhāgavata Teaches Advaita philosophy as the supreme reality Anasūyā Rāmāyaṇa (Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa) Ascetic wife of Atri; instructs Sītā on a wife’s duties and gives her ornaments. (The later Purāṇic legend makes her turn the three gods into infants.) Draupadī Mahābhārata (Āraṇyaka Parva) Discourses on dharma, fate and divine justice Śabarī Rāmāyaṇa Female ascetic; ascends to heaven after receiving Rāma

Draupadī’s Question: The Philosophical Heart of the Mahābhārata

In the Āraṇyaka Parva, Draupadī asks the question that the Mahābhārata never fully answers: if dharma protects the righteous, why do the virtuous suffer while the wicked prosper? The Creator, she says, plays with creatures as a child plays with toys. Yudhiṣṭhira answers that he does not practise dharma for its rewards, and rebukes her for doubting; but her question — an Indian formulation of the problem of theodicy — is never fully answered within the text, and the war that follows only sharpens it.

docs.title: 10.10.2 Motherhood as a Source of Power
docs.text: The epics also present motherhood as a source of moral authority. Kuntī’s decisions, traced in Section 10.3, shape the whole course of the Mahābhārata. In the Rāmāyaṇa, Kausalyā’s blessing of Rāma before his departure for exile and Kaikeyī’s fateful demands demonstrate how maternal agency drives the epic’s central plot. The Strī Parva of the Mahābhārata gives voice to the collective grief of mothers, wives, and daughters after the war, presenting the female perspective on martial glory and its devastating human cost.

docs.title: 10.10.3 Women and the Tradition of Pātivratya
docs.text:
The concept of pātivratya (devotion to one’s husband) is the most debated aspect of the epics’ portrayal of women. The epics themselves present it as a form of spiritual power (tapas) that grants superhuman abilities: Sāvitrī wins her husband back from Death; Damayantī’s fidelity protects her in the wilderness. Critics have pointed out that the same ideal served to make a wife’s whole religious life consist in service to her husband, to justify her abandonment or punishment on suspicion, and, in its most extreme later form, to glorify the self-immolation of widows (satī). See Table 10.4.

Table 10.4. Pātivratās and the Powers Ascribed to Them Woman Trial Endured Power Demonstrated Sāvitrī Followed Yama to reclaim her husband’s soul Conquered death through argumentation and devotion Anasūyā Tested, in later Purāṇic legend, by the three gods Turns them into infants through her tapas (not in the epics) Damayantī Abandoned in the forest by Nala Survived through inner strength; her virtue attracted divine protection Arundhatī Lifelong devotion through cosmic ages Became the guiding star; shown to brides as an ideal Sītā The ordeal by fire Fire refuses to harm her; the earth finally receives her

docs.title: 10.11 Feminist and Other Critical Readings
docs.text:
Since the late nineteenth century, the women of the epics have been central to Indian debates about the status of women. Reformers and nationalists held up Sītā and Sāvitrī as models of the chaste, self-sacrificing Indian wife; critics have argued that these ideals served to discipline women.

  • Textual scholarship: Sally J. Sutherland (Goldman) contrasted Sītā, who turns her anger inwards and endures, with Draupadī, who expresses it openly and demands vengeance, and argued that Indian culture made the former its preferred model for women (Sutherland 1989).

  • Popular responses: Linda Hess’s study of audiences of the Rāmlīlā and of the Rāmacaritamānas documents the range of Indian responses to Rāma’s treatment of Sītā, from elaborate justification to open rejection (Hess 1999). Madhu Kishwar’s essay “Yes to Sita, No to Ram” found that many women revere Sītā while condemning Rāma’s conduct towards her (Richman 2001).

  • Women’s retellings: Telugu, Bengali and Maithili women’s songs, the sixteenth-century Bengali Rāmāyaṇa of Candrāvatī, and modern works such as Pratibha Ray’s Odia novel Yājñasenī (1984), told from Draupadī’s point of view, and Volga’s Telugu stories Vimukta (The Liberation of Sita), retell the epics from the women’s side (Narayana Rao 1991).

  • Dalit and Adivasi readings: Mahasweta Devi’s Bengali story “Draupadi” (1978), in which a Santal woman named Dopdi, tortured and raped in police custody, refuses to cover herself before the officer — a deliberate inversion of the epic disrobing — connected the epic to the violence suffered by tribal and Dalit women. The mutilation of Śūrpaṇakhā, a forest woman, has likewise been read as an emblem of caste and gender violence.

These readings do not displace the devotional understanding of Sītā, Draupadī and Sāvitrī, which remains central for millions of women; they show how the epics continue to be the ground on which questions of gender are argued (Chakravarti 2003). See Figure 10.1.

Figure 10.1. Rāma enthroned with Sītā, attended by Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, Śatrughna and Hanumān: chromolithograph bearing Raja Ravi Varma’s signature (late nineteenth or early twentieth century) Raja Ravi Varma, Ram Panchayatan (lithograph, before 1906), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: Chapter 11: Philosophical Content Embedded in the Epics
docs.text:
nāsti buddhir ayuktasya na cāyuktasya bhāvanā / na cābhāvayataḥ śāntir aśāntasya kutaḥ sukham // “The undisciplined has no wisdom, nor has he contemplation; without contemplation there is no peace, and for one without peace, how can there be happiness?”

— Bhagavad Gītā 2.66

The epics teach philosophy in dialogue and in situations of crisis: Bhīṣma teaches from his deathbed, Kṛṣṇa on the battlefield, Sanatsujāta in the sleepless night before a war. Because the Mahābhārata took shape before the classical philosophical systems (darśanas) were codified in their sūtras and commentaries, these passages are a principal source for the early history of Sāṅkhya, Yoga and Vedāntic thought, and of devotional theism (Brockington 1998; Sutton 2000). The Bhagavad Gītā has its own chapter (Chapter 6); the political teaching of the Śānti Parva is summarised in Section 4.17, and Vidura’s practical wisdom in Section 9.4. This chapter is concerned with the Mokṣadharma, the third and longest section of the Śānti Parva (Section 5.12), with the shorter philosophical texts of the epic, and with the philosophy of the Purāṇas.

docs.title: 11.1 The Mokṣadharma
docs.text: The Mokṣadharma (“the dharma of liberation”) is a vast collection of dialogues on the nature of the self and the means of release from rebirth. Bhīṣma rarely speaks in his own voice; he answers Yudhiṣṭhira’s questions with old stories (itihāsa purātana), in which named teachers instruct a pupil or a king. The sage Bhṛgu teaches Bharadvāja on creation, the elements and the soul; Vasiṣṭha, Yājñavalkya and Pañcaśikha each instruct a King Janaka of Videha; Vyāsa teaches his son Śuka; and a woman ascetic, Sulabhā, refutes Janaka’s claim to be liberated (Section 10.10.1). The collection is not a system. Its dialogues offer different and sometimes incompatible accounts of the world, the self and God, and it ends with the Nārāyaṇīya (Section 11.5), which subordinates them all to devotion.

docs.title: 11.1.1 Consolation and the Problem of Suffering
docs.text:
The occasion of the Mokṣadharma is grief, and much of it is consolation. In the Strī Parva Vidura has already consoled the blind king with the parable of the man in the well: fleeing a wild elephant through a forest full of beasts, a man falls into a well and hangs from a creeper, with a great snake below and the elephant above, while black and white mice gnaw at the creeper; bees above him drip honey, and he goes on tasting it. The forest is the world, Vidura explains, the elephant old age, the snake death, the mice the nights and days, and the honey the pleasures that keep people from thinking of their end. In the Śānti Parva Bhīṣma recounts how a brahmin consoled King Senajit, mourning his son, with verses on the impermanence of every union, among them the song of the courtesan Piṅgalā, who waits all night for lovers who do not come and finds peace at dawn when she gives up hope. Other “songs” in the same part of the book make the same point, such as that of Maṅki, who learns from the loss of the two young bulls he had bought that desire is the root of suffering.

The dialogues also debate what causes suffering and success. Some teachers ascribe them to past action (karman), others to fate (daiva), to a being’s own nature (svabhāva) or to time (kāla). In one dialogue the demon king Bali, stripped of his sovereignty, tells the gloating Indra that it is time, not Indra’s prowess, that has brought him low, and that time will humble Indra in his turn. Time is also measured on a cosmic scale: the four ages (yugas) succeed each other in decline, dharma losing one “foot” in each, and the cycle repeats (Table 7.6). Comparable schemes of declining ages are found elsewhere, as in Hesiod’s ages of gold, silver, bronze and iron. Against all these powers the Mokṣadharma sets the possibility of release: the self that knows itself to be distinct from body, mind and the world is not touched by them.

docs.title: 11.2 Sāṅkhya and Yoga in the Mokṣadharma
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata contains the most extensive pre-classical exposition of Sāṅkhya and Yoga. The classical systems are known from Īśvarakṛṣṇa’s Sāṅkhyakārikā (c. 4th–5th century CE) and Patañjali’s Yogasūtra (c. 325–425 CE); the epic dialogues are older in large part, and they show both traditions before they were fixed.

What the two words mean.

Franklin Edgerton argued in a classic article that in the epic “Sāṅkhya” and “Yoga” are not yet the names of two philosophical systems but of two methods of reaching liberation: Sāṅkhya is the way of knowledge, reached by reasoning, reckoning (saṅkhyā) and discrimination; Yoga is the way of disciplined practice and meditation (Edgerton 1924). The metaphysics behind both, he held, is largely that of the Upaniṣads, and it is usually theistic or monist rather than the dualism without God of classical Sāṅkhya. The epic’s teachers insist that the two methods lead to the same goal, as the Gītā does when it says that only the unlearned speak of Sāṅkhya and Yoga as different, and that whoever sees them as one sees truly (5.4–5).

The enumerations.

The dialogues count the constituents of the world and the person in different ways — seventeen, twenty-four or twenty-five principles (tattvas). The fullest lists, in the teachings given to Janaka, come close to the classical scheme. From unmanifest nature (avyakta, prakṛti), composed of the three guṇas, evolve the intellect (mahat or buddhi), the sense of self (ahaṃkāra), the mind (manas), the senses and organs of action, and the subtle and gross elements; the conscious self (puruṣa) is the twenty-fifth. Liberation comes from discriminating the self from all that it is not, and the teachers describe in detail how the evolutes dissolve back into their source at the end of a cosmic cycle. The dialogue of Vasiṣṭha with King Karāla Janaka adds a decisive further step: it distinguishes the twenty-fifth principle, the individual self that “is awakening” (budhyamāna), from a twenty-sixth, the “awakened” (buddha), the supreme self or God, with whom the liberated soul is united. This is a theistic Sāṅkhya, close in spirit to the Gītā’s supreme person beyond the perishable and the imperishable (Gītā 15.16–18) and to the theology of the Nārāyaṇīya. The teacher Pañcaśikha, whom the later Sāṅkhya tradition counts, after Kapila and Āsuri, among the founders of the school (Sāṅkhyakārikā 70), appears here instructing Janaka in the discrimination of the self from the elements and faculties.

Yoga.

The Mokṣadharma’s yoga passages describe a recognisable discipline: a solitary place, a light diet, the restraint of the senses, the control of breath (prāṇāyāma), and the fixing of the mind (dhāraṇā) until the yogin sees the self within himself. They also describe the powers that the yogin acquires and the dangers of becoming attached to them. Two narratives show yoga in action. Sulabhā, the woman ascetic, enters King Janaka’s mind by yogic power in order to show him that he is not yet free (Section 10.10.1); and Vyāsa’s son Śuka, having learned Sāṅkhya and Yoga, rises by yoga into the sky and passes beyond the world, leaving his father calling after him. Bhīṣma’s own teaching on the self, given through dialogues of earlier sages and in his own voice, echoes the Kaṭha and other Upaniṣads: the self is unborn and undying, subtler than the subtle, hidden in the cave of the heart, and known by those who are free from desire.

The scholarly debate.

E. Washburn Hopkins, who catalogued the epic’s philosophical vocabulary at the beginning of the twentieth century, stressed its variety and its lack of system (Hopkins 1901). Erich Frauwallner tried to reconstruct from the Mokṣadharma a sequence of stages through which Sāṅkhya developed before Īśvarakṛṣṇa (Frauwallner 1973); Gerald Larson traced a movement from the speculative thought of the Upaniṣads and the epic, which he called “proto-Sāṅkhya,” to the classical system (Larson 1969). Scholars still disagree whether a single original Sāṅkhya ever existed, or whether the epic preserves several related traditions that the classical system later unified; and the dating of individual dialogues is uncertain (Brockington 1998). What is not disputed is that the Mokṣadharma is the main evidence for the period in which the vocabulary of Sāṅkhya and Yoga — prakṛti and puruṣa, the guṇas, the evolutes, discrimination and the disciplined mind — became the common language of Indian thought about liberation, shared by theists and non-theists alike.

docs.title: 11.3 The Sanatsujātīya
docs.text:
The Sanatsujātīya (Udyoga Parva, chapters 41–45 in the CE) is a philosophical dialogue between the ancient sage Sanatsujāta and the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which follows Vidura’s counsel on the sleepless night before Sañjaya reports the Pāṇḍavas’ response. When Dhṛtarāṣṭra asks about death, Vidura declares himself unqualified to teach on it, since he is a Śūdra by birth, and summons Sanatsujāta — an instance of the epic’s acknowledgement of caste limits on teaching.

Sanatsujāta teaches that death, in the sense that matters, is not the end of the body but heedlessness (pramāda) about one’s true nature; that the self is unborn and imperishable; that liberation comes through knowledge of Brahman, not through ritual alone; and he discusses the meaning of mauna, the silence of the sage, and the virtues and faults of the ascetic.

Sanatsujātīya on Death — Udyoga Parva 5.42.4 (Critical Edition)

pramādaṃ vai mṛtyum ahaṃ bravīmi sadāpramādam amṛtatvaṃ bravīmi Translation: “Heedlessness, I say, is death; constant heedfulness, I say, is immortality.”

A commentary on the Sanatsujātīya is attributed to Śaṅkara, which made the text an important source for later Advaitins; the attribution, like that of several works ascribed to him, is debated.

docs.title: 11.4 The Anu Gītā — Kṛṣṇa’s Second Discourse
docs.text: After the war and the horse sacrifice, Arjuna, who confesses that he has forgotten what Kṛṣṇa taught him on the battlefield, asks him to repeat it. Kṛṣṇa replies that he cannot repeat it exactly, and instead gives the Anugītā (Āśvamedhika Parva), a long discourse that revisits many Gītā themes with a different emphasis: more on yoga, the subtle body and the path of knowledge, with the teaching of a perfected sage (siddha) to the brahmin Kāśyapa on rebirth and liberation, and the Brāhmaṇagītā, a dialogue between a brahmin and his wife on the inner sacrifice.

docs.title: 11.5 The Nārāyaṇīya — Early Vaiṣṇava Theology in the Epic
docs.text: Near the end of the Mokṣadharma stands a group of chapters (12.321–339 in the Critical Edition) that the tradition calls the Nārāyaṇīya. It is the fullest statement in the epic of a theology centred on Nārāyaṇa, and it is the earliest substantial witness to the ideas of the Pāñcarātra tradition, whose later scriptures are treated in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama. Most scholars regard it as one of the later layers of the Śānti Parva; a collaborative study edited by Peter Schreiner has examined its structure, its sources and its place in the history of Vaiṣṇavism in detail (Schreiner 1997).

docs.title: 11.5.1 The Narrative Frame
docs.text:
The section is built, like the epic itself, of stories within stories. Yudhiṣṭhira asks Bhīṣma which god the four stages of life should worship. Bhīṣma answers with a tale. The sage Nārada visits the twin sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa in their hermitage at Badarī in the Himalaya and finds Nārāyaṇa engaged in worship; asked whom the supreme god himself worships, Nārāyaṇa replies that he honours his own highest self. Nārada then travels to Śvetadvīpa, the “White Island” that lies north of the ocean of milk (12.322.8), whose radiant inhabitants are devoted to the one god with undivided minds. There Nārāyaṇa appears to him in a cosmic form and teaches him the doctrine that Nārada carries back to the world.

Within this frame is set the story of King Uparicara Vasu, a devotee who performs a great horse sacrifice in which no animal is killed. In a related episode, when the gods and the sages dispute whether the word aja in the injunction to sacrifice means “goat” or “seed grain that will not sprout again”, Vasu decides in favour of the goat and as a result falls from the sky into a chasm in the earth, until his devotion to Nārāyaṇa restores him. The episode is one of several places in the epic where non-violence is set against the Vedic sacrifice of animals.

docs.title: 11.5.2 The Teaching
docs.text:
The doctrine revealed at Śvetadvīpa combines devotion with the cosmology of Sāṅkhya. The supreme god Vāsudeva is the highest self of all beings. From him proceed, in succession, three further forms, each named after a member of the Vṛṣṇi clan and each identified with a Sāṅkhya principle: Saṃkarṣaṇa with the individual soul (jīva), Pradyumna with mind (manas), and Aniruddha with the sense of self (ahaṃkāra).
